# DataFusion Advanced — 19) Logical plans

Style target follows the uploaded advanced-reference pattern. 

## 19.0 Mental model: `LogicalPlan` = semantic relational program

```text
SQL / DataFrame / custom query language
  → Expr + LogicalPlan
      ├─ TableScan / EmptyRelation / Values
      ├─ Projection
      ├─ Filter
      ├─ Aggregate / Window
      ├─ Join / CrossJoin / Union / Distinct
      ├─ Sort / Limit / Repartition
      ├─ Ddl / Dml / Copy / Explain / Analyze / DescribeTable
      ├─ Unnest / RecursiveQuery / SubqueryAlias
      └─ Extension(custom node)
  → analyzer + logical optimizer
  → physical planner
  → ExecutionPlan
```

A `LogicalPlan` is a tree of relational operators such as `Projection` and `Filter`; each node transforms an input relation into an output relation with a potentially different schema, and data conceptually flows from leaves up to the root. Logical plans can be created by the SQL planner, the DataFrame API, or programmatically, such as from a custom query language. ([Docs.rs][1])

---

## 19.1 Value case

| Need                     | Logical-plan value                                                                         |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| SQL compiler target      | `SqlToRel` lowers SQL AST into `LogicalPlan`                                               |
| DataFrame implementation | DataFrame methods delegate to `LogicalPlanBuilder`                                         |
| custom query language    | emit `LogicalPlan` directly, bypass SQL                                                    |
| optimizer input          | logical optimizer rewrites tree while preserving results                                   |
| authorization/policy     | inspect table refs, columns, filters, functions before execution                           |
| custom operators         | use `LogicalPlan::Extension`                                                               |
| testing                  | snapshot/compare semantic plan before physical algorithms                                  |
| portability              | logical plans do not encode hash join vs sort-merge join, file openers, runtime partitions |

The library guide says DataFrame is a higher-level API that delegates to `LogicalPlanBuilder`; it also states that logical plans must be compiled into physical `ExecutionPlan`s before execution because physical plans contain algorithmic and execution-specific details. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 19.2 Creation paths

| Path        | API                                                                | When to use                                       |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
| SQL         | `ctx.sql("SELECT ...").await?` → `DataFrame` → `df.logical_plan()` | user-authored query text                          |
| DataFrame   | `ctx.table(...).await?.filter(...).select(...)`                    | typed Rust plan construction                      |
| Builder     | `LogicalPlanBuilder::scan(...).filter(...).project(...).build()?`  | custom compilers, optimizer tests, extension code |
| Direct enum | `LogicalPlan::Filter(Filter::try_new(...))`                        | rare low-level tests / exact node construction    |
| Extension   | `LogicalPlan::Extension(Extension { node })`                       | custom logical operators                          |

DataFusion docs explicitly say it is possible to create logical plans by directly constructing the `LogicalPlan` enum, but it is usually easier to use `LogicalPlanBuilder`; the builder supports roots such as `empty`, `values`, `scan`, and `scan_with_filters`, then transformation methods such as `filter`, `limit`, `sort`, `distinct`, and `join`. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

## 19.3 Core imports

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::arrow::datatypes::{DataType, Field, Schema, SchemaRef};
use datafusion::common::{DFSchema, DFSchemaRef, Result};
use datafusion::logical_expr::{
    col, lit, Expr, JoinType, LogicalPlan, LogicalPlanBuilder, LogicalTableSource,
};
use datafusion::prelude::*;
```

Prefer `datafusion::logical_expr::*` re-exports for app code. Use direct subcrates such as `datafusion-expr` only when building lower-level extension crates and pin all DataFusion subcrates to the same version.

---

## 19.4 `LogicalPlan` variants: map of major nodes

Current `LogicalPlan` variants listed in docs include: `Aggregate`, `Analyze`, `Copy`, `Ddl`, `DescribeTable`, `Distinct`, `Dml`, `EmptyRelation`, `Explain`, `Extension`, `Filter`, `Join`, `Limit`, `Projection`, `RecursiveQuery`, `Repartition`, `Sort`, `Statement`, `Subquery`, `SubqueryAlias`, `TableScan`, `Union`, `Unnest`, `Values`, and `Window`. ([Docs.rs][1])

| Variant                | Semantic role            | SQL/DataFrame source                                 |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `TableScan`            | read table/source        | `FROM t`, `ctx.table`, `LogicalPlanBuilder::scan`    |
| `Projection`           | compute/select columns   | `SELECT expr`, `df.select`, `builder.project`        |
| `Filter`               | row predicate            | `WHERE`, `df.filter`, `builder.filter`               |
| `Aggregate`            | group + aggregate        | `GROUP BY`, `df.aggregate`, `builder.aggregate`      |
| `Window`               | window expressions       | `OVER (...)`, `builder.window`                       |
| `Join`                 | relational join          | `JOIN`, `df.join`, `builder.join`                    |
| `Sort`                 | ordering                 | `ORDER BY`, `df.sort`, `builder.sort`                |
| `Limit`                | skip/fetch               | `LIMIT/OFFSET`, `df.limit`, `builder.limit`          |
| `Union`                | set append               | `UNION`, `df.union`, `builder.union`                 |
| `Distinct`             | deduplication            | `SELECT DISTINCT`, `df.distinct`, `builder.distinct` |
| `Values`               | inline rows              | `VALUES (...)`, `builder.values`                     |
| `EmptyRelation`        | empty/one-row relation   | constants/planner internals, `builder.empty`         |
| `Extension`            | custom operator          | user-defined logical node                            |
| `Ddl` / `Dml` / `Copy` | catalog/write statements | `CREATE`, `INSERT`, `COPY`                           |
| `Explain` / `Analyze`  | explain/analyze plan     | `EXPLAIN`, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`                         |
| `Unnest`               | nested expansion         | `UNNEST`, `builder.unnest_*`                         |

Agent rule:

```text
LogicalPlan expresses "what"; ExecutionPlan expresses "how".
Never infer physical algorithm, parallelism, or file I/O behavior from LogicalPlan alone.
```

---

## 19.5 Logical plan root construction

### `empty`

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::empty(false).build()?;
```

`LogicalPlanBuilder::empty(produce_one_row)` creates an empty relation; `produce_one_row=true` means the node produces a placeholder row. ([Docs.rs][4])

Use cases:

```text
SELECT literal-only plans
optimizer tests
synthetic plans
existence/no-op plans
```

### `values`

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::values(vec![
    vec![lit(1i64), lit("alice")],
    vec![lit(2i64), lit("bob")],
])?
.build()?;
```

`values` creates a `VALUES`-style relation and infers schema from the data; the docs note default column names such as `column1`, `column2`, so it is usually better to override names with an alias list or supplied schema. ([Docs.rs][4])

### `values_with_schema`

```rust
let schema = Arc::new(DFSchema::try_from(Schema::new(vec![
    Field::new("id", DataType::Int64, false),
    Field::new("name", DataType::Utf8, true),
]))?);

let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::values_with_schema(
    vec![
        vec![lit(1i64), lit("alice")],
        vec![lit(2i64), lit("bob")],
    ],
    &schema,
)?
.build()?;
```

Use `values_with_schema` when output names/types are part of the contract.

### `scan`

```rust
let schema = Schema::new(vec![
    Field::new("id", DataType::Int32, true),
    Field::new("name", DataType::Utf8, true),
]);

let table_source = LogicalTableSource::new(SchemaRef::new(schema));

let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan(
    "person",
    Arc::new(table_source),
    None, // optional projection indices
)?
.filter(col("id").gt(lit(500)))?
.build()?;
```

The logical-plan guide shows this exact pattern: build a `LogicalTableSource`, call `LogicalPlanBuilder::scan`, apply `filter`, then `build`; at this stage no query execution happens. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

### Table-name normalization caveat

```rust
// Treated as SQL identifier and normalized.
LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("MyTable", table_source.clone(), None)?;

// Preserves mixed case by quoted identifier parsing.
LogicalPlanBuilder::scan(r#""MyTable""#, table_source.clone(), None)?;
```

`LogicalPlanBuilder::scan` treats string table names as SQL identifiers, so unquoted strings are normalized; use quoted identifiers or `TableReference` if case/name preservation matters. ([Docs.rs][4])

---

## 19.6 Relation operators: scan → filter → projection

### Builder chain

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("person", Arc::new(table_source), None)?
    .filter(col("id").gt(lit(500)))?
    .project(vec![
        col("id"),
        col("name"),
        (col("id") + lit(1)).alias("next_id"),
    ])?
    .build()?;
```

### Equivalent shape

```text
Projection: person.id, person.name, person.id + Int32(1) AS next_id
  Filter: person.id > Int32(500)
    TableScan: person
```

`filter` applies a predicate to the plan; `project` applies a projection expression list. The builder API has `project`, `select` by column indices, and `filter` as transformation methods. ([Docs.rs][4])

Agent rules:

```text
filter = WHERE-stage row predicate.
project = SELECT-stage output expression list.
Always alias computed expressions.
Use select(indices) only when you intentionally project by ordinal.
```

---

## 19.7 Aggregate plans

```rust
use datafusion::functions_aggregate::expr_fn::{sum, count};

let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("sales", Arc::new(table_source), None)?
    .filter(col("amount").gt(lit(0.0)))?
    .aggregate(
        vec![col("region")],
        vec![
            count(lit(1)).alias("row_count"),
            sum(col("amount")).alias("total_amount"),
        ],
    )?
    .build()?;
```

`LogicalPlanBuilder::aggregate(group_expr, aggr_expr)` groups by the supplied expressions and calculates aggregate expressions for each distinct group-expression value. ([Docs.rs][4])

Agent rules:

```text
group_expr = GROUP BY keys.
aggr_expr = aggregate output expressions.
Alias aggregate outputs.
Use Filter before Aggregate for WHERE semantics.
Use another Filter after Aggregate for HAVING-like semantics.
```

Post-aggregate filter:

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::from(plan)
    .filter(col("total_amount").gt(lit(1000.0)))?
    .build()?;
```

---

## 19.8 Sort and limit

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("events", Arc::new(table_source), None)?
    .sort(vec![
        col("event_ts").sort(false, false), // DESC NULLS LAST
        col("event_id").sort(true, true),   // ASC NULLS FIRST
    ])?
    .limit(0, Some(100))?
    .build()?;
```

`sort_by` sorts by expressions using default direction, `sort` accepts `Sort` expressions, `sort_with_limit` combines sort and optional fetch, and `limit(skip, fetch)` skips rows then fetches a maximum row count. ([Docs.rs][4])

Agent rules:

```text
Use sort before limit for deterministic top-N.
Use sort_with_limit for top-K-like plans where appropriate.
limit(skip, fetch): skip = offset, fetch = max rows after offset.
Do not assume output order without Sort.
```

---

## 19.9 Joins

### Explicit equijoin

```rust
let left = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("orders", Arc::new(orders_source), None)?
    .build()?;

let right = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("customers", Arc::new(customers_source), None)?
    .build()?;

let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::from(left)
    .join(
        right,
        JoinType::Inner,
        (
            vec![datafusion::common::Column::from_qualified_name("orders.customer_id")],
            vec![datafusion::common::Column::from_qualified_name("customers.id")],
        ),
        None,
    )?
    .build()?;
```

`join(right, join_type, join_keys, filter)` applies a join with explicitly specified equijoin columns and an optional filter expression; the docs note the optional filter is applied only to matched rows for outer joins. ([Docs.rs][4])

### Expression join

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::from(left)
    .join_on(
        right,
        JoinType::Inner,
        vec![
            col("orders.customer_id").eq(col("customers.id")),
            col("orders.region").eq(col("customers.region")),
        ],
    )?
    .build()?;
```

`join_on` accepts join expressions directly, and DataFusion automatically identifies and optimizes equality predicates, so there is no performance difference versus explicit `join` for equality predicates. ([Docs.rs][4])

### Detailed joins

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::from(left)
    .join_detailed(
        right,
        JoinType::Inner,
        (left_keys, right_keys),
        None,
        null_equality,
    )?
    .build()?;
```

`join_detailed` adds explicit null-equality behavior; `join_with_expr_keys` is a lower-level API where equijoin predicates and residual filters are supplied separately, and the docs recommend `join_on` for most users because it identifies predicates automatically. ([Docs.rs][4])

Agent rules:

```text
Prefer join_on for generated expression joins.
Prefer join for simple named equijoins.
Use join_detailed only when null equality semantics matter.
Alias/qualify duplicate columns before/after join.
Test outer-join filter semantics carefully.
```

---

## 19.10 Union, distinct, and set-like logical operators

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::from(left_plan)
    .union(right_plan)?
    .build()?;
```

`union` preserves duplicate rows; `union_by_name` preserves duplicate rows but aligns by column name; `union_distinct` removes duplicates; `union_by_name_distinct` aligns by name and removes duplicates. ([Docs.rs][4])

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::from(left_plan)
    .distinct()?
    .build()?;
```

`distinct` applies deduplication. `distinct_on(on_expr, select_expr, sort_expr)` selects first values by distinct-on expressions according to optional sort expressions. ([Docs.rs][4])

Static set functions:

```rust
let intersect = LogicalPlanBuilder::intersect(left_plan, right_plan, false)?;
let except = LogicalPlanBuilder::except(left_plan, right_plan, false)?;
```

`intersect` and `except` build set-operation logical plans, with an `is_all` flag. ([Docs.rs][4])

Agent rules:

```text
Use union for UNION ALL semantics with identical schemas.
Use union_by_name for schema-evolution/column-order mismatch.
Use distinct variants only when deduplication is required.
Normalize schemas explicitly before set operations.
```

---

## 19.11 Window and unnest

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("events", Arc::new(source), None)?
    .window(vec![
        // window expression built elsewhere
    ])?
    .build()?;
```

`window` applies window functions and extends the schema. ([Docs.rs][4])

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("users", Arc::new(source), None)?
    .unnest_column(datafusion::common::Column::from_name("tags"))?
    .build()?;
```

`unnest_column`, `unnest_column_with_options`, and `unnest_columns_with_options` add `Unnest` logical operations for nested columns. ([Docs.rs][4])

Agent rules:

```text
Window extends row-level output with analytic expressions.
Unnest can change row cardinality or expand struct columns.
Add LIMIT / filters before unnest where possible.
```

---

## 19.12 Display methods and plan diagnostics

### Human readable node only

```rust
println!("{}", plan.display());
```

`display()` returns a human-readable description of the current logical-plan node, not including children. ([Docs.rs][1])

### Indented tree

```rust
println!("{}", plan.display_indent());
```

`display_indent()` produces one line per node in an indented logical-plan tree. ([Docs.rs][1])

### Indented tree with schema

```rust
println!("{}", plan.display_indent_schema());
```

`display_indent_schema()` produces one line per node and includes each node’s output schema. ([Docs.rs][1])

### PostgreSQL JSON format

```rust
let pg_json = format!("{}", plan.display_pg_json());
```

`display_pg_json()` returns a PostgreSQL-style JSON plan representation that can be used with existing visualization tools. ([Docs.rs][1])

### Graphviz DOT

```rust
let dot = format!("{}", plan.display_graphviz());
std::fs::write("/tmp/plan.dot", dot)?;
```

`display_graphviz()` returns DOT-language output for graphical visualization; docs note it currently produces both a basic-structure graph and a graph with additional details such as schema. ([Docs.rs][1])

Agent rules:

```text
display_indent() = concise semantic snapshot.
display_indent_schema() = debugging schema evolution.
display_graphviz() = complex tree visualization.
display_pg_json() = plan visualization tooling.
Do not snapshot exact display strings across DataFusion upgrades unless pinned.
```

---

## 19.13 LogicalPlanBuilder vs SQL vs DataFrame

| Path                      | Strength                              | Weakness                                         |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| SQL                       | user-facing, compact, full SQL syntax | string validation, injection, dialect governance |
| DataFrame                 | typed Rust flow, simple to compose    | hides some logical-plan construction details     |
| `LogicalPlanBuilder`      | explicit semantic plan construction   | lower-level, less ergonomic than DataFrame       |
| direct `LogicalPlan` enum | exact node control                    | most fragile/verbose                             |
| custom `Extension` node   | new operators                         | requires physical planning + optimizer support   |

DataFusion’s top-level docs say projects can build their own query languages or plans with `LogicalPlanBuilder`, rather than using the built-in SQL planner `SqlToRel`. They list `LogicalPlanBuilder` alongside other extension points such as custom table providers, catalogs, UDFs, optimizer rules, and custom planner nodes. ([Docs.rs][5])

Agent decision rules:

```text
Human-authored query language -> SQL.
Rust-generated business logic -> DataFrame / Expr.
Custom compiler target -> LogicalPlanBuilder.
Custom relational operator -> LogicalPlan::Extension.
Optimizer rule tests -> LogicalPlanBuilder or direct enum.
```

---

## 19.14 Building logical plans directly

### Direct enum construction

```rust
use datafusion::logical_expr::{Filter, LogicalPlan, TableScan};

let projection = None;
let filters = vec![];
let fetch = None;

let table_scan = LogicalPlan::TableScan(TableScan::try_new(
    "person",
    Arc::new(table_source),
    projection,
    filters,
    fetch,
)?);

let filter_expr = col("id").gt(lit(500));

let plan = LogicalPlan::Filter(Filter::try_new(
    filter_expr,
    Arc::new(table_scan),
)?);

println!("{}", plan.display_indent_schema());
```

The logical-plan guide shows manual construction of `TableScan` and `Filter` variants, then `display_indent_schema()` output. It also says this is possible but `LogicalPlanBuilder` is easier in most cases. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

### Builder equivalent

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("person", Arc::new(table_source), None)?
    .filter(col("id").gt(lit(500)))?
    .build()?;
```

Use direct enum construction only when:

```text
testing a specific node constructor
constructing a variant not exposed ergonomically by builder
working inside optimizer/planner internals
debugging schema behavior at exact node boundary
```

---

## 19.15 Table sources: `LogicalTableSource` vs `TableProvider`

`LogicalTableSource` is useful for tests, docs, and building logical plans when you do not intend to use DataFusion’s physical planner. In normal applications, use a `TableProvider`; to turn a `TableProvider` into a `TableSource`, use `provider_as_source` or `DefaultTableSource`. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

### Test-only / logical-only

```rust
let schema = Schema::new(vec![
    Field::new("id", DataType::Int32, true),
]);

let source = LogicalTableSource::new(SchemaRef::new(schema));

let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("t", Arc::new(source), None)?
    .filter(col("id").gt(lit(10)))?
    .build()?;
```

### Application provider source

```rust
use datafusion::catalog::TableProvider;
use datafusion::datasource::provider_as_source;

let provider: Arc<dyn TableProvider> = Arc::new(my_provider);
let table_source = provider_as_source(provider);

let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("t", table_source, None)?
    .build()?;
```

Agent rules:

```text
LogicalTableSource = schema-only test/logical planning source.
TableProvider = real DataFusion scan/execution source.
If plan must execute through DataFusion physical planner, prefer TableProvider-backed source.
```

---

## 19.16 Preserving schemas

### Inspect builder schema during construction

```rust
let builder = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("events", table_source, None)?
    .filter(col("amount").gt(lit(0.0)))?;

println!("{:?}", builder.schema());
```

`LogicalPlanBuilder::schema()` returns the output schema of the plan built so far, while `plan()` returns the current `LogicalPlan` held by the builder. ([Docs.rs][4])

### Inspect final plan schema

```rust
let schema = plan.schema();
for field in schema.fields() {
    println!("{}: {:?}", field.name(), field.data_type());
}
```

`LogicalPlan` exposes `schema()` and schema-recomputing/normalization methods; schema is central to expression resolution and optimizer correctness. ([Docs.rs][1])

### Output schema contract

```text
Projection:
  output fields derived from select expressions and aliases

Filter:
  output schema unchanged from input

Aggregate:
  output fields = grouping expressions + aggregate expressions

Join:
  output fields = left + right fields according to join type/constraint

Sort:
  output schema unchanged from input

Limit:
  output schema unchanged from input

Union:
  output schema based on compatible inputs

Extension:
  schema is supplied by custom node
```

Agent rules:

```text
Preserve field names and types across rewrites.
Use alias() on computed expressions before projection/aggregate.
Never assume expression display name is stable enough for public schema.
Check plan.check_invariants() in tests when manipulating plans directly.
```

`LogicalPlan` exposes `check_invariants`, `with_new_exprs`, `recompute_schema`, and tree-node traversal/rewrite APIs, reflecting that schema/expression consistency is a first-class invariant. ([Docs.rs][1])

---

## 19.17 Preserving expression names

### Good

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("sales", source, None)?
    .project(vec![
        col("region"),
        (col("amount") * lit(1.08)).alias("amount_with_tax"),
    ])?
    .build()?;
```

### Bad

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("sales", source, None)?
    .project(vec![
        col("region"),
        col("amount") * lit(1.08), // output name likely expression-derived
    ])?
    .build()?;
```

Expression names affect parent references, output fields, error messages, and snapshot stability. Optimizer docs also emphasize that expression names must be preserved during rewrites; changing names while preserving semantic values can still break downstream plan references and output schema expectations. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

Agent rules:

```text
Alias every computed projection.
Alias every aggregate.
Alias every window expression.
When rewriting Exprs, preserve aliases unless intentionally changing output schema.
Use unalias only for semantic comparison, not output-building.
```

---

## 19.18 Plan traversal and rewrite

### Collect expressions

```rust
use std::collections::HashSet;
use datafusion::common::tree_node::TreeNodeRecursion;

let mut expressions = HashSet::new();

plan.apply(|node| {
    node.apply_expressions(|expr| {
        expressions.insert(expr.clone());
        Ok(TreeNodeRecursion::Continue)
    })?;
    Ok(TreeNodeRecursion::Continue)
})?;
```

The `LogicalPlan` docs show using the tree-node API to recursively walk the plan and collect expressions via `apply` and `apply_expressions`. ([Docs.rs][7])

### Top-down / bottom-up rewrite

```rust
use datafusion::common::tree_node::{Transformed, TreeNode};

let transformed = plan.transform_up(|node| {
    // inspect/replace node
    Ok(Transformed::no(node))
})?;

let plan = transformed.data;
```

`LogicalPlan` implements tree rewrite methods such as `transform_down` and `transform_up`, which recursively rewrite nodes top-down or bottom-up and return `Transformed<LogicalPlan>`. ([Docs.rs][7])

Agent rules:

```text
Use transform_up for child-aware rewrites.
Use transform_down for context/ancestor-aware rewrites.
Use apply/apply_expressions for analysis-only passes.
Maintain schema and aliases.
Do not duplicate volatile expressions unsafely.
```

---

## 19.19 Parameters / placeholders

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("t1", table_source, None)?
    .filter(col("id").eq(placeholder("$1")))?
    .build()?;

let plan = plan.with_param_values(vec![
    ScalarValue::from(3i32),
])?;
```

`LogicalPlan::with_param_values` replaces placeholder parameters such as `$1` or named parameters with `ScalarValue`s; docs show building a filter with `$1` and then replacing it with `Int32(3)`. `get_parameter_names`, `get_parameter_types`, and `get_parameter_fields` inspect placeholders. ([Docs.rs][1])

Agent rules:

```text
Use placeholders for prepared/generic plans.
Use with_param_values for binding.
Use get_parameter_types/fields for validation before binding.
Do not string-concatenate literal user values into SQL or logical expressions.
```

---

## 19.20 Extension nodes

### Purpose

```text
LogicalPlan::Extension
  = custom logical operator
  = unsupported by built-in relational algebra
  = requires custom planning/optimization rules if it should execute
```

`LogicalPlan` contains an `Extension` variant that lets projects add custom logical operators. `UserDefinedLogicalNodeCore` is the recommended trait for implementing custom nodes; it requires methods such as `name`, `inputs`, `schema`, `expressions`, `fmt_for_explain`, and `with_exprs_and_inputs`. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

### Skeleton

```rust
use std::{fmt, sync::Arc};
use datafusion::common::{DFSchemaRef, Result};
use datafusion::logical_expr::{Expr, LogicalPlan, UserDefinedLogicalNodeCore};

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct MyNode {
    input: LogicalPlan,
    schema: DFSchemaRef,
    predicate: Expr,
}

impl UserDefinedLogicalNodeCore for MyNode {
    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "MyNode"
    }

    fn inputs(&self) -> Vec<&LogicalPlan> {
        vec![&self.input]
    }

    fn schema(&self) -> &DFSchemaRef {
        &self.schema
    }

    fn expressions(&self) -> Vec<Expr> {
        vec![self.predicate.clone()]
    }

    fn fmt_for_explain(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "MyNode: predicate={}", self.predicate)
    }

    fn with_exprs_and_inputs(
        &self,
        exprs: Vec<Expr>,
        inputs: Vec<LogicalPlan>,
    ) -> Result<Self> {
        Ok(Self {
            input: inputs.into_iter().next().expect("one input"),
            schema: self.schema.clone(),
            predicate: exprs.into_iter().next().expect("one expr"),
        })
    }
}
```

### Extension-node invariants

```text
inputs() returns child plans only.
expressions() returns node-local expressions only.
schema() is output schema, not input schema unless identical.
with_exprs_and_inputs must preserve semantic order.
fmt_for_explain must be stable enough for diagnostics.
Pushdown hooks must be conservative.
```

Custom extension nodes require a physical planner extension or custom query planner before they can execute; otherwise DataFusion can represent but not necessarily lower them to a runnable `ExecutionPlan`.

---

## 19.21 Logical plans to physical plans

```rust
let physical_plan = ctx
    .state()
    .create_physical_plan(&plan)
    .await?;
```

Logical plans cannot be directly executed; they must be compiled into a physical `ExecutionPlan`. The logical-plan guide says the easiest path is `SessionState::create_physical_plan`, and it emphasizes that physical plans include more detail such as specific algorithms and optimizations. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

Agent rules:

```text
LogicalPlan is not executable.
Use SessionState::create_physical_plan for explicit compile.
DataFrame collect/show/stream compile automatically.
Custom logical Extension needs custom physical planning.
```

---

## 19.22 End-to-end: direct logical plan → physical plan → stream

```rust
use futures::StreamExt;
use datafusion::prelude::*;
use datafusion::logical_expr::{LogicalPlanBuilder, LogicalTableSource};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let ctx = SessionContext::new();

    let schema = Schema::new(vec![
        Field::new("id", DataType::Int32, true),
        Field::new("name", DataType::Utf8, true),
    ]);

    let source = Arc::new(LogicalTableSource::new(SchemaRef::new(schema)));

    let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("person", source, None)?
        .filter(col("id").gt(lit(500)))?
        .project(vec![col("name")])?
        .limit(0, Some(100))?
        .build()?;

    println!("{}", plan.display_indent_schema());

    let physical = ctx.state().create_physical_plan(&plan).await?;
    let task_ctx = ctx.task_ctx();

    let mut stream = physical.execute(0, task_ctx)?;

    while let Some(batch) = stream.next().await {
        let batch = batch?;
        println!("rows={}", batch.num_rows());
    }

    Ok(())
}
```

For real execution, use a `TableProvider`-backed source rather than `LogicalTableSource` where possible; the guide notes `LogicalTableSource` is suitable for tests/docs and for building logical plans without DataFusion’s physical planner, while `TableProvider` is the common path for actual planning/execution. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 19.23 Logical-plan policy validation

### Example: deny scans outside allowlist

```rust
use datafusion::common::tree_node::{TreeNode, TreeNodeRecursion};

fn validate_tables(plan: &LogicalPlan, allowed: &std::collections::HashSet<String>)
    -> datafusion::error::Result<()>
{
    plan.apply(|node| {
        if let LogicalPlan::TableScan(scan) = node {
            let name = scan.table_name.to_string();
            if !allowed.contains(&name) {
                return Err(datafusion::error::DataFusionError::Plan(
                    format!("table not allowed: {name}")
                ));
            }
        }
        Ok(TreeNodeRecursion::Continue)
    })?;

    Ok(())
}
```

### Example: collect column refs from expressions

```rust
let mut refs = std::collections::HashSet::new();

plan.apply(|node| {
    node.apply_expressions(|expr| {
        for col in expr.column_refs() {
            refs.insert(col.clone());
        }
        Ok(TreeNodeRecursion::Continue)
    })?;
    Ok(TreeNodeRecursion::Continue)
})?;
```

Use logical-plan inspection for:

```text
table allowlists
column allowlists
function allowlists
unbounded query rejection
DML/DDL detection
direct path table detection
tenant schema enforcement
extension-node denial/approval
```

---

## 19.24 Building plans directly vs via SQL/DataFrame

### Prefer SQL when

```text
humans write the query
CTEs/window syntax dominate
SQL dialect is the product interface
query text must be stored/audited
tooling emits SQL
```

### Prefer DataFrame when

```text
application code generates filters/projections
you want Rust type checking and no SQL string concatenation
policy filters/masks are appended after user SQL
query shape is simple relational composition
```

### Prefer LogicalPlanBuilder when

```text
writing a compiler from another language
testing optimizer rules
creating reusable plan templates
needing direct plan inspection/modification
building logical plans independent of SessionContext
```

### Prefer direct `LogicalPlan` enum when

```text
testing exact node behavior
constructing special variants manually
working in optimizer internals
creating extension nodes
```

Agent rule:

```text
Use the highest-level API that preserves required control.
Do not drop to direct enum construction just because it looks precise.
```

---

## 19.25 Plan names, qualifiers, and output identity

### Alias tables / subqueries

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("orders", orders_source, None)?
    .alias("o")?
    .build()?;
```

`LogicalPlanBuilder::alias` applies a relation alias using a `TableReference`. ([Docs.rs][4])

### Alias expressions

```rust
let plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::scan("sales", source, None)?
    .project(vec![
        col("region"),
        sum(col("amount")).alias("total_amount"),
    ])?
    .build()?;
```

### Rules

```text
Relation aliases affect column qualification.
Expression aliases affect output field names.
Computed expressions without aliases generate expression-derived names.
Optimizers and parent nodes may rely on output expression names.
```

---

### Snapshot semantic shape

```rust
assert_eq!(
    plan.display_indent().to_string(),
    "Projection: person.name\n  Filter: person.id > Int32(500)\n    TableScan: person"
);
```

### Snapshot schema evolution

```rust
insta::assert_snapshot!(
    plan.display_indent_schema().to_string()
);
```

### Validate invariants

```rust
plan.check_invariants()?;
```

### Test optimized plan

```rust
let optimized = ctx.state().optimize(&plan)?;
println!("{}", optimized.display_indent_schema());
```

Agent test matrix:

```text
[ ] unoptimized plan shape
[ ] optimized plan shape
[ ] schema at each critical node
[ ] aliases preserved
[ ] qualified columns after joins
[ ] parameters bind correctly
[ ] custom extension node reconstructs with_exprs_and_inputs
[ ] physical plan can be created if execution is expected
[ ] result batches match expected output
```

Snapshot warning:

```text
Plan display strings are diagnostics, not stable cross-version API.
Pin DataFusion version for golden plan snapshots.
Prefer semantic checks for long-lived tests.
```

## 19.27 Deployment advisory

```text
Query services:
  parse/build plan
  validate logical plan for table/function/policy
  add service filters/limits/masks as DataFrame/LogicalPlan rewrites
  optimize
  physical plan / execute stream

Custom query languages:
  emit LogicalPlanBuilder chains
  preserve aliases and schema
  validate output schema before execution
  add tests against equivalent SQL if possible

Optimizer extensions:
  use tree_node transform APIs
  maintain schema/name invariants
  check volatile expressions before duplication/reordering
  test with EXPLAIN and results

Catalog/source extensions:
  TableProvider first
  LogicalPlan::Extension only for new relational semantics
```

---

## 19.28 Anti-pattern inventory

* Treating `LogicalPlan` as executable.
* Inferring physical join algorithm from `LogicalPlan::Join`.
* Dropping aliases during optimizer rewrites.
* Using expression-derived field names as public API.
* Constructing `LogicalPlan` enum nodes directly when `LogicalPlanBuilder` suffices.
* Using `LogicalTableSource` for real execution when a `TableProvider` is required.
* Reporting extension-node schema incorrectly.
* Returning child expressions from `UserDefinedLogicalNodeCore::expressions()` instead of node-local expressions.
* Implementing `with_exprs_and_inputs` with changed ordering.
* Claiming pushdown/limit behavior for extension nodes without semantic proof.
* Snapshotting exact plan strings across DataFusion upgrades without pinning.
* Using unqualified column names after joins.
* Mutating logical plans without `check_invariants`.
* Running `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on expensive queries just to inspect logical shape.
* Building direct plans with normalized table names accidentally due to unquoted identifier strings.

---

```text
[ ] Decide creation path: SQL / DataFrame / LogicalPlanBuilder / direct enum / Extension.
[ ] Treat LogicalPlan as semantic tree, not executable runtime.
[ ] Use LogicalPlanBuilder for programmatic construction.
[ ] Use scan with TableProvider-backed source for executable plans.
[ ] Use filter/project/aggregate/join/sort/limit builder methods for relation operators.
[ ] Alias computed, aggregate, window, and case expressions.

[ ] Use display_indent for concise plan snapshots.

[ ] Validate allowed tables/functions/columns at logical-plan level.
```

# DataFusion Advanced — 20) Physical plans and execution operators

Style target follows the uploaded advanced-reference pattern. 

## 20.0 Physical-plan mental model

```text id="dns2lm"
Optimized LogicalPlan
  → PhysicalPlanner
  → ExecutionPlan DAG/tree
      ├─ concrete operator choices
      │   ├─ DataSourceExec / FilterExec / ProjectionExec
      │   ├─ AggregateExec / SortExec / LimitExec
      │   ├─ HashJoinExec / SortMergeJoinExec / ...
      │   └─ custom ExecutionPlan
      ├─ PhysicalExpr nodes
      ├─ PlanProperties
      │   ├─ output partitioning
      │   ├─ output ordering
      │   ├─ boundedness
      │   └─ emission / pipeline behavior
      └─ execute(partition, TaskContext)
          → SendableRecordBatchStream
              → RecordBatch
              → RecordBatch
              → ...
```

`ExecutionPlan` represents nodes in DataFusion’s physical plan. Calling `execute(partition, context)` produces an async `SendableRecordBatchStream` of Arrow `RecordBatch`es that incrementally computes one partition of the operator’s output. `schema()` and `properties()` communicate output shape/order/partitioning to the optimizer, while input-requirement methods communicate distribution and ordering needs from child operators. ([Docs.rs][1])

---

## 20.1 Logical vs physical plan

| Layer     | Type                        | Contains                                                                                               | Does not contain                                               |
| --------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| logical   | `LogicalPlan`               | semantic relational operators: scan/filter/project/join/aggregate/sort/limit                           | concrete algorithms, partitions, sortedness, runtime resources |
| physical  | `ExecutionPlan`             | concrete algorithms, partitions, child plans, physical expressions, ordering/distribution requirements | SQL syntax, abstract relation names                            |
| execution | `SendableRecordBatchStream` | actual async production of `RecordBatch` values                                                        | planning / optimizer decisions                                 |

A physical plan is generated from a logical plan with awareness of hardware configuration and data organization, such as CPU count and number of files; the same logical query can produce different physical plans on different data layouts or hardware. DataFusion’s explain docs explicitly distinguish logical plans as language/query-specific and physical plans as data/hardware-specific. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 20.2 `ExecutionPlan`: required contract

Current DataFusion-55 contract, simplified to the methods extension authors must consciously handle:

```rust id="dm824n"
pub trait ExecutionPlan: Any + Debug + DisplayAs + Send + Sync {
    fn name(&self) -> &str;
    fn properties(&self) -> &Arc<PlanProperties>;
    fn children(&self) -> Vec<&Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>>;

    // Preferred child replacement API in 55. The trait provides a default
    // implementation; override when the node can honor the requested property mode
    // more precisely than the compatibility path.
    fn replace_children(
        self: Arc<Self>,
        children: Vec<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>>,
        options: ReplaceChildrenOptions,
    ) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> { /* provided default */ }

    // Required in 55: visit every root PhysicalExpr owned/evaluated by this node.
    fn apply_expressions(
        &self,
        f: &mut dyn FnMut(&Arc<dyn PhysicalExpr>) -> Result<TreeNodeRecursion>,
    ) -> Result<TreeNodeRecursion>;

    fn execute(
        &self,
        partition: usize,
        context: Arc<TaskContext>,
    ) -> Result<SendableRecordBatchStream>;

    // Still required for compatibility in 55, but deprecated. Implement it as a
    // shim delegating to replace_children(..., Recompute).
    #[deprecated]
    fn with_new_children(
        self: Arc<Self>,
        children: Vec<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>>,
    ) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>>;
}
```

**DataFusion-55 compatibility note:** examples later in this document that focus on another concern may abbreviate the trait implementation. A deployable custom `ExecutionPlan` must implement `apply_expressions`; new rewrite code should call/implement `replace_children` and keep `with_new_children` only as the required deprecated compatibility shim. If the node owns no physical expressions, `apply_expressions` returns `TreeNodeRecursion::Continue`; if it owns expressions, visit the expression roots it actually evaluates or updates.

The actual trait also provides many default methods, but the key invariants are: `children()` exposes child plans, `with_new_children()` reconstructs the node for optimizer rewrites, `properties()` describes output properties, and `execute()` returns a stream for one partition. `children()` is empty for leaf scans, one child for unary operators, and typically two children for binary operators such as joins. In DataFusion 54 the trait declares `Any` as a supertrait instead of a `fn as_any` method; optimizer rules and inspection code downcast with trait upcasting, e.g. `plan.downcast_ref::<ProjectionExec>()` on a `&dyn ExecutionPlan`. ([Docs.rs][1])

Agent invariants:

```text id="0wpm5f"
ExecutionPlan is immutable execution metadata.
execute(...) creates a stream; it should not eagerly compute the full result.
Each partition is executed independently through execute(partition, TaskContext).
Returned batches must match plan.schema().
with_new_children must preserve operator semantics while replacing inputs.
```

---

## 20.3 `PlanProperties`: output contract

`PlanProperties` is the physical operator’s compact contract to DataFusion’s physical optimizer and downstream operators.

```text id="v7nr0z"
PlanProperties
  ├─ EquivalenceProperties
  ├─ Partitioning
  ├─ EmissionType
  └─ Boundedness
```

`ExecutionPlanProperties` exposes `output_partitioning()`, `output_ordering()`, `boundedness()`, `pipeline_behavior()`, and `equivalence_properties()`. `output_partitioning()` says how output is split into partitions; `output_ordering()` returns local ordering within each partition when guaranteed; `boundedness()` indicates whether the stream is bounded; `pipeline_behavior()` indicates how results are emitted. ([Docs.rs][1])

Example construction:

```rust id="6hj6mo"
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::arrow::datatypes::SchemaRef;
use datafusion::physical_expr::EquivalenceProperties;
use datafusion::physical_plan::{
    execution_plan::{Boundedness, EmissionType},
    Partitioning, PlanProperties,
};

fn plan_properties(schema: SchemaRef, partitions: usize) -> Arc<PlanProperties> {
    Arc::new(PlanProperties::new(
        EquivalenceProperties::new(schema),
        Partitioning::UnknownPartitioning(partitions),
        EmissionType::Incremental,
        Boundedness::Bounded,
    ))
}
```

Agent rules:

```text id="z5eggo"
Partitioning must describe actual output partition count/layout.
Ordering must be reported only if guaranteed within each partition.
Boundedness must distinguish finite table scans from unbounded streams.
EmissionType should reflect pipelined vs blocking behavior.
False ordering/partitioning metadata can produce incorrect query results.
```

---

## 20.4 Partitioning

### Meaning

```text id="5xb40v"
Logical row set
  → physical output split into N partitions
      partition 0 -> stream of RecordBatch
      partition 1 -> stream of RecordBatch
      ...
```

`execute(partition, context)` is called for each partition. Partitioning encodes how parallelism is exposed to the runtime and how downstream operators such as joins/aggregates can assume data is distributed. The `ExecutionPlan` docs state that output partitioning describes how output is split into partitions. ([Docs.rs][1])

### Common partitioning patterns

| Source/operator         | Natural partitioning                                   |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| file scan               | file groups / row groups / object chunks               |
| object-store dataset    | file groups / partition directories                    |
| SQL database federation | shard / range / page partition                         |
| Kafka/stream            | topic partition                                        |
| repartition             | hash / round-robin / unknown partitioning              |
| aggregate final stage   | often single partition                                 |
| global sort/merge       | may collapse or preserve partitions depending operator |
| custom API              | tenant/region/date-range/page partition                |

### Agent rules

```text id="czffzo"
Expose natural partitions; do not serialize a parallel source into one partition unnecessarily.
Do not over-partition if every partition contends on the same lock/connection.
If partition count changes, properties must change.
If partitions are sorted independently, output_ordering is local, not global.
```

---

## 20.5 Ordering and input requirements

`output_ordering()` returns `Some(keys)` only if the output within each partition is sorted by those keys; `None` means no ordering assumptions are allowed. `required_input_ordering()` describes local ordering requirements for children, and `maintains_input_order()` states whether a node preserves input row order; the docs warn that overriding order-preservation incorrectly can cause incorrect results. ([Docs.rs][1])

```rust id="bn879x"
// Conceptual:
// ProjectionExec and FilterExec often maintain input order.
// HashJoinExec generally does not promise input row order.
// SortExec produces specified ordering.
// RepartitionExec may disrupt ordering unless order-preserving mode applies.
```

Agent rules:

```text id="a0gb4l"
Only report output ordering that is guaranteed by implementation.
Order is local per partition unless a merge/global operator enforces global ordering.
Filter/Projection can preserve order if implemented row-preserving/order-preserving.
Hashing, repartitioning, parallel merging, joins often break order.
If order matters for LIMIT/top-K, test physical plan with EXPLAIN.
```

---

## 20.6 Children and tree rewrites

`children()` exposes child `ExecutionPlan`s; `replace_children()` is the DataFusion-55 preferred API for reconstructing an operator with new children; `with_new_children()` remains a required but deprecated compatibility method. Physical optimizer rules use these methods to transform plan trees, insert `RepartitionExec`, remove unnecessary `SortExec`, or substitute custom nodes. ([Docs.rs][1])

### Unary operator pattern

```rust id="d7779l"
#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyUnaryExec {
    input: Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>,
    properties: Arc<PlanProperties>,
}

impl ExecutionPlan for MyUnaryExec {
    fn apply_expressions(
        &self,
        _f: &mut dyn FnMut(
            &std::sync::Arc<dyn datafusion::physical_expr::PhysicalExpr>,
        ) -> datafusion::common::Result<datafusion::common::tree_node::TreeNodeRecursion>,
    ) -> datafusion::common::Result<datafusion::common::tree_node::TreeNodeRecursion> {
        // This illustrated node owns no PhysicalExpr roots.
        Ok(datafusion::common::tree_node::TreeNodeRecursion::Continue)
    }

    fn children(&self) -> Vec<&Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        vec![&self.input]
    }

    fn with_new_children(
        self: Arc<Self>,
        children: Vec<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>>,
    ) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        if children.len() != 1 {
            return internal_err!("MyUnaryExec expects one child");
        }

        Ok(Arc::new(Self::try_new(children[0].clone())?))
    }

    // ...
}
```

### Binary operator pattern

```rust id="czfzh4"
fn children(&self) -> Vec<&Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
    vec![&self.left, &self.right]
}

fn with_new_children(
    self: Arc<Self>,
    children: Vec<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>>,
) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
    if children.len() != 2 {
        return internal_err!("MyJoinLikeExec expects two children");
    }

    Ok(Arc::new(Self::try_new(
        children[0].clone(),
        children[1].clone(),
        self.join_on.clone(),
    )?))
}
```

Agent rules:

```text id="x4c5ex"
Child order is semantic.
Recompute PlanProperties when children change.
Do not retain stale child-derived schema/order/partitioning.
Leaf nodes must return empty children.
with_new_children must validate arity.
```

---

## 20.7 `execute(partition, context)`

### Contract

```rust id="p1d6ki"
fn execute(
    &self,
    partition: usize,
    context: Arc<TaskContext>,
) -> Result<SendableRecordBatchStream>;
```

`execute` begins execution of one partition and returns an async stream of `RecordBatch` values. The method itself is not `async`; it should return a stream quickly, and most execution plans should do no work before the first `RecordBatch` is requested from the stream. Execution errors are returned as `Err` items in the stream. ([Docs.rs][1])

Correct boundary:

```text id="7s6j1e"
execute() time:
  validate partition id
  clone Arc handles
  create stream object
  wire metrics / reservations / child stream
  return stream

stream poll time:
  perform async I/O
  compute batches
  pull child batches
  allocate buffers
  update metrics
  yield RecordBatch
```

Agent rules:

```text id="emmif3"
execute() should not read all data.
execute() should not block on remote APIs.
execute() should not allocate full output.
stream drop must free resources and stop background work.
errors should appear as stream Err values after execution starts.
```

---

## 20.8 Stream production

### Type

```rust id="9kpqbx"
pub type SendableRecordBatchStream =
    Pin<Box<dyn RecordBatchStream<Item = Result<RecordBatch, DataFusionError>> + Send>>;
```

### Precomputed batch stream

```rust id="1ez8ke"
use datafusion::physical_plan::stream::RecordBatchStreamAdapter;
use futures::stream;

fn one_batch_stream(
    schema: SchemaRef,
    batch: RecordBatch,
) -> SendableRecordBatchStream {
    let s = stream::once(async move { Ok(batch) });
    Box::pin(RecordBatchStreamAdapter::new(schema, s))
}
```

The `ExecutionPlan` docs show returning a precomputed `RecordBatch` by wrapping a futures stream in `RecordBatchStreamAdapter`; the same docs also show lazy async batch computation and flattening an async-created stream. ([Docs.rs][1])

### Lazy async batch stream

```rust id="d9h3oq"
use datafusion::physical_plan::stream::RecordBatchStreamAdapter;
use futures::stream;

fn lazy_one_batch_stream(
    schema: SchemaRef,
) -> SendableRecordBatchStream {
    let schema_for_batch = schema.clone();

    let s = stream::once(async move {
        let batch = produce_batch(schema_for_batch).await?;
        Ok(batch)
    });

    Box::pin(RecordBatchStreamAdapter::new(schema, s))
}
```

### Async stream from remote pages

```rust id="azlwug"
use async_stream::try_stream;
use datafusion::physical_plan::stream::RecordBatchStreamAdapter;

fn remote_page_stream(
    schema: SchemaRef,
    client: Arc<MyClient>,
    request: MyRequest,
) -> SendableRecordBatchStream {
    let stream_schema = schema.clone();

    let s = try_stream! {
        let mut cursor = None;

        loop {
            let page = client.fetch_page(&request, cursor.clone()).await?;
            if page.rows.is_empty() {
                break;
            }

            yield rows_to_record_batch(stream_schema.clone(), page.rows)?;

            cursor = page.next_cursor;
            if cursor.is_none() {
                break;
            }
        }
    };

    Box::pin(RecordBatchStreamAdapter::new(schema, s))
}
```

Agent stream rules:

```text id="dtdg98"
Every yielded RecordBatch must match stream schema.
Batch production should be incremental.
Use bounded channels for background producers.
Stop work when receiver/stream is dropped.
Yield to Tokio for long CPU loops.
Use RecordBatchStreamAdapter for most custom streams.
```

---

## 20.9 Cancellation, errors, and background tasks

The returned stream must free allocated resources when dropped; this is critical for spawned tasks or threads. DataFusion docs explicitly state that `spawn` is disallowed in this context unless care is taken to abort, and recommend `SpawnedTask`, `JoinSet`, and `RecordBatchReceiverStreamBuilder`-style structures to ensure background tasks are cancelled. They also warn streams must not block the CPU indefinitely and must yield to the Tokio runtime regularly. ([Docs.rs][1])

Agent cancellation rules:

```text id="d6bl6p"
Never spawn orphan tasks from execute().
Tie every background task lifetime to stream lifetime.
Drop receiver -> producer exits.
Error -> stop polling children / stop additional work.
Long CPU loops -> yield_now or cooperative budget.
Blocking APIs -> spawn_blocking or dedicated pool + bounded channel.
```

---

## 20.10 Physical expressions

`PhysicalExpr` is the physical counterpart to logical `Expr`: it knows its type/nullability and can be evaluated directly on a `RecordBatch`. It represents expressions such as `A + 1` or `CAST(c1 AS int)` and is normally created by a physical planner, though APIs such as `SessionContext::create_physical_expr` and lower-level `create_physical_expr` can create them directly. ([Docs.rs][3])

### Create and evaluate a physical expression

```rust id="3pdl5p"
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::arrow::{
    array::{ArrayRef, Int32Array},
    datatypes::{DataType, Field, Schema},
    record_batch::RecordBatch,
};
use datafusion::common::DFSchema;
use datafusion::physical_expr::create_physical_expr;
use datafusion::prelude::*;

let expr = col("a").gt(lit(1));

let schema = Schema::new(vec![
    Field::new("a", DataType::Int32, true),
]);
let df_schema = DFSchema::try_from(schema)?;

let props = datafusion::execution::context::ExecutionProps::new();

let physical_expr = create_physical_expr(
    &expr,
    &df_schema,
    &props,
    &datafusion::logical_expr::physical_planning_context::PhysicalPlanningContext::default(),
)?;

let batch = RecordBatch::try_from_iter(vec![
    ("a", Arc::new(Int32Array::from(vec![1, 2, 3])) as ArrayRef),
])?;

let value = physical_expr.evaluate(&batch)?;
```

The low-level `create_physical_expr` path uses a `DFSchema`, query-wide `ExecutionProps`, and a `PhysicalPlanningContext`, then evaluates the resulting `PhysicalExpr` against Arrow `RecordBatch` values to produce a `ColumnarValue`. In DataFusion 55, `ExecutionProps` no longer carries scalar-subquery/lambda scope; that state lives in `PhysicalPlanningContext`. Create `ExecutionProps` with `ExecutionProps::new()` and use `PhysicalPlanningContext::default()` only when the expression genuinely needs no scalar-subquery/lambda planning state. ([Docs.rs][4])

### `ColumnarValue`

`ColumnarValue::Array` holds an Arrow `ArrayRef`; `ColumnarValue::Scalar` represents a single `ScalarValue` repeated logically across rows, which is an important performance optimization for constant values. Implementations should avoid unnecessarily expanding scalars into arrays in hot paths. ([Docs.rs][5])

Agent rules:

```text id="oaop28"
PhysicalExpr evaluates batches, not logical rows.
PhysicalExpr result = ColumnarValue::Array or ColumnarValue::Scalar.
Use SessionContext::create_physical_expr when you want DataFusion coercion.
Use low-level create_physical_expr only when expression is already type-coerced.
Custom operators should preserve scalar fast paths where possible.
```

The `ExecutionPlan` implementor list in current docs includes many of these nodes, including source/sink, aggregates, async functions, coalescing, filters, joins, limits, projection, recursive query, and other physical operators. The physical-plan module docs also identify operator modules such as projection, repartition, sort, stream wrappers, streaming table execution, union, unnest, and windows. ([Docs.rs][1])

Operator role map:

| Node family                          | Role                                    |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| `DataSourceExec`                     | scan file/table/custom sources          |
| `FilterExec`                         | evaluate boolean predicate over batches |
| `ProjectionExec`                     | compute output expressions/columns      |
| `AggregateExec`                      | partial/final/group aggregate execution |
| `HashJoinExec`                       | hash-based join                         |
| `SortMergeJoinExec`                  | sorted-input merge join                 |
| `NestedLoopJoinExec`                 | non-equi/small/cross-like join paths    |
| `RepartitionExec`                    | change partitioning/distribution        |
| `CoalesceBatchesExec`                | normalize batch sizes                   |
| `CoalescePartitionsExec`             | merge partitions                        |
| `SortExec` / sort family             | order rows                              |
| `GlobalLimitExec` / `LocalLimitExec` | enforce limits                          |
| `DataSinkExec`                       | consume stream and write to sink        |
| `ExplainExec` / `AnalyzeExec`        | plan/runtime diagnostics                |
| `UnionExec`                          | combine same-schema inputs              |
| `UnnestExec`                         | expand nested list/struct values        |

## 20.12 Custom operator skeleton

> This is a compile-shape reference; pin exact trait imports and method set to your DataFusion version.

```rust id="ecemkq"
use std::{any::Any, sync::Arc};

use datafusion::arrow::{
    datatypes::SchemaRef,
    record_batch::RecordBatch,
};
use datafusion::common::{internal_err, Result};
use datafusion::execution::TaskContext;
use datafusion::physical_expr::EquivalenceProperties;
use datafusion::physical_plan::{
    execution_plan::{Boundedness, EmissionType},
    stream::RecordBatchStreamAdapter,
    DisplayAs, DisplayFormatType, ExecutionPlan, Partitioning, PlanProperties,
    SendableRecordBatchStream,
};
use futures::stream;

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct MyExec {
    schema: SchemaRef,
    properties: Arc<PlanProperties>,
    partitions: usize,
}

impl MyExec {
    pub fn try_new(schema: SchemaRef, partitions: usize) -> Result<Self> {
        let properties = Arc::new(PlanProperties::new(
            EquivalenceProperties::new(schema.clone()),
            Partitioning::UnknownPartitioning(partitions),
            EmissionType::Incremental,
            Boundedness::Bounded,
        ));

        Ok(Self {
            schema,
            properties,
            partitions,
        })
    }

    async fn make_batch(
        &self,
        partition: usize,
    ) -> Result<RecordBatch> {
        // produce one partition batch
        todo!()
    }
}

impl DisplayAs for MyExec {
    fn fmt_as(
        &self,
        _t: DisplayFormatType,
        f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>,
    ) -> std::fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "MyExec: partitions={}", self.partitions)
    }
}

impl ExecutionPlan for MyExec {
    fn apply_expressions(
        &self,
        _f: &mut dyn FnMut(
            &std::sync::Arc<dyn datafusion::physical_expr::PhysicalExpr>,
        ) -> datafusion::common::Result<datafusion::common::tree_node::TreeNodeRecursion>,
    ) -> datafusion::common::Result<datafusion::common::tree_node::TreeNodeRecursion> {
        // This illustrated node owns no PhysicalExpr roots.
        Ok(datafusion::common::tree_node::TreeNodeRecursion::Continue)
    }

    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "MyExec"
    }

    fn properties(&self) -> &Arc<PlanProperties> {
        &self.properties
    }

    fn children(&self) -> Vec<&Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        vec![]
    }

    fn with_new_children(
        self: Arc<Self>,
        children: Vec<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>>,
    ) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        if !children.is_empty() {
            return internal_err!("MyExec is a leaf node");
        }
        Ok(self)
    }

    fn execute(
        &self,
        partition: usize,
        _context: Arc<TaskContext>,
    ) -> Result<SendableRecordBatchStream> {
        if partition >= self.partitions {
            return internal_err!("invalid partition {partition}");
        }

        let schema = self.schema.clone();
        let this = self.clone_for_stream();

        let s = stream::once(async move {
            this.make_batch(partition).await
        });

        Ok(Box::pin(RecordBatchStreamAdapter::new(schema, s)))
    }
}
```

Implementation rules:

```text id="e59lkv"
Leaf node: children() = [].
Unary node: children() = [input].
Binary node: children() = [left, right].
Recompute properties if children change.
Return stream quickly.
Yield batches with exact schema.
Expose DisplayAs text for EXPLAIN.
```

## 20.13 Custom operator tied to `TableProvider`

```text id="n5b8pf"
TableProvider::scan(...)
  receives:
    projection
    filters
    limit
  returns:
    Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>

ExecutionPlan::execute(partition, TaskContext)
  creates:
    SendableRecordBatchStream

RecordBatchStream::poll_next(...)
  actually:
    calls remote API / reads source / decodes data / computes batches
```

The custom table provider guide frames these as the three layers and emphasizes where work belongs: `scan()` creates a plan during planning, `execute()` creates a partition stream, and the stream is where rows are produced. It also describes physical planning as the point where choices such as hash join vs sort-merge join and number of scan partitions are made. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

Agent provider/operator rules:

```text id="8zmnuj"
Push projection/filter/limit into ExecutionPlan metadata.
Do remote I/O only inside stream polling.
Use partition ids to map to shards/files/ranges/pages.
Use EXPLAIN to verify FilterExec/ProjectionExec/RepartitionExec placement.
```

## 20.14 Operator metrics

DataFusion operators expose runtime metrics so users can understand where time is spent and how much data flows through the pipeline; DataFusion docs point users to `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` for viewing these metrics. ([Apache DataFusion][7])

The metrics module includes `BaselineMetrics`, counters, gauges, timers, pruning metrics, spill metrics, expression-evaluator metrics, and `ExecutionPlanMetricsSet`; `BaselineMetrics` is a helper for common per-operator metrics, and counters record quantities such as input/output rows. ([Docs.rs][8])

`ExecutionPlan::metrics()` returns an optional snapshot `MetricsSet`; if no metrics are available, return `None`. The set of metric names is stable for the plan while values can change during execution. ([Docs.rs][9])

### Metrics skeleton

```rust id="cs0d90"
use datafusion::physical_plan::metrics::{
    BaselineMetrics, ExecutionPlanMetricsSet,
};

#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyExec {
    metrics: ExecutionPlanMetricsSet,
    // ...
}

impl MyExec {
    fn baseline_metrics(&self, partition: usize) -> BaselineMetrics {
        BaselineMetrics::new(&self.metrics, partition)
    }
}

// in ExecutionPlan impl:
fn metrics(&self) -> Option<MetricsSet> {
    Some(self.metrics.clone_inner())
}
```

### Stream metric usage concept

```rust id="w9duqe"
let baseline = exec.baseline_metrics(partition);

let timer = baseline.elapsed_compute().timer();
// compute / poll / transform batch
drop(timer);

baseline.record_output(batch.num_rows());
```

Exact helper method names vary by version; use the pinned docs.rs API for `BaselineMetrics`, `ExecutionPlanMetricsSet`, `Count`, and `Time`.

Agent metrics rules:

```text id="3w1tsb"
Expose output rows.
Expose elapsed compute time.
Expose source-specific counters: bytes read, pages read, API calls, retries, cache hits.
Expose pruning metrics for sources that skip work.
Expose spill metrics for spillable operators.
Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE in tests and production diagnostics.
```

## 20.15 Resource reservations and memory pools

DataFusion’s memory model has `MemoryPool`, `MemoryConsumer`, `SharedRegistration`, and `MemoryReservation`. A `MemoryConsumer` is a named allocation traced for an operator/partition; each consumer can have multiple `MemoryReservation`s for different internal structures; reservations are RAII-based and freed by dropping them. ([Docs.rs][10])

The memory-pool module includes `FairSpillPool`, `GreedyMemoryPool`, `UnboundedMemoryPool`, `TrackConsumersPool`, `MemoryConsumer`, and `MemoryReservation`; `MemoryPool` tracks and potentially limits memory use across operators during execution. ([Docs.rs][11])

### Reservation pattern

```rust id="peiejw"
use datafusion::execution::memory_pool::MemoryConsumer;

fn make_reservation(
    context: &TaskContext,
    operator_name: &str,
) -> datafusion::error::Result<MemoryReservation> {
    let consumer = MemoryConsumer::new(operator_name.to_string());
    let reservation = consumer.register(context.memory_pool());
    Ok(reservation)
}
```

### Growth / shrink concept

```rust id="zmpwsc"
reservation.try_grow(bytes_needed)?;

// allocate buffer / hash table / batch cache

reservation.shrink(bytes_freed);

// drop(reservation) frees remaining reservation automatically
```

Agent memory rules:

```text id="4eo4gp"
Track memory for custom operators that buffer data.
Use one MemoryConsumer per operator partition when possible.
Use separate reservations for separate internal structures.
try_grow before allocating large buffers.
shrink/drop reservations when memory is released.
Do not bypass memory pool for unbounded buffers in service workloads.
```

---

## 20.16 Physical filter pushdown

Physical filter pushdown is opt-in and proceeds in phases. The default behavior blocks parent filters from being pushed down. Nodes can gather filters for child pushdown and handle child pushdown results on the way back up; `DataSourceExec` may absorb filters for late materialization, `FilterExec` may combine residual filters or remove itself if no filters remain, and join nodes may push filters to one side or add their own filters. ([Docs.rs][1])

Agent rules:

```text id="bkrrkm"
Do not implement physical filter pushdown casually.
Only absorb filters your node can enforce exactly or report residuals correctly.
Preserve SQL null semantics.
Residual filters must remain above the scan/operator.
Use EXPLAIN to verify FilterExec removal/retention.
```

---

## 20.17 Physical planning from a logical plan

```rust id="gq8dzt"
let logical_plan = df.into_optimized_plan()?;

// or from builder / SQL / custom compiler

let physical_plan = ctx
    .state()
    .create_physical_plan(&logical_plan)
    .await?;
```

Logical plans cannot be directly executed; DataFusion compiles them into `ExecutionPlan`s. The logical-plan guide says `SessionState::create_physical_plan` is the easiest way to translate logical plans into physical plans and notes that physical plans include concrete choices such as algorithms and detailed optimizations. ([Apache DataFusion][12])

Manual execution:

```rust id="9z1shw"
use futures::StreamExt;

let task_ctx = ctx.task_ctx();
let mut stream = physical_plan.execute(0, task_ctx)?;

while let Some(batch) = stream.next().await {
    let batch = batch?;
    // consume batch
}
```

Agent rules:

```text id="c7kqmb"
Prefer DataFrame actions for normal apps.
Use create_physical_plan for custom execution, diagnostics, and extension tests.
Manual execute must iterate all partitions unless intentionally executing one partition.
```

## 20.20 Custom operator resource pattern

```rust id="fdk3sy"
struct MyStream {
    schema: SchemaRef,
    reservation: MemoryReservation,
    baseline: BaselineMetrics,
    input: SendableRecordBatchStream,
}

impl Stream for MyStream {
    type Item = Result<RecordBatch, DataFusionError>;

    fn poll_next(
        self: Pin<&mut Self>,
        cx: &mut Context<'_>,
    ) -> Poll<Option<Self::Item>> {
        let this = self.project();

        let timer = this.baseline.elapsed_compute().timer();

        match this.input.poll_next_unpin(cx) {
            Poll::Ready(Some(Ok(batch))) => {
                let bytes = estimate_batch_memory(&batch);

                if let Err(e) = this.reservation.try_grow(bytes) {
                    return Poll::Ready(Some(Err(e)));
                }

                let out = transform(batch)?;

                this.baseline.record_output(out.num_rows());

                this.reservation.shrink(bytes);
                drop(timer);

                Poll::Ready(Some(Ok(out)))
            }
            other => {
                drop(timer);
                other
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Conceptual only: exact helper methods and pin projection utilities depend on the pinned DataFusion and stream implementation. The pattern remains: reserve before buffering, track compute time/output rows, shrink/drop memory, and propagate errors through the stream.

## 20.22 Tying to `TaskContext` and runtime state

`TaskContext` supplies execution-time state such as `SessionConfig`, function registries, and `RuntimeEnv`, including the memory pool, disk manager, cache manager, and object-store registry. Custom physical operators should use `TaskContext` rather than global state when accessing execution resources.

```rust id="fddm8z"
fn execute(
    &self,
    partition: usize,
    context: Arc<TaskContext>,
) -> Result<SendableRecordBatchStream> {
    let memory_pool = context.memory_pool();
    let runtime = context.runtime_env();

    // use runtime.object_store(...) / disk manager / cache manager as needed
    // use memory_pool for reservations
    todo!()
}
```

Agent rules:

```text id="yftqrr"
TaskContext is execution resource boundary.
Do not hard-code global runtime resources inside operators.
Use context.memory_pool() for operator reservations.
Use runtime object-store registry for remote reads.
Use session config from context for batch sizes and execution behavior.
```

## 20.23 Physical operator design policy

| Operator type | Key property                                  | Key risk                                |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| source        | partitions, schema, pruning, object-store use | too much work in execute/scan           |
| projection    | expression evaluation, order preservation     | wrong expression type/nullability       |
| filter        | predicate correctness, null semantics         | claiming pushdown incorrectly           |
| aggregate     | memory/spill/state merge                      | untracked state memory                  |
| join          | distribution/order requirements               | wrong partitioning/order assumptions    |
| sort          | ordering guarantee, spill                     | unbounded memory                        |
| limit         | global vs local semantics                     | wrong top-N semantics across partitions |
| sink          | commit/rollback/count metrics                 | partial writes                          |
| custom        | properties, metrics, cancellation             | optimizer misuse / resource leaks       |

---

## 20.25 Anti-pattern inventory

* Doing remote reads inside `execute()` before returning a stream.
* Returning all rows as one huge `RecordBatch`.
* Returning batches whose schema differs from `plan.schema()`.
* Reporting `output_ordering` because the current test data happens to be sorted.
* Reporting `maintains_input_order = true` without proof.
* Forgetting to recompute `PlanProperties` in `with_new_children`.
* Using `tokio::spawn` without cancellation binding to stream lifetime.
* Blocking CPU indefinitely in `poll_next`.
* Buffering unbounded data without `MemoryReservation`.
* Ignoring `TaskContext` memory/runtime resources.
* Returning `None` metrics for production custom operators.
* Treating `EXPLAIN` string snapshots as stable across DataFusion versions without pinning.
* Implementing physical filter pushdown without residual-filter correctness tests.
* Assuming local partition ordering is global ordering.
* Manually executing only partition `0` of a multi-partition plan and treating it as full output.
