## 20.27 `ScalarSubqueryExec`: physical uncorrelated scalar subqueries (DataFusion 54)

DataFusion 54 changed how **uncorrelated scalar subqueries** execute. Under 53 they had to be optimized away at plan time (or the query failed); under 54 they survive to the final logical plan and execute physically, **once**, through dedicated operators:

* `ScalarSubqueryExec` (`datafusion_physical_plan::scalar_subquery`) — wraps the main input plan plus the subquery plan(s); on execution it runs each subquery to completion, stores the resulting scalar values into the shared `ScalarSubqueryResults` container carried by `PhysicalPlanningContext`, then streams the main input through.
* `ScalarSubqueryExpr` (`datafusion_physical_expr::scalar_subquery`) — the `PhysicalExpr` that reads the computed scalar from the results container by index (`data_type`/`nullable` fixed at planning time).

Behavior contract:

* The subquery executes **exactly once per query**, not per row or per partition.
* **One-row cardinality is enforced at runtime**: a scalar subquery yielding more than one row raises an execution error instead of picking an arbitrary row.
* Scalar subqueries now work in positions that previously failed to plan: `ORDER BY (SELECT ...)`, join `ON` conditions, and aggregate arguments.
* Gated by `datafusion.optimizer.enable_physical_uncorrelated_scalar_subquery` (default `true`); disabling restores the 53-style rewrite-only behavior.

```sql
-- plans in 54; executes the scalar subquery once
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (SELECT avg(salary) FROM employees);
```

Transport/serialization note: plans containing `ScalarSubqueryExec` / `ScalarSubqueryExpr` require a `datafusion-proto` codec that understands these nodes — see §36.26. Custom `ExecutionPlan` tree-walkers should note that `ScalarSubqueryExec::children()` returns the main input **plus every subquery plan**, so operators can now have more children than the "one input" intuition suggests. Full planning treatment: `docs/library_ref/datafusion_planning_rust.md` (§41/§49).

# DataFusion Advanced — 21) Streaming execution model

Style target follows the uploaded advanced-reference pattern. 

## 21.0 Mental model: streaming by `RecordBatch` polling

```text id="5ksg16"
ExecutionPlan DAG
  ├─ execute(partition=0, TaskContext) -> SendableRecordBatchStream
  ├─ execute(partition=1, TaskContext) -> SendableRecordBatchStream
  └─ ...

Each stream:
  poll_next()
    → pull child batch(es)
    → compute output batch
    → yield RecordBatch
    → repeat until None or Err
```

DataFusion is a streaming query engine: `ExecutionPlan`s incrementally read inputs and compute output one `RecordBatch` at a time by continually polling `SendableRecordBatchStream`s. Output and intermediate batches usually contain approximately `batch_size` rows, amortizing per-batch overhead while avoiding full-result materialization. ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/))

---

## 21.1 Value case: why streaming execution matters

| Requirement                 | Streaming value                                                  |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| large result sets           | avoid `Vec<RecordBatch>` full buffering                          |
| HTTP/gRPC/Arrow Flight APIs | send batches as soon as produced                                 |
| cancellation                | dropping stream aborts execution and frees resources             |
| remote sources              | overlap async I/O with compute                                   |
| low-latency first row       | pipeline-friendly operators can emit before reading all input    |
| bounded memory              | operators process batch-sized chunks when not pipeline-breaking  |
| parallelism                 | partitions execute as separate streams/tasks                     |
| custom sources              | implement stream over API pages, files, queues, shards           |
| unbounded data              | source and operators can model streams that do not naturally end |

DataFrame docs describe three execution modes: `collect` buffers all output into `Vec<RecordBatch>`, `execute_stream` returns a `SendableRecordBatchStream` that incrementally computes output on `next()`, and `cache` materializes results in memory for repeated use. ([datafusion.apache.org](https://datafusion.apache.org/library-user-guide/using-the-dataframe-api.html))

---

## 21.2 `SendableRecordBatchStream`

### Type

```rust id="dy045u"
pub type SendableRecordBatchStream =
    Pin<Box<dyn RecordBatchStream<Item = Result<RecordBatch, DataFusionError>> + Send>>;
```

`SendableRecordBatchStream` is a pinned, boxed, sendable async stream of `RecordBatch` results; it is the normal output of physical execution. `RecordBatchStream` implementations must guarantee all returned batches have the same schema as `schema()`. ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/execution/trait.RecordBatchStream.html))

### Consumption

```rust id="1n3rku"
use futures::StreamExt;
use datafusion::prelude::*;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let ctx = SessionContext::new();

    let mut stream = ctx
        .read_csv("events.csv", CsvReadOptions::new())
        .await?
        .execute_stream()
        .await?;

    while let Some(batch) = stream.next().await {
        let batch = batch?;
        process_batch(batch).await?;
    }

    Ok(())
}
```

`DataFrame::execute_stream()` begins execution and returns a stream; dropping that stream aborts execution and frees allocated resources. ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/dataframe/struct.DataFrame.html))

### Schema-before-data

```rust id="he2gwp"
let stream = df.execute_stream().await?;
let schema = stream.schema();

println!("schema={schema:?}");
```

`RecordBatchStream::schema()` is available before any batches are produced, which is essential for protocols such as Arrow Flight, IPC, and HTTP schemas where clients need schema metadata before body chunks.

### Agent rules

```text id="aryp06"
Always iterate until stream returns None.
Do not assume a fixed batch count.
Do not assume a fixed row count per batch.
Handle Err items and stop/propagate according to product policy.
Use stream.schema() for response headers / protocol setup.
Dropping stream is cancellation.
```

---

## 21.3 Batch size

### Default

```text id="nhpjt6"
datafusion.execution.batch_size = 8192
```

The config reference documents `datafusion.execution.batch_size` with default `8192`; it controls the default batch size when creating new batches and helps avoid excessive metadata overhead from tiny batches. ([datafusion.apache.org](https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/configs.html))

### Configure in Rust

```rust id="r1kxzo"
use datafusion::prelude::*;

let config = SessionConfig::new()
    .with_batch_size(16_384);

let ctx = SessionContext::new_with_config(config);
```

### Configure by key

```rust id="xetd4e"
let mut config = SessionConfig::new();
config.set_usize("datafusion.execution.batch_size", 16_384)?;

let ctx = SessionContext::new_with_config(config);
```

### Configure in SQL / CLI

```sql id="k31fqq"
SET datafusion.execution.batch_size = '16384';
```

### Configure by environment variable

```bash id="7r6r4m"
export DATAFUSION_EXECUTION_BATCH_SIZE=16384
```

The CLI usage docs show environment variables use uppercase config names with `.` converted to `_`, such as `DATAFUSION_EXECUTION_BATCH_SIZE`. ([datafusion.apache.org](https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/cli/usage.html))

### Agent rules

```text id="f3u0lv"
Batch size is a target, not a promise.
Sources/operators may produce different batch sizes.
Always handle any batch.num_rows(), including 0-row batches if emitted.
Larger batches reduce per-batch overhead but increase latency/memory.
Smaller batches can improve cancellation/latency but increase metadata/dispatch cost.
Benchmark with real operators and output protocols.
```

DataFusion’s Arrow intro warns users not to assume a particular batch size; different files or sources can produce different batch sizes such as 8192 rows or 1024 rows. ([datafusion.apache.org](https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/arrow-introduction.html))

---

## 21.4 Incremental polling and backpressure

### Polling chain

```text id="u24t6z"
consumer.next().await
  → root operator poll_next()
    → child operator poll_next()
      → source stream poll_next()
        → file/API/DB/page decode
        → RecordBatch
      → compute transform
    → RecordBatch
```

### Backpressure model

```text id="malcf5"
Consumer slow:
  next().await not called
  root stream not polled
  child streams not polled
  source fetch/decode pauses if implementation is poll-driven

Consumer drops:
  stream dropped
  query aborted
  resources freed
```

DataFusion’s execution docs state that dropping the stream aborts the query and frees allocated resources; this makes `execute_stream` naturally cancellation-aware for services when response consumers disconnect. ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/physical_plan/fn.execute_stream.html))

### Service pattern

```rust id="4k7l03"
use futures::StreamExt;
use datafusion::arrow::record_batch::RecordBatch;

pub async fn write_batches_to_response(
    mut stream: datafusion::execution::SendableRecordBatchStream,
    mut sink: impl BatchResponseSink,
) -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let schema = stream.schema();
    sink.write_schema(schema).await?;

    while let Some(batch) = stream.next().await {
        let batch = batch?;
        sink.write_batch(batch).await?;
    }

    sink.finish().await?;
    Ok(())
}
```

Agent rules:

```text id="ojdk3g"
Do not collect before streaming to response.
Do not spawn unbounded producers ahead of consumer demand.
Use bounded channels if bridging blocking systems.
Tie spawned producer lifetime to stream/sink lifetime.
```

---

## 21.5 `collect` vs `execute_stream`

| Method                         | Execution                                 | Memory                              | Use                              |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `collect()`                    | executes and buffers all output           | O(total output)                     | tests, small bounded results     |
| `execute_stream()`             | executes and yields batches incrementally | O(operator state + current batches) | services, exports, large results |
| `execute_stream_partitioned()` | returns one stream per output partition   | O(partition stream state)           | partition-aware sinks/processors |
| `collect_partitioned()`        | buffers output by partition               | O(total output)                     | bounded partition-aware tests    |

DataFusion’s DataFrame guide explicitly contrasts `collect`, which buffers all output into memory, with `execute_stream`, which computes output incrementally with each `next()` call. ([datafusion.apache.org](https://datafusion.apache.org/library-user-guide/using-the-dataframe-api.html))

### Rust example: collect

```rust id="x2rytx"
let batches = df.collect().await?;
```

### Rust example: stream

```rust id="h82qpm"
use futures::StreamExt;

let mut stream = df.execute_stream().await?;

while let Some(batch) = stream.next().await {
    let batch = batch?;
    // process batch
}
```

### Agent rules

```text id="mgkzae"
Default to execute_stream for service endpoints.
Use collect for bounded tests and small admin queries.
Use collect only after explicit LIMIT / known finite small result.
Use execute_stream_partitioned when downstream can exploit partitions.
```

---

## 21.6 Partitioned streaming

```rust id="gxj0t1"
let streams = df.execute_stream_partitioned().await?;

for (partition, mut stream) in streams.into_iter().enumerate() {
    while let Some(batch) = stream.next().await {
        let batch = batch?;
        process_partition_batch(partition, batch).await?;
    }
}
```

`execute_stream_partitioned()` executes the DataFrame without buffering and returns one `SendableRecordBatchStream` per partition. Use it when partition boundaries matter, such as writing one file per partition, maintaining source shard identity, or running partition-local postprocessing. ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/dataframe/struct.DataFrame.html))

Agent rules:

```text id="tq6ofv"
execute_stream() usually coalesces into one output stream for consumer simplicity.
execute_stream_partitioned() preserves partition stream boundaries.
Partition-local ordering is not global ordering.
Do not assume partitions are balanced.
```

---

## 21.7 Blocking vs async boundaries

### Correct split

```text id="za2zda"
async / poll-friendly source:
  implement stream that awaits I/O on poll

blocking source:
  offload to spawn_blocking / dedicated thread pool
  send RecordBatch values over bounded channel
  wrap receiver as RecordBatchStream

CPU-heavy custom operator:
  process in chunks
  yield periodically
  track memory
```

The `ExecutionPlan` docs warn that streams must not block the CPU indefinitely and should yield to the Tokio runtime regularly. They also emphasize cleanup on stream drop, especially for spawned tasks. ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html))

### Blocking bridge pattern

```rust id="mqxiuu"
use datafusion::physical_plan::stream::RecordBatchStreamAdapter;
use tokio_stream::wrappers::ReceiverStream;

fn blocking_source_stream(
    schema: SchemaRef,
    config: BlockingConfig,
) -> SendableRecordBatchStream {
    let (tx, rx) = tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(2);

    tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || {
        for batch_result in blocking_read_record_batches(config) {
            if tx.blocking_send(batch_result).is_err() {
                break; // stream receiver dropped: stop producing
            }
        }
    });

    Box::pin(RecordBatchStreamAdapter::new(
        schema,
        ReceiverStream::new(rx),
    ))
}
```

### Async source pattern

```rust id="gby1hq"
use async_stream::try_stream;
use datafusion::physical_plan::stream::RecordBatchStreamAdapter;

fn async_api_stream(
    schema: SchemaRef,
    client: Arc<MyClient>,
    request: Request,
) -> SendableRecordBatchStream {
    let schema_for_batches = schema.clone();

    let s = try_stream! {
        let mut cursor = None;

        loop {
            let page = client.fetch_page(&request, cursor.clone()).await?;
            if page.rows.is_empty() {
                break;
            }

            yield rows_to_batch(schema_for_batches.clone(), page.rows)?;
            cursor = page.next_cursor;

            if cursor.is_none() {
                break;
            }
        }
    };

    Box::pin(RecordBatchStreamAdapter::new(schema, s))
}
```

Agent rules:

```text id="4gdway"
Never block Tokio worker threads with synchronous DB/file/API loops.
Use bounded channels for blocking bridges.
Stop producer on receiver drop.
Batch rows before yielding.
Avoid one remote call per row.
```

---

## 21.8 Memory benefits and limits

### What streaming reduces

```text id="1z0sxp"
Avoids:
  buffering all output rows
  building Vec<RecordBatch> for full result
  waiting for complete query before first output
  materializing full intermediate for pipeline-friendly operators

Still may require:
  hash table for hash join
  aggregate state for GROUP BY
  sort buffer for global ORDER BY
  window frame/partition state
  distinct/dedup state
  spill files for memory-limited operations
```

DataFusion is streaming, but some operations remain pipeline breakers or large-state operators. The core docs explicitly say full sort and hash aggregation may need to consume all input before producing output. ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/))

### Memory/resource config

```rust id="j7jj1o"
use datafusion::execution::{
    runtime_env::RuntimeEnvBuilder,
    session_state::SessionStateBuilder,
};
use datafusion::prelude::*;

let runtime = RuntimeEnvBuilder::new()
    .with_memory_limit(8 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024, 0.8)
    .with_temp_file_path("/mnt/spill/datafusion")
    .build_arc()?;

let state = SessionStateBuilder::new()
    .with_runtime_env(runtime)
    .with_default_features()
    .build();

let ctx = SessionContext::from(state);
```

### Agent rules

```text id="13srmt"
Streaming output != no memory use.
Stateful operators can still hold large state.
Set memory limits and spill paths in services.
Prefer streaming-friendly query shapes for large/unbounded sources.
Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE metrics for memory/row-flow diagnostics.
```

---

## 21.9 Pipeline behavior and boundedness

`ExecutionPlanProperties` exposes `boundedness()` and `pipeline_behavior()`. `boundedness` describes whether the corresponding stream is bounded, and `pipeline_behavior` reports how the plan emits results. These are based on `PlanProperties` and inform streaming/physical-optimizer behavior. ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html))

### Conceptual categories

| Property                   | Meaning                                              |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `Bounded`                  | finite input/output; eventually ends                 |
| `Unbounded`                | input/output may not end                             |
| `Incremental` emission     | operator can emit output as input arrives            |
| pipeline-breaking emission | operator may need to consume all input before output |

### Custom source properties

```rust id="8vld1b"
use datafusion::physical_plan::{
    execution_plan::{Boundedness, EmissionType},
    Partitioning, PlanProperties,
};
use datafusion::physical_expr::EquivalenceProperties;

let properties = PlanProperties::new(
    EquivalenceProperties::new(schema.clone()),
    Partitioning::UnknownPartitioning(num_partitions),
    EmissionType::Incremental,
    Boundedness::Unbounded,
);
```

Agent rules:

```text id="6y2rzz"
Boundedness must reflect source reality.
Do not mark an infinite stream as bounded.
Do not mark a pipeline-breaking operator as incremental.
Incorrect boundedness/emission metadata can break unbounded execution planning.
```

---

## 21.10 Bounded vs unbounded sources

### Bounded source

```text id="7bmhe2"
files
finite object-store datasets
finite database query
in-memory RecordBatch list
finite REST export
```

### Unbounded source

```text id="x2lpl8"
Kafka topic
WebSocket stream
tailing log
message queue
long-running RPC stream
streaming table
```

### SQL DDL for unbounded external source

```sql id="otjzvs"
CREATE UNBOUNDED EXTERNAL TABLE taxi
STORED AS PARQUET
LOCATION '/mnt/nyctaxi/tripdata.parquet';
```

DataFusion’s DDL docs describe `CREATE UNBOUNDED EXTERNAL TABLE` as marking a source as unbounded; DataFusion then tries to execute queries in streaming fashion and fails plan generation if a query cannot be executed in streaming mode. It also warns that supported queries over unbounded sources are a subset of those supported over bounded sources. ([datafusion.apache.org](https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/sql/ddl.html))

### Agent rules

```text id="ez1r75"
Unbounded source:
  avoid global sort
  avoid final-only aggregates unless windowed/bounded
  prefer filters, projections, streaming windows, stream-friendly joins
  test plan generation failure as expected for unsupported queries
  configure joins carefully
```

---

## 21.11 Streaming aggregation and grouping

### Streaming-friendly aggregation patterns

```sql id="wge00k"
-- bounded source: fine
SELECT region, count(*) AS n
FROM events
GROUP BY region;
```

```sql id="df4iaf"
-- unbounded-like stream: prefer window/time-bounded aggregation, if supported by source/query shape
SELECT
  date_bin(INTERVAL '1 minute', event_ts, TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:00') AS bucket,
  region,
  count(*) AS n
FROM events
GROUP BY bucket, region;
```

Hash aggregation may require maintaining state for all active groups, and final/global aggregates over unbounded streams may never complete. The core docs call out hash aggregation as an operation that may need to consume all input before producing output; therefore, unbounded sources require special care with aggregate shapes. ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/))

### Agent rules

```text id="wpv0vy"
Bounded source:
  normal GROUP BY is fine subject to memory/spill.

Unbounded source:
  global count/sum without window = no natural completion.
  group state can grow without bound.
  use time/key windows or bounded state if product requires streaming.
  test physical plan boundedness and memory behavior.
```

---

## 21.12 Streaming window execution

### Window-function example

```sql id="jvy1yk"
SELECT
  account_id,
  event_ts,
  amount,
  sum(amount) OVER (
    PARTITION BY account_id
    ORDER BY event_ts
    ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS rolling_7_row_amount
FROM account_events;
```

Window functions compute row-level results with access to surrounding rows; supported frame types and memory behavior depend on the frame. Row-bounded frames such as `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` are more stream-friendly than unbounded frames requiring full partition state. DataFusion’s window-function docs describe partitioning, ordering, row/range/groups frames, and aggregate-window filtering. ([datafusion.apache.org](https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/sql/window_functions.html))

### Agent rules

```text id="6umosi"
Stream-friendly:
  finite ROWS preceding/following frames
  partitioned by bounded-cardinality key
  deterministic ORDER BY

Less stream-friendly:
  UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  full-partition windows
  high-cardinality unbounded partitions
  global windows over unbounded sources
```

---

## 21.13 Streaming joins and symmetric hash join

### Join categories

| Join shape                 | Streaming friendliness                                              |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| bounded hash join          | common for finite inputs; may buffer build side                     |
| stream-static join         | stream side joined to bounded/dimension side                        |
| symmetric hash join        | both sides can be streamed, with pruning/window constraints         |
| sort-merge join            | stream-friendly if inputs arrive ordered and bounds allow progress  |
| cross join                 | usually dangerous for streams                                       |
| unbounded full/outer joins | can require retaining unmatched rows until end or pruning condition |

`SymmetricHashJoinExec` is documented as hashing both input streams on join keys and using hash tables from both streams to join rows; it is symmetric because hash tables are built on both sides. ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/physical_plan/joins/struct.SymmetricHashJoinExec.html))

### Relevant config

```sql id="amjhcf"
SET datafusion.optimizer.allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning = true;
```

The config docs describe `allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning`: it controls whether symmetric hash joins are allowed for unbounded data sources when inputs lack ordering or filtering. If disabled, some join types cannot prune internal buffers and may produce results only at the end of execution, which is not typical stream processing behavior. ([datafusion.apache.org](https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/configs.html))

### Agent join rules

```text id="yq655q"
For unbounded joins:
  require time/range predicates or ordering enabling pruning.
  avoid full outer joins unless retention policy is clear.
  avoid cross joins.
  prefer stream-static joins when possible.
  inspect physical plan for SymmetricHashJoinExec / SortMergeJoinExec.
  monitor hash table memory and pruning metrics.
```

---

## 21.14 Custom streaming source pattern

### TableProvider → ExecutionPlan → stream

```rust id="jz6unu"
#[async_trait::async_trait]
impl TableProvider for MyStreamingTable {
    fn schema(&self) -> SchemaRef {
        self.schema.clone()
    }

    fn table_type(&self) -> TableType {
        TableType::Base
    }

    async fn scan(
        &self,
        _state: &dyn Session,
        projection: Option<&Vec<usize>>,
        filters: &[Expr],
        limit: Option<usize>,
    ) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        Ok(Arc::new(MyStreamingExec::new(
            self.schema.clone(),
            projection.cloned(),
            filters.to_vec(),
            limit,
            self.source.clone(),
        )?))
    }
}
```

The custom table provider guide describes exactly this layering: the `TableProvider` describes schema/capabilities and creates an `ExecutionPlan`; the `ExecutionPlan` describes partitioning/ordering/children and returns streams; the stream actually yields `RecordBatch`es. ([datafusion.apache.org](https://datafusion.apache.org/library-user-guide/custom-table-providers.html))

### Stream implementation pattern

```rust id="288jw4"
use async_stream::try_stream;
use datafusion::physical_plan::stream::RecordBatchStreamAdapter;

fn make_source_stream(
    schema: SchemaRef,
    receiver: MyAsyncReceiver,
) -> SendableRecordBatchStream {
    let schema_for_batches = schema.clone();

    let s = try_stream! {
        loop {
            match receiver.recv().await {
                Some(msgs) => {
                    yield messages_to_batch(schema_for_batches.clone(), msgs)?;
                }
                None => break,
            }
        }
    };

    Box::pin(RecordBatchStreamAdapter::new(schema, s))
}
```

Agent rules:

```text id="g24lyl"
Unbounded stream must set Boundedness::Unbounded in PlanProperties.
Use bounded batches.
Use polling/awaiting model, not busy loop.
Implement cancellation on stream drop.
Expose partitioning by source partitions when possible.
```

---

## 21.15 Streaming sinks / exports

### Stream to custom sink

```rust id="zxibpm"
use futures::StreamExt;

let mut stream = df.execute_stream().await?;

while let Some(batch) = stream.next().await {
    let batch = batch?;
    sink.write_record_batch(batch).await?;
}
```

### Stream to Arrow IPC / HTTP / Flight

```text id="9gk7d8"
response headers:
  stream.schema()

body:
  for each RecordBatch:
    encode batch
    write chunk
    flush according to protocol
```

Agent rules:

```text id="0revz4"
Use stream.schema() before first batch.
Do not convert all batches to rows unless response format requires it.
Apply backpressure through await on sink write.
If client disconnects, drop stream to cancel query.
```

## 21.16 Operator classes: pipeline-friendly vs pipeline-breaking

| Operator            | Streaming behavior                                  |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| scan/source         | usually incremental                                 |
| projection          | incremental                                         |
| filter              | incremental                                         |
| limit               | incremental and can terminate early                 |
| local repartition   | can be streaming but may buffer/reroute             |
| hash aggregate      | stateful; may emit final only depending mode        |
| global sort         | pipeline-breaking                                   |
| top-K sort          | bounded memory relative to K; still stateful        |
| hash join           | can buffer one/build side or both sides             |
| symmetric hash join | stream-stream possible with pruning/windowing       |
| window functions    | frame-dependent; finite frames more stream-friendly |
| distinct            | stateful; memory grows with distinct keys           |
| union               | incremental across inputs depending implementation  |

DataFusion’s core docs explicitly state that full sort and hash aggregation may need to consume all input before producing output, which is the key distinction between a streaming engine and every operator being non-blocking. ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/))

Agent rules:

```text id="ovng0k"
Streaming engine ≠ every query emits early.
Check physical plan for blocking operators.
Rewrite user queries for streaming:
  filter/projection early
  limit early where semantically valid
  avoid full global sort
  use bounded windows
  avoid unbounded distinct/group states
```

---

## 21.17 `execute_stream` and cancellation examples

### Timeout wrapper

```rust id="45pj80"
use tokio::time::{timeout, Duration};

let mut stream = df.execute_stream().await?;

loop {
    let next = timeout(Duration::from_secs(5), stream.next()).await;

    match next {
        Ok(Some(Ok(batch))) => process(batch).await?,
        Ok(Some(Err(e))) => return Err(e),
        Ok(None) => break,
        Err(_) => {
            drop(stream); // abort query
            return Err(datafusion::error::DataFusionError::Execution(
                "query timed out waiting for next batch".to_string(),
            ));
        }
    }
}
```

### Early termination

```rust id="vc0b33"
let mut stream = df.execute_stream().await?;
let mut rows = 0usize;

while let Some(batch) = stream.next().await {
    let batch = batch?;
    rows += batch.num_rows();

    if rows >= 10_000 {
        drop(stream); // cancel remaining work
        break;
    }
}
```

DataFusion’s Rust docs state dropping the stream aborts execution and frees allocated resources, so early termination should be implemented by dropping the stream rather than continuing to poll and discard. ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/dataframe/struct.DataFrame.html))

---

| Config                                                       | Default / role                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `datafusion.execution.batch_size`                            | default 8192 rows per new batch                |
| `datafusion.execution.target_partitions`                     | desired query parallelism / partitions         |
| `datafusion.execution.coalesce_batches`                      | whether to coalesce small batches              |
| `datafusion.execution.coalesce_target_batch_size`            | target size for coalesced batches              |
| `datafusion.execution.max_buffered_batches_per_output_file`  | write-output buffering                         |
| `datafusion.optimizer.allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning` | unbounded symmetric join pruning policy        |
| memory limit / temp path                                     | runtime resource safety for stateful streaming |

The configuration docs list these execution and optimizer settings, including batch size, target partitions, batch coalescing behavior, and the unbounded symmetric join flag. ([datafusion.apache.org](https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/configs.html))

## 21.19 Diagnostics: verifying streaming behavior

### Explain

```sql id="rhhixv"
EXPLAIN
SELECT *
FROM events
WHERE region = 'us'
LIMIT 100;
```

### Analyze

```sql id="4ilcbs"
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT *
FROM events
WHERE region = 'us'
LIMIT 100;
```

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and includes runtime metrics collected by operators, which is essential for diagnosing row flow, pruning, buffer sizes, and pipeline breakers. ([datafusion.apache.org](https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/explain-usage.html))

### Rust physical plan display

```rust id="655pww"

let physical = df.create_physical_plan().await?;
println!("{}", displayable(physical.as_ref()).indent(true));
```

### What to inspect

```text id="10jj6c"
[ ] SortExec present?
[ ] AggregateExec partial/final shape?
[ ] HashJoinExec vs SymmetricHashJoinExec vs SortMergeJoinExec?
[ ] RepartitionExec inserted?
[ ] CoalesceBatchesExec inserted?
[ ] DataSourceExec partition count?
[ ] FilterExec above scan or pushed down?
[ ] boundedness/emission properties in custom nodes?
[ ] EXPLAIN ANALYZE row counts per operator?
```

## 21.20 Stream-friendly SQL patterns

### Good: projection + filter + limit

```sql id="iwxkd9"
SELECT event_id, event_ts
FROM events
WHERE region = 'us'
LIMIT 1000;
```

### Good: bounded top-K

```sql id="shg3fl"
SELECT event_id, score
FROM events
WHERE event_date = DATE '2026-05-22'
ORDER BY score DESC, event_id ASC
LIMIT 100;
```

### Good: time-bucketed aggregation over bounded source

```sql id="ckjnwa"
SELECT
  date_bin(INTERVAL '5 minutes', event_ts, TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01') AS bucket,
  count(*) AS n
FROM events
WHERE event_date = DATE '2026-05-22'
GROUP BY bucket
ORDER BY bucket;
```

### Risky for unbounded streams

```sql id="nl70bg"
SELECT *
FROM events
ORDER BY event_ts;
```

```sql id="lfr96j"
SELECT count(*)
FROM unbounded_events;
```

```sql id="0pzbpw"
SELECT DISTINCT user_id
FROM unbounded_events;
```

```text id="csvqjz"
Add LIMIT where acceptable.
Replace full global sort with top-K if possible.

Avoid unbounded DISTINCT.
```

## 21.23 Anti-pattern inventory

* Using `collect()` in a service endpoint for arbitrary queries.
* Assuming every query emits before consuming all input.
* Assuming batch size is exactly 8192.
* Returning one huge batch from a custom stream.
* Doing blocking I/O directly in stream poll without offloading.
* Spawning producer tasks that continue after stream drop.
* Marking unbounded sources as bounded.
* Using global `ORDER BY` over unbounded data.
* Using unbounded `COUNT(*)` and expecting completion.
* Joining two unbounded streams without pruning/window constraints.
* Ignoring `allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning` risk in unbounded joins.
* Treating partition-local ordering as global ordering.
* Not handling `Err` stream items.
* Converting every `RecordBatch` to rows eagerly when Arrow batch output is acceptable.
* Testing only `collect()` and never `execute_stream()`.

---

```text id="jb9p2b"
[ ] Use execute_stream_partitioned when partition identity matters.
[ ] Never assume exact batch size.
[ ] Configure batch_size for throughput/latency tradeoff.
[ ] Implement custom streams with RecordBatchStreamAdapter where possible.
[ ] Ensure stream.schema() matches all yielded batches.
[ ] Keep execute() lightweight; do work during stream polling.
[ ] Avoid blocking Tokio; offload blocking sources.
[ ] Use bounded channels for producer/consumer bridges.
[ ] Drop stream to cancel execution.
[ ] Set Boundedness and EmissionType correctly for custom plans.
[ ] Inspect EXPLAIN for blocking operators.
[ ] Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE for row-flow/runtime metrics.
[ ] For unbounded sources, restrict query shapes to stream-friendly operators.
[ ] For joins on streams, require pruning/order/window constraints.
```

## 21.25 Morsel-driven scans and file-stream work stealing (introduced in 54; revised in DataFusion 55)

DataFusion file scans can share a per-execution queue of unopened files across sibling output partitions. A fast partition can therefore take work that would otherwise be stranded behind a slow sibling, reducing skew from uneven file sizes.

### DataFusion 55 control plane

DataFusion 55 adds an explicit execution option:

```text
datafusion.execution.enable_file_stream_work_stealing = true   # default
```

`FileScanConfig::create_sibling_state(&ConfigOptions)` returns no shared sibling state when **any** of these are true:

```text
preserve_order == true
output_partitioning.is_some()
enable_file_stream_work_stealing == false
```

Otherwise sibling streams may share `SharedWorkSource` state and dynamically reassign unopened files.

`FileScanConfig::partitioned_by_file_group` was removed in 55. If file groups themselves define an output-partitioning contract, declare that contract through `FileScanConfig::output_partitioning` / `FileScanConfigBuilder::with_output_partitioning`. A declared output partitioning both tells the optimizer what partitioning exists and prevents file-group reshuffling that would violate the partition-to-file-group contract.

### Distributed execution rule

Executors such as Ballista-style/distributed runtimes that execute plan partitions as isolated tasks rather than polling sibling partitions in one process should set:

```text
datafusion.execution.enable_file_stream_work_stealing = false
```

so each output partition reads only its own planned file group. Do not attempt to preserve this behavior using the removed `partitioned_by_file_group` flag.

### Agent checklist

```text
Use work stealing for in-process sibling scan partitions when file order/distribution allows it.
Disable it for isolated per-partition distributed execution.
Use output_partitioning to declare a real file-group partitioning contract.
Use preserve_order when execution correctness depends on planned file order.
Do not rely on deterministic file->partition assignment when work stealing is enabled.
```


# DataFusion Advanced — 22) Query optimizer

Style target follows the uploaded advanced-reference pattern. 

## 22.0 Optimizer mental model

```text id="sxtcu1"
SQL / DataFrame / LogicalPlanBuilder
  → initial LogicalPlan
      ├─ AnalyzerRule / function rewrites
      │   └─ semantic validity: type coercion, grouping resolution, function rewrites
      ├─ OptimizerRule
      │   └─ semantic-preserving logical rewrites
      │      projection pushdown, predicate pushdown, limit pushdown,
      │      expression simplification, join rewrites, subquery decorrelation, ...
      ├─ PhysicalPlanner
      │   └─ ExecutionPlan
      └─ PhysicalOptimizerRule
          └─ physical rewrites
             distribution, ordering, join selection, TopK, pushdown, coalescing, ...
```

DataFusion has analyzer rules, logical optimizer rules, and physical optimizer rules. Analyzer rules make a logical plan valid for later planning, logical optimizer rules rewrite `LogicalPlan`s and expressions while preserving results, and physical optimizer rules rewrite `ExecutionPlan`s while preserving results. The official optimizer guide says DataFusion contains extensive `OptimizerRule`s and `PhysicalOptimizerRule`s that may rewrite plans/expressions so they run faster while computing the same result. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 22.1 Value case

| Optimization family         | Value                                                                  |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| analyzer rules              | make plan valid: type coercion, grouping resolution, function rewrites |
| expression simplification   | replace constants/algebraic no-ops before execution                    |
| predicate pushdown          | fewer rows flow through the plan                                       |
| projection pushdown         | fewer columns scanned/copied/materialized                              |
| limit pushdown              | stop earlier; enable top-K / limited operators                         |
| join reordering             | reduce intermediate result size and runtime                            |
| physical distribution rules | add/remove repartitioning to meet join/aggregate requirements          |
| physical ordering rules     | add/remove sorts, exploit source/order properties                      |
| dynamic filters             | feed runtime TopK/join/aggregate state back into scans to skip work    |
| statistics-aware planning   | better join/order/scan/pruning decisions                               |
| custom rules                | domain-specific rewrites and source-aware improvements                 |

Predicate pushdown moves filters earlier so fewer rows are processed; projection pushdown keeps only needed columns earlier, especially valuable for columnar formats like Parquet; limit pushdown pushes row limits earlier and can replace full sort + limit with TopK-like execution. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 22.2 Optimizer phases

| Phase              | Input                   | Output                            | Rule trait              | Can change semantics?                    |
| ------------------ | ----------------------- | --------------------------------- | ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Analyzer           | initial `LogicalPlan`   | valid analyzed `LogicalPlan`      | `AnalyzerRule`          | may resolve/transform to valid semantics |
| Logical optimizer  | valid `LogicalPlan`     | faster equivalent `LogicalPlan`   | `OptimizerRule`         | must preserve result semantics           |
| Physical planner   | optimized `LogicalPlan` | `ExecutionPlan`                   | `PhysicalPlanner`       | lowers semantics to algorithms           |
| Physical optimizer | `ExecutionPlan`         | faster equivalent `ExecutionPlan` | `PhysicalOptimizerRule` | must preserve result semantics           |

DataFusion’s architecture docs describe planning as: analyzer rules enforce semantic rules such as type coercion; optimizer rules rewrite logical plans such as projection/filter pushdown; the physical planner creates an execution plan; physical optimizer rules such as sort and join selection improve that execution plan. ([Docs.rs][3])

---

## 22.3 Analyzer rules

### Role

```text id="rrigaf"
AnalyzerRule:
  initial LogicalPlan
    → semantically valid LogicalPlan
```

`AnalyzerRule`s transform `LogicalPlan`s to make them valid before the rest of the optimizer runs. They differ from `OptimizerRule`s because optimizer rules must preserve existing logical semantics, while analyzer rules may resolve expressions into more specific forms or do type coercion to ensure operand types are valid. Built-in analyzer rule implementors include function rewrites, grouping-function resolution, and type coercion. ([Docs.rs][4])

### Trait shape

```rust id="ep8gef"
use std::fmt::Debug;

use datafusion::common::{config::ConfigOptions, Result};
use datafusion::logical_expr::LogicalPlan;
use datafusion::optimizer::analyzer::AnalyzerRule;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyAnalyzerRule;

impl AnalyzerRule for MyAnalyzerRule {
    fn analyze(
        &self,
        plan: LogicalPlan,
        config: &ConfigOptions,
    ) -> Result<LogicalPlan> {
        // rewrite plan into a semantically valid/analyzed form
        Ok(plan)
    }

    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "my_analyzer_rule"
    }
}
```

The released 55.0.0 `AnalyzerRule` trait requires `analyze(plan, config) -> Result<LogicalPlan>` and `name() -> &str`; use `SessionState::add_analyzer_rule` to register additional analyzer rules. ([Docs.rs][4])

### Analyzer use cases

```text id="j2fj2p"
type coercion
function rewrite, e.g. syntax/operator → function call
grouping function resolution
custom semantic validation
domain-specific expression normalization required before optimizer rules
custom placeholder / parameter semantics
```

### Agent rules

```text id="up2fc6"
Use AnalyzerRule only when the input plan is not yet semantically ready.
Use OptimizerRule for performance-only rewrites.
Analyzer rules may change semantic representation but must preserve user-intended query meaning.
Analyzer rules must run before logical optimizer assumptions are relied on.
```

---

## 22.4 Logical optimizer rules

### Role

```text id="qdx7vx"
OptimizerRule:
  LogicalPlan -> LogicalPlan
  same results, better plan
```

`OptimizerRule` transforms one `LogicalPlan` into another that computes the same result, possibly more efficiently. If no transformation applies, the rule must return the input unchanged; the optimizer calls `rewrite` repeatedly until a fixed point, so returning `Transformed::no` when nothing changed is important. ([Docs.rs][5])

### Trait shape

```rust id="42xwcm"
use datafusion::common::{
    tree_node::Transformed,
    Result,
};
use datafusion::logical_expr::LogicalPlan;
use datafusion::optimizer::{OptimizerConfig, OptimizerRule};

#[derive(Default, Debug)]
struct MyOptimizerRule;

impl OptimizerRule for MyOptimizerRule {
    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "my_optimizer_rule"
    }

    fn rewrite(
        &self,
        plan: LogicalPlan,
        config: &dyn OptimizerConfig,
    ) -> Result<Transformed<LogicalPlan>> {
        // Return Transformed::yes(new_plan) if changed.
        // Return Transformed::no(plan) if unchanged.
        Ok(Transformed::no(plan))
    }
}
```

The `OptimizerRule` trait exposes `name`, `apply_order`, `supports_rewrite` (deprecated), and `rewrite`; docs warn rules should avoid function-name-specific transformations because UDFs can override names and semantics, and should use function implementation traits where possible. ([Docs.rs][5])

---

## 22.5 Physical optimizer rules

### Role

```text id="csiaj0"
PhysicalOptimizerRule:
  Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan> -> Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>
  same results, better executable plan
```

`PhysicalOptimizerRule` transforms an `ExecutionPlan` into a more efficient plan that computes the same results. Required methods are `optimize(plan, config)`, `name()`, and `schema_check()`. `schema_check()` tells the physical optimizer whether to validate that the rule did not change the plan schema; some rules may alter nullable properties and should disable schema checking. ([Docs.rs][6])

### Trait shape

```rust id="0ybkwv"
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::common::{config::ConfigOptions, Result};
use datafusion::physical_optimizer::PhysicalOptimizerRule;
use datafusion::physical_plan::ExecutionPlan;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyPhysicalRule;

impl PhysicalOptimizerRule for MyPhysicalRule {
    fn optimize(
        &self,
        plan: Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>,
        config: &ConfigOptions,
    ) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        Ok(plan)
    }

    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "my_physical_rule"
    }

    fn schema_check(&self) -> bool {
        true
    }
}
```

The physical optimizer module includes rules for limit pushdown, projection pushdown, sort pushdown, sanity checking, aggregation-related optimizations, and output/distribution requirements; the module docs also state that `SanityCheckPlan` rejects non-runnable plans with infinite sources and checks ordering/distribution requirements. ([Docs.rs][7])

---

## 22.6 Running the logical optimizer manually

```rust id="yx42jg"
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::logical_expr::{col, lit, LogicalPlan, LogicalPlanBuilder};
use datafusion::optimizer::{Optimizer, OptimizerContext, OptimizerRule};

let initial_logical_plan = LogicalPlanBuilder::empty(false)
    .project(vec![(lit(1i64) + lit(2i64)).alias("x")])?
    .build()?;

let rules: Vec<Arc<dyn OptimizerRule + Send + Sync>> = vec![
    Arc::new(MyOptimizerRule::default()),
];

let optimizer = Optimizer::with_rules(rules);
let config = OptimizerContext::new().with_max_passes(16);

let optimized_plan = optimizer.optimize(
    initial_logical_plan.clone(),
    &config,
    |plan: &LogicalPlan, rule: &dyn OptimizerRule| {
        println!("after {}:\n{}", rule.name(), plan.display_indent());
    },
)?;
```

The optimizer guide demonstrates creating an optimizer with custom rules, using `OptimizerContext::new().with_max_passes(16)`, and supplying an observer callback that prints the plan after each rule application. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 22.7 Registering custom rules in `SessionState`

```rust id="8p3y41"
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::execution::session_state::SessionStateBuilder;
use datafusion::prelude::*;

let state = SessionStateBuilder::new()
    .with_default_features()
    .with_optimizer_rule(Arc::new(MyOptimizerRule::default()))
    .with_physical_optimizer_rule(Arc::new(MyPhysicalRule))
    .build();

let ctx = SessionContext::from(state);
```

`OptimizerRule` docs say additional logical optimizer rules can be registered on `SessionState`; physical optimizer docs similarly state additional `PhysicalOptimizerRule`s can be registered on `SessionState`. In codebases using `SessionStateBuilder`, prefer central rule registration during engine construction rather than ad hoc mutation after queries are planned. ([Docs.rs][5])

---

## 22.8 Rule ordering and fixed points

```text id="mb92dh"
optimizer pass:
  for rule in rules:
    apply rule
    if changed:
      continue
  repeat until fixed point or max passes
```

`OptimizerRule::rewrite` docs state the optimizer calls `rewrite` several times until a fixed point is reached, so rules must return `Transformed::no` when the output is unchanged. `OptimizerRule::apply_order()` can specify how the rule should be applied; if it returns `None`, the rule must handle recursion itself. ([Docs.rs][5])

Agent rules:

```text id="jx92hk"
Return Transformed::no for no-op.
Avoid oscillating rewrites: A -> B -> A.
Keep rules idempotent when possible.
Use max_passes as a guard, not as a correctness crutch.
Rule order matters when rules expose opportunities for later rules.
```

---

## 22.9 Expression rewrites and constant folding

### Example rewrite: `BETWEEN` → comparisons

```rust id="7owrcv"
use datafusion::common::{
    tree_node::{Transformed, TreeNode},
    Result,
};
use datafusion::logical_expr::{Between, Expr};

fn rewrite_between(expr: Expr) -> Result<Transformed<Expr>> {
    expr.transform_up(|expr| {
        let Expr::Between(Between {
            negated,
            expr,
            low,
            high,
        }) = expr
        else {
            return Ok(Transformed::no(expr));
        };

        if negated {
            Ok(Transformed::no(Expr::Between(Between::new(
                expr, negated, low, high,
            ))))
        } else {
            let rewritten = expr.clone()
                .gt_eq(*low)
                .and(expr.lt_eq(*high));

            Ok(Transformed::yes(rewritten))
        }
    })
}
```

The optimizer guide shows this `BETWEEN` rewrite pattern using the `TreeNode` API and `transform_up`, and it also shows `EXPLAIN VERBOSE` demonstrating type coercion and expression simplification reducing `CAST(1 + 2.2 AS string)` into the constant `"3.2"`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Expression-name preservation

```rust id="sua60y"
// Semantically simplify:
lit(1i64) + lit(2i64)  ->  lit(3i64)

// But preserve output field name:
lit(3i64).alias("Int64(1) + Int64(2)")
```

DataFusion identifies columns by expression names inside logical plans, subqueries, and output schemas, so optimizer rewrites must preserve expression names. The optimizer guide explicitly says expression names must not change when rewriting expressions, typically by adding an alias; it shows `1 + 2` optimized to `3 AS "1 + 2"`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rules:

```text id="q5q8vs"
Use canonical_name for expression equivalence.
Use display_name for schema/output field names.
When simplifying an output expression, alias it to the original display name.
Do not drop aliases in optimizer rewrites.
Do not duplicate volatile expressions.
```

---

## 22.10 Predicate / filter pushdown

### Logical purpose

```text id="04p2qq"
Filter above expensive plan:
  Aggregate
    Filter(city = 'BOSTON')
      Scan

better:
  Aggregate
    Scan with filter city = 'BOSTON'
```

Predicate pushdown moves filters down so they run earlier; the optimizer blog notes that earlier filtering reduces work for the rest of the plan and can combine with partition/storage pruning. It gives the example of pushing a `HAVING city = 'BOSTON'` predicate before aggregation because filtering first avoids computing all cities. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

### TableProvider interaction

```rust id="tmx28u"
fn supports_filters_pushdown(
    &self,
    filters: &[&Expr],
) -> Result<Vec<TableProviderFilterPushDown>> {
    Ok(filters.iter().map(|f| {
        if source_can_exactly_apply(f) {
            TableProviderFilterPushDown::Exact
        } else if source_can_prune_partitions(f) {
            TableProviderFilterPushDown::Inexact
        } else {
            TableProviderFilterPushDown::Unsupported
        }
    }).collect())
}
```

### Agent rules

```text id="vvdnnn"
Exact pushdown: source enforces predicate exactly; residual filter can be removed.
Inexact pushdown: source prunes candidates; DataFusion must retain residual FilterExec.
Unsupported: DataFusion evaluates the filter.
Do not claim Exact unless SQL null semantics are preserved.
```

---

## 22.11 Projection pushdown

### Logical purpose

```text id="i3dfc8"
Projection high in plan:
  Projection(a)
    Filter(b > 10)
      Scan(a,b,c,d,e)

better:
  Projection(a)
    Filter(b > 10)
      Scan(a,b)   -- c,d,e not needed
```

Projection pushdown moves column narrowing earlier so unused columns are not copied/scanned/materialized. The optimizer blog emphasizes this is especially powerful for columnar storage such as Parquet, where readers can fetch only required columns; it is still useful but less effective for row formats such as JSON/CSV. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

### Physical projection pushdown

The physical optimizer module documents `ProjectionPushdown`, which tries to push projections down through physical operators, and if a projection reaches a source it can disappear from the plan entirely. ([Docs.rs][7])

### Agent rules

```text id="8jaebp"
Avoid SELECT * in generated SQL.
Track columns needed by final projection, filters, joins, group keys, sorts, windows.
Custom TableProvider must map projection indices to remote selected fields.
For nested Parquet, project nested leaves where supported.
```

---

## 22.12 Limit pushdown and TopK

### Logical purpose

```text id="eefk4p"
Full sort + limit:
  Limit 10
    Sort by ts DESC
      Scan all rows

TopK / limit-aware:
  TopK 10 by ts DESC
    Scan with early-stop / dynamic pruning where possible
```

Limit pushdown pushes row limits earlier so the plan can stop generating data sooner. The optimizer blog notes a classic example: replacing a full sort + limit with a TopK operator that tracks only top values using a heap, and that DataFusion’s Parquet reader can stop opening more files once a limit has been hit. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

### Config knobs

```sql id="dk099e"
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_topk_aggregation = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_topk_repartition = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_topk_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_window_topn = false;
```

The configuration docs include top-K-related flags: `enable_topk_aggregation`, `enable_topk_repartition`, `enable_topk_dynamic_filter_pushdown`, and `enable_window_topn`; `enable_window_topn` is false by default and can improve low-cardinality partitioned row-number patterns but may regress high-cardinality cases. ([Apache DataFusion][8])

### Agent rules

```text id="9x4gga"
ORDER BY + LIMIT is a top-K candidate.
Add deterministic tie-breakers for correctness.
Do not assume LIMIT without ORDER BY means top-K.
For window row_number filters, test enable_window_topn under workload cardinality.
```

## 22.13 Dynamic filter pushdown

### Concept

```text id="sf892g"
Runtime operator state:
  TopK current cutoff
  Join build-side key/range/filter state
  Aggregate state

→ dynamic filter

→ scan operator / file scan
  skip files / row groups / pages / rows that cannot match current runtime constraint
```

DataFusion’s config docs describe dynamic filters as filters generated by operators such as TopK, Join, and Aggregate and pushed into the file scan phase; the example is `ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 10`, where once the current TopK contains 10 timestamps from 2025, files containing only 2024 timestamps can be skipped. The same config group includes umbrella `enable_dynamic_filter_pushdown` plus specific TopK, join, and aggregate dynamic filter flags. ([Apache DataFusion][8])

### Config

```sql id="6gk28x"
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_topk_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_join_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_aggregate_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
```

`enable_dynamic_filter_pushdown` suppresses or overrides the component-specific dynamic-filter flags according to the config docs; treat it as the umbrella control in service profiles. ([Apache DataFusion][8])

### TopK dynamic filter value case

The 2025 dynamic-filter blog reports that TopK dynamic filters improved a common “last K traces” pattern by more than 10x in one motivating production-like workflow, and its example shows TopK passing a current timestamp threshold to scans so files/rows outside the current candidate range can be skipped. ([Apache DataFusion][9])

### Agent rules

```text id="1slm7d"
Dynamic filters help most when:
  scan source has pruning metadata
  query has ORDER BY LIMIT / selective join / aggregate-derived constraints
  source can skip files/row groups/pages

Dynamic filters help less when:
  source cannot prune
  data is unsorted/random relative to dynamic predicate
  predicate column has no useful metadata
  overhead exceeds skipped work
```

---

## 22.14 Join optimization and cost-based choices

### Config examples

```sql id="953btw"
SET datafusion.optimizer.repartition_joins = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.filter_null_join_keys = false;
```

The configuration docs state that join-related optimizer settings influence algorithm selection; `repartition_joins` enables repartitioning by join keys to execute joins in parallel, and `filter_null_join_keys` can insert filters before joins between nullable and non-nullable join columns but may add overhead when the file format does not fully support predicate pushdown. ([Apache DataFusion][8])

### Join reordering / cost-based planning concept

```text id="iwii54"
Inputs:
  statistics:
    row counts
    byte sizes
    column min/max / distinct estimates
  predicates:
    join keys
    filters
  config:
    join algorithm preferences
    repartition settings
    null-key filtering
Output:
  join order
  join algorithm
  repartition/sort requirements
```

Statistics matter for join ordering and cost-based choices. DataFusion’s architecture docs state physical plans include concrete execution choices such as hash vs merge join and partitioning/sortedness, while `PruningPredicate` and statistical information can prove some filters can never be true. ([Docs.rs][3])

### Agent rules

```text id="na918c"
Expose accurate TableProvider statistics if building custom sources.
Keep join keys typed and cast-compatible.
Prefer equality predicates for hash/repartition joins.
Avoid hiding join keys inside functions when source/optimizer cannot reason about them.
Test join plans under EXPLAIN for large-table workloads.
```

## 22.15 Statistics

### Sources

```text id="bvkgcm"
TableProvider::statistics()
Parquet metadata statistics
catalog/metastore row counts
custom provider estimates
runtime metrics from EXPLAIN ANALYZE
```

Statistics support pruning, cost decisions, and custom optimizer rules. DataFusion’s architecture notes that pruning predicates can prove filters can never be true using statistical information, and the optimizer configs include several statistics-sensitive optimizations such as Parquet pruning and dynamic scan filters. ([Docs.rs][3])

### Agent rules

```text id="dxynfe"
Unknown statistics are safer than wrong exact statistics.
Use conservative estimates for custom providers.
Expose min/max/null counts only if semantics are reliable.
Refresh stale catalog statistics deliberately.
Avoid leaking sensitive distribution metadata through public information_schema or diagnostics.
```

## 22.16 Cost-based vs rule-based optimization

| Type              | Example                                                                     | Input required                            |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| always-good rule  | expression simplification, projection pushdown, predicate pushdown          | plan shape/expression semantics           |
| cost-aware choice | join reordering, join algorithm choice, repartitioning, file repartitioning | statistics, config, physical properties   |
| runtime/dynamic   | dynamic filter pushdown                                                     | operator runtime state + scan integration |

The optimizer blog classifies expression simplification, predicate pushdown, and limit pushdown as “always optimizations” that are generally always worth doing, while other choices depend more heavily on workload, statistics, and physical layout. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

Agent rules:

```text id="2vsi8a"
Always-on rules should be semantic-preserving and broadly beneficial.
Cost-aware rules must degrade safely when stats are unknown.
Runtime/dynamic rules need source/operator integration and metrics.
```

## 22.18 Custom logical optimizer rule: expression simplifier example

```rust id="7y7rii"
use datafusion::common::{
    tree_node::{Transformed, TreeNode},
    Result,
};
use datafusion::logical_expr::{Expr, LogicalPlan};
use datafusion::optimizer::{OptimizerConfig, OptimizerRule};

#[derive(Debug, Default)]
struct RewriteBetweenRule;

impl OptimizerRule for RewriteBetweenRule {
    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "rewrite_between_rule"
    }

    fn rewrite(
        &self,
        plan: LogicalPlan,
        _config: &dyn OptimizerConfig,
    ) -> Result<Transformed<LogicalPlan>> {
        plan.transform_up(|plan| {
            let transformed = plan.map_expressions(|expr| rewrite_between(expr))?;
            Ok(transformed)
        })
    }
}

fn rewrite_between(expr: Expr) -> Result<Transformed<Expr>> {
    expr.transform_up(|expr| {
        if let Expr::Between(between) = expr {
            if between.negated {
                return Ok(Transformed::no(Expr::Between(between)));
            }

            let rewritten = between.expr.clone()
                .gt_eq(*between.low)
                .and(between.expr.lt_eq(*between.high));

            // If this expression contributes to an output schema, preserve name at caller layer.
            Ok(Transformed::yes(rewritten))
        } else {
            Ok(Transformed::no(expr))
        }
    })
}
```

The `TreeNode` API is the documented approach for walking and rewriting expression and plan trees; the optimizer guide’s `BETWEEN` example uses bottom-up `transform_up` to rewrite expressions while returning `Transformed::yes` or `Transformed::no`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

```rust id="qn87v8"
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::common::{config::ConfigOptions, Result};
use datafusion::physical_optimizer::PhysicalOptimizerRule;
use datafusion::physical_plan::ExecutionPlan;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct RemoveMyNoOpExec;

impl PhysicalOptimizerRule for RemoveMyNoOpExec {
    fn optimize(
        &self,
        plan: Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>,
        config: &ConfigOptions,
    ) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        // transform ExecutionPlan tree;
        // preserve schema and physical semantics
        Ok(plan)
    }

    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "remove_my_noop_exec"
    }

    fn schema_check(&self) -> bool {
        true
    }
}
```

`PhysicalOptimizerRule::schema_check()` should generally be true; disable it only when a rule intentionally changes nullable schema properties and has tests proving downstream correctness. ([Docs.rs][6])

## 22.20 TableProvider pushdown integration

### Pushdown contract

```rust id="gjpnuw"
fn supports_filters_pushdown(
    &self,
    filters: &[&Expr],
) -> Result<Vec<TableProviderFilterPushDown>> {
    Ok(filters.iter().map(|f| {
        if self.can_apply_exactly(f) {
            TableProviderFilterPushDown::Exact
        } else if self.can_prune_candidates(f) {
            TableProviderFilterPushDown::Inexact
        } else {
            TableProviderFilterPushDown::Unsupported
        }
    }).collect())
}

async fn scan(
    &self,
    state: &dyn Session,
    projection: Option<&Vec<usize>>,
    filters: &[Expr],
    limit: Option<usize>,
) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
    // build custom ExecutionPlan with pushed projection/filter/limit
}
```

The optimizer can only push predicates/projections/limits into custom sources if the provider exposes accurate capabilities and `scan` implements the corresponding behavior; false `Exact` declarations can produce wrong answers, while conservative `Unsupported` leaves optimization on the table.

### Agent rules

```text id="7k12uv"
Projection pushdown: return only requested columns in requested order.
Exact predicate pushdown: source enforces predicate exactly.
Inexact predicate pushdown: source prunes but residual DataFusion filter remains.
Limit pushdown: unsafe with inexact filters unless over-fetching preserves semantics.
Statistics: expose conservative row/byte/cardinality estimates when available.
```

## 22.21 Debugging optimizer behavior

### `EXPLAIN`

```sql id="8qp6rb"
EXPLAIN
SELECT city, COUNT(*)
FROM population
GROUP BY city
HAVING city = 'BOSTON';
```

### `EXPLAIN VERBOSE`

```sql id="asxku7"
EXPLAIN VERBOSE
SELECT CAST(1 + 2.2 AS STRING) AS foo;
```

`EXPLAIN VERBOSE` shows the effect of each optimization rule. The optimizer guide shows `type_coercion` inserting a cast and `simplify_expressions` reducing a casted arithmetic expression to a constant. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`

```sql id="mu318z"
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT *
FROM hits
WHERE "URL" LIKE '%google%'
ORDER BY "EventTime"
LIMIT 10;
```

Use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` for runtime metrics after physical optimization; use `EXPLAIN VERBOSE` for logical/physical rewrite visibility. The optimizer guide specifically recommends `EXPLAIN VERBOSE` for seeing the effect of each optimizer rule. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

## 22.22 Rule testing strategy

The optimizer guide recommends unit tests in the same file as a new rule to test the rule in isolation and an integration test to test the rule as part of the overall optimization process. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Unit test: isolated rule

```rust id="3xpd1z"
#[test]
fn my_rule_rewrites_expected_plan() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let plan = make_input_plan()?;
    let rule = MyOptimizerRule::default();

    let transformed = rule.rewrite(plan, &OptimizerContext::new())?;
    assert!(transformed.transformed);

    let plan = transformed.data;
    assert_eq!(plan.display_indent().to_string(), expected);

    plan.check_invariants()?;
    Ok(())
}
```

### Integration test: optimizer pipeline

```rust id="5rtx3m"
#[tokio::test]
async fn my_rule_in_optimizer_pipeline() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let ctx = make_context_with_rule();

    let df = ctx.sql("SELECT ...").await?;
    let optimized = df.clone().into_optimized_plan()?;

    insta::assert_snapshot!(optimized.display_indent().to_string());

    let batches = df.collect().await?;
    assert_batches_eq!(expected, &batches);

    Ok(())
}
```

### Required test matrix

```text id="gemw2a"
[ ] no-op input returns Transformed::no
[ ] matching input returns Transformed::yes
[ ] rule is idempotent or converges
[ ] plan.check_invariants()
[ ] schema preserved
[ ] output expression names preserved
[ ] aliases preserved
[ ] volatile functions not duplicated/reordered
[ ] optimizer with full rule set still produces correct results
[ ] EXPLAIN VERBOSE includes expected transformation
```

---

## 22.23 Rule-ordering hazards

```text id="b4r5vy"
Rule A creates pattern for Rule B:
  A: simplify expression
  B: predicate pushdown

Rule B removes pattern expected by Rule C:
  B: projection pushdown
  C: domain-specific rewrite

Rule D oscillates:
  D1: rewrite X -> Y
  D2: rewrite Y -> X
```

Agent rules:

```text id="wmjrio"
Place domain-specific rules after analyzer/type coercion.
Place rules before physical planning if they change logical shape.
Avoid relying on display strings as matching keys.
Match on Expr/LogicalPlan structure.
Use observer callbacks and EXPLAIN VERBOSE to debug rule order.
```

## 22.27 Anti-pattern inventory

* Returning `Transformed::yes` when the plan is unchanged.
* Changing expression names during rewrites.
* Dropping aliases during expression simplification.
* Matching function names instead of function implementation semantics.
* Rewriting volatile expressions as if deterministic.
* Claiming exact predicate pushdown for approximate remote filters.
* Pushing `LIMIT` below inexact filters unsafely.
* Relying on stale/wrong statistics as exact.
* Adding custom rules without result-equivalence tests.
* Snapshotting physical plan strings across versions without pinning.
* Disabling optimizer rules globally to work around one query bug.
* Assuming dynamic filters help when the source cannot prune.
* Enabling `enable_window_topn` blindly for high-cardinality partitions.
* Writing physical optimizer rules that change schema while `schema_check()` returns true.
* Implementing custom logical nodes without correct `with_exprs_and_inputs`.

---
