## 22.29 Statistics-driven Top-K and new optimizer switches (DataFusion 54)

### Statistics-driven Top-K ordering and early termination

DataFusion 54 makes `ORDER BY ... LIMIT k` (Top-K) plans exploit **file/column statistics**: when statistics prove which files or partitions can possibly contribute to the top k rows, scan order is arranged to read the most promising data first, and execution terminates early once the Top-K heap provably cannot change (the running threshold also feeds the pre-existing dynamic-filter machinery, which improved in 54 rather than being introduced by it — the `*_dynamic_filter_pushdown` keys already existed in 53). Sorted-by-time telemetry with `ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT n` is the flagship case: recent files are read first and older files are skipped entirely.

### New optimizer configuration keys in 54

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_topk_repartition = true;   -- default true
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_window_topn = false;        -- default false
SET datafusion.optimizer.join_reordering = true;            -- default true
SET datafusion.optimizer.use_statistics_registry = false;   -- default false
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_unions_to_filter = false;   -- default false
```

| Key | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `enable_topk_repartition` | `true` | allows repartitioning below a Top-K so partial Top-K runs in parallel before the final merge |
| `enable_window_topn` | `false` | opt-in rewrite of `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) <= n`-style window filters into Top-N execution |
| `join_reordering` | `true` | statistics-informed join-order selection in the optimizer |
| `use_statistics_registry` | `false` | opt-in registry-backed statistics source for planning (experimental) |
| `enable_unions_to_filter` | `false` | opt-in `UnionsToFilter` rule: rewrites `UNION ALL` branches over the same source that differ only by predicate into a single scan with an OR-filter |

The `UnionsToFilter` rule (`datafusion_optimizer::unions_to_filter::UnionsToFilter`) ships in 54 but is **disabled by default** — enable it deliberately and verify plans, since collapsing unions changes partitioning and ordering properties of the plan.

Agent rules:

```text
Keep statistics collection on for Top-K-heavy workloads; early termination depends on it.
enable_window_topn and enable_unions_to_filter are opt-in: test plans before enabling in production.
Do not present the *_dynamic_filter_pushdown keys as new in 54; they pre-date it (behavior improved).
Re-baseline EXPLAIN snapshots: Top-K/repartition shapes changed between 53 and 54.
```

# DataFusion Advanced — 23) Join algorithms and join tuning

Style target follows the uploaded advanced-reference pattern. 

## 23.0 Join mental model

```text
SQL / DataFrame join
  → LogicalPlan::Join
      ├─ JoinType
      ├─ equijoin keys
      ├─ optional non-equi join filter
      └─ output projection/schema
  → logical optimizer
      ├─ predicate pushdown
      ├─ projection pushdown
      ├─ join reordering / null-key filtering
      └─ join predicate extraction
  → physical planner / physical optimizer
      ├─ HashJoinExec
      ├─ SortMergeJoinExec
      ├─ NestedLoopJoinExec
      ├─ PiecewiseMergeJoinExec
      ├─ SymmetricHashJoinExec
      └─ CrossJoinExec
  → ExecutionPlan::execute(partition, TaskContext)
      → SendableRecordBatchStream
```

DataFusion’s SQL reference documents inner, left/right/full outer, natural, cross, left/right semi, left/right anti, lateral, and left lateral joins. Its physical join module includes `HashJoinExec`, `SortMergeJoinExec`, `NestedLoopJoinExec`, `PiecewiseMergeJoinExec`, `SymmetricHashJoinExec`, and `CrossJoinExec`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 23.1 SQL join syntax map

### Inner join

```sql
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  c.customer_name
FROM orders AS o
INNER JOIN customers AS c
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
```

Inner joins return rows with matches on both sides. Use for normal equijoin relationships. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Left outer join

```sql
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  o.order_id
FROM customers AS c
LEFT OUTER JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

Left outer joins preserve all left rows and fill right columns with `NULL` where no match exists. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Right outer join

```sql
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  o.order_id
FROM customers AS c
RIGHT OUTER JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

Right outer joins preserve all right rows and fill left columns with `NULL` where no match exists. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Full outer join

```sql
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  o.order_id
FROM customers AS c
FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

Full outer joins preserve unmatched rows from both inputs, filling the missing side with `NULL`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Cross join

```sql
SELECT
  a.id AS a_id,
  b.id AS b_id
FROM a
CROSS JOIN b;
```

A cross join returns the Cartesian product. DataFusion’s `CrossJoinExec` buffers the left input in memory and streams right-side batches while combining them with the buffered left side. ([Docs.rs][2])

### Natural join

```sql
SELECT *
FROM x NATURAL JOIN y;
```

A natural join is an inner join based on common column names; if no common column names exist, DataFusion documents that it behaves like a cross join. Avoid natural joins in generated SQL unless the schema is tightly controlled. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Semi join

```sql
SELECT *
FROM customers AS c
LEFT SEMI JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

Semi joins return rows from one side that have a match on the other side and project only the preserved side’s columns. Use for existence predicates. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Anti join

```sql
SELECT *
FROM customers AS c
LEFT ANTI JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

Anti joins return rows from one side with no match on the other side and project only the preserved side’s columns. Use for non-existence predicates. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Lateral join

```sql
SELECT
  d.name AS department,
  e.name AS employee
FROM departments AS d,
LATERAL (
  SELECT employees.name
  FROM employees
  WHERE employees.dept_id = d.id
) AS e;
```

DataFusion requires the `LATERAL` keyword for correlated subqueries in `FROM`; the docs also document `LEFT JOIN LATERAL` and note limitations for outer references in lateral subquery `SELECT` lists and `HAVING`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 23.2 DataFrame join syntax

### Equijoin by column names

```rust
use datafusion::logical_expr::JoinType;
use datafusion::prelude::*;

let joined = left.join(
    right,
    JoinType::Inner,
    &["customer_id"],
    &["customer_id"],
    None,
)?;
```

### Expression join

```rust
let joined = left.join_on(
    right,
    JoinType::Inner,
    [
        col("orders.customer_id").eq(col("customers.id")),
        col("orders.region").eq(col("customers.region")),
    ],
)?;
```

### Outer join

```rust
let joined = left.join(
    right,
    JoinType::Left,
    &["customer_id"],
    &["customer_id"],
    None,
)?;
```

### Semi / anti join

```rust
let semi = left.join(
    right.clone(),
    JoinType::LeftSemi,
    &["customer_id"],
    &["customer_id"],
    None,
)?;

let anti = left.join(
    right,
    JoinType::LeftAnti,
    &["customer_id"],
    &["customer_id"],
    None,
)?;
```

Agent rules:

```text
Use join(...) for simple equijoins.
Use join_on(...) for generated composite predicates.
Use semi/anti joins for EXISTS / NOT EXISTS style logic.
Always disambiguate duplicate column names before or immediately after joins.
Use qualified columns after joining tables that share field names.
```

---

## 23.3 Logical join anatomy

```text
LogicalPlan::Join
  left: LogicalPlan
  right: LogicalPlan
  join_type: JoinType
  join_constraint: On | Using
  on: Vec<(left_col, right_col)>
  filter: Option<Expr>
  projection: Option<Vec<usize>>
  null_equality: NullEqualsNull | NullEqualsNothing
```

Physical join operators typically split predicates into **equijoin keys** and **join filters**. For example, `HashJoinExec` stores equijoin columns in `on` and non-equality filters in `filter`; `SortMergeJoinExec` similarly represents equijoin predicates separately from optional post-equi join filters. ([Docs.rs][3])

Example:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a
JOIN b
  ON a.id = b.id
 AND a.ts < b.expires_at;
```

Conceptual split:

```text
equijoin key:
  a.id = b.id

join filter:
  a.ts < b.expires_at
```

Agent rules:

```text
Equijoin keys enable hash join / sort-merge join.
Non-equi predicates become join filters or specialized range joins.
Avoid wrapping join keys in functions when a direct equality predicate is possible.
Prefer explicit ON predicates over NATURAL JOIN in generated SQL.
```

---

## 23.4 Physical join algorithm map

| Physical operator        | Best for                                                    | Main risk                                 |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `HashJoinExec`           | equijoins, enough memory for build side                     | build-side memory pressure                |
| `SortMergeJoinExec`      | equijoins with sorted inputs or memory-limited large inputs | sort cost / ordering requirements         |
| `NestedLoopJoinExec`     | non-equi joins without equijoin keys                        | O(left × right) cost; buffers left        |
| `PiecewiseMergeJoinExec` | single range predicate joins                                | experimental; sorted/buffered constraints |
| `SymmetricHashJoinExec`  | streaming/unbounded joins with range/window pruning         | buffer pruning correctness                |
| `CrossJoinExec`          | intentional Cartesian product                               | explosive output; buffers left            |

DataFusion’s join module documents these physical join implementations and their intended roles; notably, `HashJoinExec` evaluates equijoin predicates with hash tables, `SortMergeJoinExec` can join arbitrarily large sorted inputs, `NestedLoopJoinExec` targets joins without equijoin keys, `PiecewiseMergeJoinExec` targets a single range filter, and `SymmetricHashJoinExec` targets streaming contexts with hash tables on both sides. ([Docs.rs][4])

---

## 23.5 Hash join

### Physical role

```text
HashJoinExec
  left child  = build side
  right child = probe side
  on          = equijoin key pairs
  filter      = optional join filter
  join_type   = INNER / LEFT / RIGHT / FULL / SEMI / ANTI / ...
  mode        = PartitionMode
```

DataFusion documents the `HashJoinExec` left child as the build side and the right child as the probe side. The build side is hashed into a table; the probe side is filtered by that hash table. DataFusion explicitly warns that putting the smaller input on the build side is very important to minimize hash-table creation work. ([Docs.rs][3])

### SQL shape

```sql
SELECT *
FROM small_dim AS d
JOIN large_fact AS f
  ON d.id = f.dim_id;
```

Preferred physical build/probe intent:

```text
build side: small_dim
probe side: large_fact
```

### Config

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join = true;
```

`datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join` defaults to `true`; when true, the optimizer favors hash join for faster execution when sufficient memory is available, and when false, it may choose sort-merge join when more memory-efficient execution is needed. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

### Rust config

```rust
let mut config = SessionConfig::new();
config.set_bool("datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join", true)?;
let ctx = SessionContext::new_with_config(config);
```

### Agent tuning rules

```text
Good hash join:
  equality keys
  smaller build side
  enough memory for build hash table
  useful projection pushdown before join
  low-to-moderate duplicate explosion

Risky hash join:
  large build side
  skewed join keys
  high duplicate multiplicity
  wide build rows
  insufficient memory
```

### Build/probe side correction

```sql
-- Usually better if dim is smaller:
SELECT *
FROM dim
JOIN fact
  ON dim.id = fact.dim_id;
```

If the optimizer chooses the wrong build side, inspect statistics and physical plan. `HashJoinExec` exposes `swap_inputs`, and the docs note DataFusion’s default SQL interface uses this through the `JoinSelection` physical optimizer before distribution enforcement inserts repartitioning operators. ([Docs.rs][3])

---

## 23.6 Hash join partitioning and repartitioning

### Config

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.repartition_joins = true;
```

`repartition_joins` enables repartitioning joined data by join keys so joins can execute in parallel. Hash join has a `PartitionMode`; DataFusion’s docs note that partitioned hash join can split the build side across partitions, affecting optimizations such as dense-key array-map optimization. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

### Conceptual plan

```text
HashJoinExec
  RepartitionExec hash(left_key)
    left input
  RepartitionExec hash(right_key)
    right input
```

### Agent rules

```text
Enable repartition_joins for large parallel equijoins.
Avoid unnecessary repartitioning for tiny joins.
Expose accurate source partitioning when implementing custom providers.
If inputs are already partitioned on join keys, preserve partition metadata.
Check EXPLAIN for RepartitionExec placement.
```

---

## 23.7 Sort-merge join

### Physical role

```text
SortMergeJoinExec
  left/right inputs must be sorted on join keys
  on = equijoin key pairs
  filter = optional non-equi join filter
  join_type = join semantics
```

`SortMergeJoinExec` executes equijoin predicates on multiple partitions using the sort-merge join algorithm and can be used for arbitrarily large inputs where one or both inputs do not fit in available memory. It assumes both inputs are pre-sorted; sorting inputs is not the responsibility of the execution plan itself. ([Docs.rs][7])

### Config

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join = false;
```

When `prefer_hash_join` is false, DataFusion allows sort-merge join to be chosen when more memory-efficient execution is needed. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

### SQL pattern

```sql
SELECT *
FROM left_events AS l
JOIN right_events AS r
  ON l.user_id = r.user_id
ORDER BY l.user_id;
```

### Agent rules

```text
Good sort-merge join:
  inputs already sorted or cheaply sortable
  large inputs exceed hash-table memory
  downstream also needs join-key ordering
  memory-limited workloads

Risk:
  sorting cost can dominate
  wrong ordering metadata can produce incorrect plans
  spilled buffered side can increase disk I/O
```

### Memory behavior

Sort-merge join has streamed and buffered inputs. The streamed side memory depends on output batch size; buffered input is buffered for record batches with the same join key, and if memory limit is exceeded and spilling is enabled, buffered batches can spill to disk; otherwise execution fails. ([Docs.rs][7])

---

## 23.8 Nested loop join

### Physical role

```text
NestedLoopJoinExec
  designed for joins without equijoin keys
  buffers left side
  streams right side
  evaluates join filter over Cartesian candidates
```

`NestedLoopJoinExec` is a build-probe join for joins that do not have equijoin keys in their `ON` clause. It eagerly buffers left-side input batches, and right-side batches are streamed and compared against the buffered left side using the join filter. As of DataFusion 54, `NestedLoopJoinExec` supports memory-limited execution with spilling: when the buffered build side exceeds the memory budget, build-side data spills to disk through the `DiskManager` instead of aborting with an out-of-memory error (in 53 and earlier, a build side that did not fit was a hard OOM). Spilling requires a runtime with memory limits and a configured `DiskManager`; the changelog reports coverage for inner/left and right/full join types. Spill files honor `datafusion.execution.spill_compression` (`uncompressed`, `lz4_frame`, `zstd` — a key that pre-dates 54). ([Docs.rs][8])

### SQL pattern

```sql
SELECT *
FROM ranges AS r
JOIN events AS e
  ON e.ts >= r.start_ts
 AND e.ts < r.end_ts;
```

### Agent rules

```text
Nested loop is fallback for non-equi joins.
Keep left/build side small.
Avoid nested loop on two large tables.
Rewrite to equijoin + residual filter if possible.
Enable piecewise merge join for single range predicates if appropriate.
```

### Memory behavior

Nested loop always considers the left side as the build/buffered side; DataFusion docs say the physical optimizer should assign the smaller input to the left. Output buffering threshold is tied to batch size. Since DataFusion 54, memory-limited execution is implemented: the buffered build side spills to disk under memory pressure (requires memory limits plus a `DiskManager` on the runtime). ([Docs.rs][8])

---

## 23.9 Piecewise merge join

### Physical role

```text
PiecewiseMergeJoinExec
  specialized range join
  single comparison filter:
    <, <=, >, >=
  buffered side sorted
  streamed side sorted during processing
```

`PiecewiseMergeJoinExec` evaluates a single range filter and is documented as much faster than nested-loop join for these workloads. The physical planner may select it when there is exactly one comparison filter with `<`, `<=`, `>`, or `>=`; the buffered side must be sorted according to the operator, while streamed batches can be sorted during processing. ([Docs.rs][9])

### Enable

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_piecewise_merge_join = true;
```

`enable_piecewise_merge_join` defaults to `false` and enables the experimental piecewise merge join algorithm; the config docs state it can be selected when there is exactly one range filter and is faster than nested loop except for some cases where both tables are large and approximately equal in size. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

### SQL patterns

```sql
SELECT *
FROM left_table AS l
JOIN right_table AS r
  ON l.ts < r.ts;
```

```sql
SELECT *
FROM intervals AS i
JOIN events AS e
  ON e.ts >= i.start_ts;
```

### Agent rules

```text
Use only for single range-filter join shapes.
Do not expect it for compound range conditions.
Benchmark before enabling globally.
Prefer equijoin + residual filter when equality keys exist.
Avoid for two similarly large tables without benchmarks.
```

---

## 23.10 Symmetric hash join

### Physical role

```text
SymmetricHashJoinExec
  hash both input streams
  probe both directions
  range conditions can prune stale state
  designed for streaming/unbounded contexts
```

`SymmetricHashJoinExec` hashes both input streams on join keys. DataFusion’s docs describe it as efficient for streaming because it avoids scanning one or both streams for matches and can consider only elements within a sliding window when range conditions are present, enabling operation on unbounded streaming data without unbounded stale state. ([Docs.rs][10])

### Config

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning = true;
```

`allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning` controls whether symmetric hash joins are allowed for unbounded data sources when inputs lack ordering or filtering; disabling it prevents symmetric hash join plans that cannot prune internal buffers and may only produce results at the end. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

### Streaming SQL shape

```sql
SELECT *
FROM left_stream AS l
JOIN right_stream AS r
  ON l.user_id = r.user_id
 AND l.event_ts BETWEEN r.event_ts - INTERVAL '5 minutes'
                    AND r.event_ts + INTERVAL '5 minutes';
```

### Agent rules

```text
Use symmetric hash join for stream-stream joins only when pruning/window constraints exist.
Require time/range predicates or ordering that bounds state.
Avoid unbounded joins with no pruning condition.
Monitor internal buffer growth.
Inspect EXPLAIN for SymmetricHashJoinExec.
```

---

## 23.11 Cross join

### SQL

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a
CROSS JOIN b;
```

`CrossJoinExec` returns the Cartesian product, buffers the left input in memory, then streams right-side batches and combines them with the buffered left input. ([Docs.rs][2])

### Agent rules

```text
Cross join is output-multiplicative: rows = left_rows × right_rows.
Use only when intentional.
Apply filters and projections before cross join.
Use LIMIT only for exploration, not correctness.
Avoid cross joins in generated SQL unless explicitly requested.
```

---

## 23.12 Join filters

### Meaning

```text
Equijoin condition:
  a.id = b.id
  → physical on keys

Join filter:
  a.ts < b.ts
  a.score + b.score > 100
  → optional JoinFilter evaluated after/on match candidates
```

`HashJoinExec` and `SortMergeJoinExec` both expose optional filters; `SortMergeJoinExec` docs describe non-equality predicates as filter expressions evaluated after equijoin predicates. ([Docs.rs][3])

### SQL

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a
JOIN b
  ON a.id = b.id
 AND a.ts < b.ts
 AND a.region = 'us';
```

Optimizer split:

```text
equi keys:
  a.id = b.id

join filter / other pushdown candidates:
  a.ts < b.ts
  a.region = 'us'
```

Agent rules:

```text
Keep equality join keys syntactically visible.
Move single-table predicates to WHERE when possible for pushdown.
Do not hide equijoin keys in CASE/lower/cast unless required.
Non-equi filters can force nested-loop or piecewise/range algorithms.
```

---

## 23.13 Dynamic join filters

### Concept

```text
Runtime join state
  → build-side keys / ranges / min-max
  → dynamic filter
  → scan/probe side pruning
```

DataFusion’s dynamic filter config describes dynamic filters generated by operators such as TopK, Join, and Aggregate and pushed into file scans; `enable_join_dynamic_filter_pushdown` controls join-derived dynamic filters. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

### Config

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_join_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
```

### Good use case

```sql
SELECT *
FROM fact AS f
JOIN small_dim AS d
  ON f.dim_id = d.id
WHERE d.category = 'active';
```

Conceptual runtime effect:

```text
small_dim filtered keys
  → dynamic key/range filter
  → fact scan prunes irrelevant files/row groups/pages if source can use metadata
```

Agent rules:

```text
Dynamic join filters help only if scan source can prune.
Best with Parquet statistics, partition columns, or indexed custom sources.
Less useful for CSV/JSON without metadata.
Enable and benchmark under real file layout.
```

---

## 23.14 Build/probe side concerns

### Hash join

```text
HashJoinExec:
  left  = build side
  right = probe side
```

DataFusion’s `HashJoinExec` docs state the build side is the first child and the probe side is the second child, and smaller input should be placed on the build side to reduce hash-table work. ([Docs.rs][3])

### Nested loop / cross join

```text
NestedLoopJoinExec:
  left = buffered/build side
  right = streamed/probe side

CrossJoinExec:
  left = loaded in memory
  right = streamed/combined with left
```

Nested loop and cross join docs both describe buffering the left input and streaming the right input. ([Docs.rs][8])

### Sort-merge join

```text
SortMergeJoinExec:
  both inputs sorted on join keys
  streamed/probe side determined by join type
  buffered side may spill if spilling enabled
```

Sort-merge join docs describe streamed and buffered sides and note that buffered batches can spill to disk if spilling is enabled and memory is exceeded. ([Docs.rs][7])

### Agent rules

```text
Put smaller side left/build for hash, nested-loop, and cross joins when possible.
Use statistics so optimizer can choose/swap sides.
After repartitioning, avoid manual child swapping unless partition requirements are recomputed.
Project only needed columns before join to reduce build memory.
```

---

## 23.15 Join memory behavior and spilling

| Operator                 | Memory behavior                                                                                 |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `HashJoinExec`           | builds hash table from build side; memory proportional to build rows/width and key multiplicity |
| `SortMergeJoinExec`      | requires sorted inputs; buffers matching-key groups; buffered input can spill if enabled        |
| `NestedLoopJoinExec`     | buffers left side; since DataFusion 54 spills to disk under memory pressure instead of erroring |
| `CrossJoinExec`          | buffers entire left side                                                                        |
| `SymmetricHashJoinExec`  | maintains hash tables for both streams; needs pruning/window constraints to bound memory        |
| `PiecewiseMergeJoinExec` | buffers one sorted side; streams the other                                                      |

Sort-merge join has documented spill behavior for buffered batches; nested-loop join docs currently describe out-of-memory failure when left-side batches cannot fit, with memory-limited fallback as future work. ([Docs.rs][7])

### Runtime config

```rust
use datafusion::execution::{
    runtime_env::RuntimeEnvBuilder,
    session_state::SessionStateBuilder,
};
use datafusion::prelude::*;

let runtime = RuntimeEnvBuilder::new()
    .with_memory_limit(16 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024, 0.8)
    .with_temp_file_path("/mnt/ssd/datafusion-spill")
    .build_arc()?;

let state = SessionStateBuilder::new()
    .with_runtime_env(runtime)
    .with_default_features()
    .build();

let ctx = SessionContext::from(state);
```

### Agent memory rules

```text
Minimize build-side width with projection pushdown.
Filter before join.
Use semi/anti joins for existence checks.
Use sort-merge when memory-limited and sorted/sortable inputs are acceptable.
Avoid nested-loop/cross joins on large inputs.
Configure memory limit and spill path for service/batch workloads.
```

---

## 23.16 Join algorithm configuration

### SQL

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.repartition_joins = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_piecewise_merge_join = false;
SET datafusion.optimizer.allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.filter_null_join_keys = false;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_join_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
```

### Rust

```rust
let mut config = SessionConfig::new();

config.set_bool("datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join", true)?;
config.set_bool("datafusion.optimizer.repartition_joins", true)?;
config.set_bool("datafusion.optimizer.enable_piecewise_merge_join", false)?;
config.set_bool(
    "datafusion.optimizer.allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning",
    true,
)?;
config.set_bool("datafusion.optimizer.filter_null_join_keys", false)?;
config.set_bool(
    "datafusion.optimizer.enable_join_dynamic_filter_pushdown",
    true,
)?;

let ctx = SessionContext::new_with_config(config);
```

The current configuration reference documents join-specific optimizer settings including `allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning`, `prefer_hash_join`, and `enable_piecewise_merge_join`; broader optimizer settings also include join repartitioning, null-key filtering, and dynamic filter pushdown. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

---

## 23.17 Null join-key behavior

### SQL null semantics

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a
JOIN b
  ON a.key = b.key;
```

Default SQL equality does not match `NULL = NULL`. DataFusion physical joins expose `null_equality` / `NullEquality` fields, and `HashJoinExec` docs include null-aware and null-equality fields in its physical operator. ([Docs.rs][3])

### Config

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.filter_null_join_keys = true;
```

`filter_null_join_keys` can insert filters before joins where nullable and non-nullable columns are joined, but the config docs warn it may add overhead when the file format does not fully support predicate pushdown. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

### Agent rules

```text
Do not assume NULL keys match.
Use explicit null-safe logic only if the query semantics require it.
Consider filter_null_join_keys for large joins with many nullable keys.
Benchmark null-key filtering; it can add filters that do not push down well.
```

---

## 23.18 Semi/anti joins as performance tools

### Existence query

```sql
SELECT *
FROM customers AS c
LEFT SEMI JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

### Non-existence query

```sql
SELECT *
FROM customers AS c
LEFT ANTI JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

Semi and anti joins avoid materializing right-side columns and can reduce duplication compared to `JOIN + DISTINCT`. DataFusion SQL docs explicitly support left/right semi and left/right anti joins. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rules:

```text
Use SEMI for EXISTS.
Use ANTI for NOT EXISTS.
Avoid inner join + DISTINCT for existence logic.
Prefer semi/anti joins when only preserved-side columns are needed.
```

---

## 23.19 Lateral joins

### Correlated right relation

```sql
SELECT
  d.name,
  e.name
FROM departments AS d
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT name
  FROM employees
  WHERE employees.dept_id = d.id
) AS e ON true;
```

Lateral joins permit the right-hand relation to refer to columns from the left side. DataFusion docs require the `LATERAL` keyword and document `LEFT JOIN LATERAL` support. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rules:

```text
Use LATERAL for correlated FROM subqueries.
Expect less optimization freedom than ordinary joins.
Avoid lateral joins for simple equijoins; use JOIN ON.
Test physical plan and row counts carefully.
```

---

## 23.20 Natural join warning

```sql
SELECT *
FROM x NATURAL JOIN y;
```

Natural join automatically chooses common column names as join keys; if there are no common columns, it behaves like a cross join. This is dangerous for generated SQL because schema changes can silently change join predicates. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rules:

```text
Never generate NATURAL JOIN by default.
Use explicit JOIN ... ON.
If user requests natural join, snapshot common-column list before execution.
Validate output cardinality risk.
```

---

## 23.21 Join explain diagnostics

### Logical/physical explain

```sql
EXPLAIN
SELECT *
FROM fact AS f
JOIN dim AS d
  ON f.dim_id = d.id
WHERE d.category = 'active';
```

### Analyze

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT *
FROM fact AS f
JOIN dim AS d
  ON f.dim_id = d.id
WHERE d.category = 'active';
```

Inspect for:

```text
HashJoinExec vs SortMergeJoinExec vs NestedLoopJoinExec
RepartitionExec on join keys
FilterExec before join
ProjectionExec before join
build/probe side ordering
JoinFilter presence
Dynamic filter / scan filter behavior if visible
spills / memory / elapsed metrics in EXPLAIN ANALYZE
```

DataFusion’s `EXPLAIN` documentation distinguishes logical and physical plan output, and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes the query and reports operator metrics. ([Apache DataFusion][11])

---

## 23.22 Join tuning profiles

### Default analytics profile

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.repartition_joins = true;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_join_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
```

Use for equijoin-heavy bounded analytics with sufficient memory.

### Memory-limited profile

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join = false;
SET datafusion.optimizer.repartition_joins = true;
```

Use when large build-side hash tables create memory pressure and sort-merge join is acceptable.

### Range-join experimental profile

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_piecewise_merge_join = true;
```

Use only when workloads contain single range predicates and benchmarks prove benefit. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

### Streaming join profile

```sql
SET datafusion.optimizer.allow_symmetric_joins_without_pruning = false;
SET datafusion.optimizer.enable_join_dynamic_filter_pushdown = true;
```

Use for unbounded/streaming sources where buffer pruning and bounded state are required.

---

## 23.23 Query-shape rewriting rules

### Bad: function-wrapped keys

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a
JOIN b
  ON lower(a.email) = lower(b.email);
```

Better if data can be normalized earlier:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a_norm AS a
JOIN b_norm AS b
  ON a.email_norm = b.email_norm;
```

### Bad: existence through join + distinct

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT c.*
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.id = o.customer_id;
```

Better:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM customers AS c
LEFT SEMI JOIN orders AS o
  ON c.id = o.customer_id;
```

### Bad: accidental cross join

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a, b;
```

Better:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM a
JOIN b
  ON a.id = b.a_id;
```

Agent rules:

```text
Expose equality keys plainly.
Normalize join keys before join.
Prefer semi/anti for existence.
Avoid implicit comma joins.
Use explicit ON predicates.
```

---

## 23.24 Custom provider considerations for joins

If implementing a `TableProvider`, your metadata strongly affects join planning.

```text
Provide:
  accurate schema
  conservative statistics
  row count if known
  byte size if known
  sortedness if guaranteed
  partitioning if guaranteed
  filter pushdown capabilities
  projection pushdown
```

The optimizer uses statistics and physical properties to make choices such as join side, algorithm, repartitioning, and sort requirements; DataFusion physical join docs also rely on child ordering, partitioning, and memory behavior. ([Docs.rs][4])

Agent rules:

```text
Wrong stats can make the optimizer pick a bad build side.
False ordering metadata can remove necessary sorts.
False partitioning metadata can break distributed join correctness.
Unsupported filters should be Unsupported, not Exact.
```

---

## 23.25 Testing matrix

```text
[ ] inner equijoin result
[ ] left/right/full outer unmatched rows and nulls
[ ] semi/anti output schema and row count
[ ] NULL join-key behavior
[ ] duplicate key multiplicity
[ ] join filter correctness
[ ] non-equi join fallback/algorithm
[ ] piecewise merge range join if enabled
[ ] lateral join correlated semantics
[ ] natural join common-column detection if allowed
[ ] cross join row explosion safeguards
[ ] EXPLAIN operator selection
[ ] EXPLAIN ANALYZE metrics
[ ] memory-limited hash join behavior
[ ] sort-merge join with sorted inputs
[ ] streaming symmetric hash join bounded-state behavior
```

---

## 23.26 Deployment advisory

```text
Bounded analytics:
  prefer hash join by default.
  use repartition_joins for large parallel equijoins.
  provide stats for better build/probe selection.
  configure memory limit and spill path.

Memory-constrained workloads:
  consider prefer_hash_join=false.
  exploit sorted inputs.
  inspect SortMergeJoinExec plans.

Streaming/unbounded workloads:
  avoid unbounded cross/full joins.
  require time/range pruning.
  consider symmetric hash join with pruning.
  disable symmetric joins without pruning if unbounded buffers are unacceptable.

Generated SQL:
  never use NATURAL JOIN by default.
  never generate comma joins.
  use SEMI/ANTI for existence.
  qualify columns.
  alias duplicate output columns.
```

---

## 23.27 Anti-pattern inventory

* Natural join in generated SQL.
* Accidental comma/cross join.
* Joining two huge tables with no equality key and no range specialization.
* Function-wrapped join keys that block equijoin extraction.
* Wide `SELECT *` before joins.
* Build side larger than probe side in hash join.
* Relying on hash join in memory-limited settings without spill/resource planning.
* Enabling piecewise merge join globally without benchmark coverage.
* Unbounded symmetric hash join without pruning/window constraints.
* Treating join physical plan strings as stable across versions without pinning.
* Ignoring `NULL` join-key semantics.
* Using inner join + distinct for existence checks.
* Exposing lateral joins in generated SQL when simple equijoin suffices.
* False custom-source statistics leading to bad join choices.
* False ordering/partitioning metadata in custom providers.

---

## 23.28 Agent checklist

```text
[ ] Choose join type: inner / left / right / full / semi / anti / cross / lateral.
[ ] Prefer explicit JOIN ... ON.
[ ] Avoid NATURAL JOIN unless user explicitly requests it.
[ ] Avoid CROSS JOIN unless Cartesian product is intended.
[ ] Use SEMI for EXISTS and ANTI for NOT EXISTS.
[ ] Keep equijoin keys syntactically visible.
[ ] Move single-table predicates to WHERE for pushdown.
[ ] Alias/qualify duplicate columns.
[ ] Inspect EXPLAIN for HashJoinExec / SortMergeJoinExec / NestedLoopJoinExec / PiecewiseMergeJoinExec / SymmetricHashJoinExec.
[ ] For hash join, ensure smaller side can be build side.
[ ] For memory pressure, consider sort-merge join and spill configuration.
[ ] For single range predicate, optionally test piecewise merge join.
[ ] For streaming, require pruning/window constraints before symmetric hash join.
[ ] Configure repartition_joins for large parallel equijoins.
[ ] Test NULL keys, duplicate keys, outer unmatched rows, and join filters.
[ ] Validate custom provider stats/ordering/partitioning before trusting join plans.
```

## 23.29 Join and exchange operator improvements in DataFusion 54

### Nested-loop join: memory-limited execution with spilling

`NestedLoopJoinExec` gained spilling in 54 (details in §23.8 and §28.28): the buffered build side spills to disk under memory pressure instead of raising an out-of-memory error. Requirements: a runtime with memory limits and a `DiskManager`; coverage per the changelog spans inner/left and right/full join types. Spill files honor `datafusion.execution.spill_compression` (`uncompressed` / `lz4_frame` / `zstd` — a pre-54 key). A previously OOM-doomed non-equi join over a large build side now degrades to disk instead of failing, which changes capacity planning: budget spill disk, not just memory, for non-equi joins.

### Sort-merge join: match tracking and deferred filtering

`SortMergeJoinExec` received two correctness/performance overhauls in 54:

* **Per-row match tracking for semi/anti/mark joins.** Semi, anti, and mark joins track matches per row rather than per key-run, fixing edge cases and avoiding redundant filter re-evaluation across duplicate keys.
* **Batched deferred filtering for left/full outer joins.** For near-unique join keys, the join filter is applied in a batched, deferred pass instead of row-at-a-time during the merge; the changelog reports 20–50× improvements on filter-heavy SMJ workloads with mostly-unique keys.

No new configuration is involved — `prefer_hash_join = false` (or ordering-based selection) still chooses SMJ; the improvements apply automatically.

### `RepartitionExec` batch coalescing

`RepartitionExec` now coalesces small batches **before** pushing them into the per-partition distributor channels. Hash repartitioning fragments input batches into per-target slivers; under 53 those slivers crossed the channel individually and downstream operators paid per-batch overhead on tiny batches. In 54, slivers are accumulated toward `batch_size` first — the changelog reports up to 50% improvement on repartition-heavy plans (high `target_partitions` with many small input batches). This is automatic; expect fewer, larger batches at operators downstream of a repartition, and re-baseline any test asserting exact batch counts.

Agent rules:

```text
Provision spill disk for non-equi joins; NLJ now spills instead of erroring at the memory limit.
Re-run SMJ-heavy benchmarks after upgrading; deferred filtering changes the profile substantially.
Do not assert exact batch counts downstream of RepartitionExec across versions.
Spill compression applies to NLJ spill files via the pre-existing spill_compression key.
```

# DataFusion Advanced — 24) User-defined functions

## 24.0 UDF family map

```text
DataFusion function extension surface
  ├─ Scalar UDF
  │   ├─ create_udf(...)
  │   └─ ScalarUDFImpl
  ├─ Async scalar UDF
  │   └─ AsyncScalarUDFImpl
  ├─ Aggregate UDF / UDAF
  │   ├─ create_udaf(...)
  │   └─ Accumulator / GroupsAccumulator
  ├─ Window UDF / UDWF
  │   ├─ create_udwf(...)
  │   └─ PartitionEvaluator
  └─ Table UDF / UDTF
      └─ TableFunctionImpl -> Arc<dyn TableProvider>
```

DataFusion’s UDF guide classifies user-defined functions as scalar, window, aggregate, table, and async scalar functions; scalar UDFs are vectorized over Arrow arrays, table UDFs return `TableProvider`s, and async scalar UDFs are intended for async work such as network or I/O calls. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 24.1 Selection matrix

| Need                                   | Use              | Output cardinality      |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------- | ----------------------- |
| row-wise deterministic transform       | scalar UDF       | one value per input row |
| row-wise async API/I/O lookup          | async scalar UDF | one value per input row |
| custom grouped metric                  | aggregate UDF    | one value per group     |
| custom frame-aware analytic            | window UDF       | one value per input row |
| parameterized table source             | table UDF        | relation / table        |
| advanced return typing, docs, coercion | `ScalarUDFImpl`  | function-specific       |
| quick fixed-type function              | `create_udf`     | fixed return type       |

Agent default:

```text
simple scalar function       -> create_udf
production scalar function   -> ScalarUDFImpl
custom aggregate             -> create_udaf + Accumulator
custom window function       -> create_udwf + PartitionEvaluator
FROM-clause function         -> TableFunctionImpl
external async lookup        -> AsyncScalarUDFImpl
```

---

## 24.2 Core imports

```rust
use std::{any::Any, sync::Arc};

use datafusion::arrow::{
    array::{ArrayRef, Int64Array, StringArray},
    datatypes::DataType,
};
use datafusion::common::{
    cast::as_int64_array,
    plan_err,
    Result,
    ScalarValue,
};
use datafusion::logical_expr::{
    col,
    create_udf,
    create_udaf,
    create_udwf,
    ColumnarValue,
    Expr,
    ScalarFunctionArgs,
    ScalarUDF,
    ScalarUDFImpl,
    Signature,
    Volatility,
};
use datafusion::physical_plan::Accumulator;
use datafusion::prelude::*;
```

Use `datafusion::arrow` re-exports for Arrow arrays and datatypes in DataFusion UDF code to avoid Arrow version mismatches. The `datafusion 55.0.0` crate manifest declares a caret Arrow requirement of `59.2.0` — satisfied by this baseline's `59.2.0` — and DataFusion subcrates pinned at `55.0.0`, so direct subcrate use should be version-aligned. ([Docs.rs][2])

---

## 24.3 Scalar UDFs: vectorized Arrow input/output

Scalar UDFs are logically row-wise, but physically batch/vector functions: DataFusion passes Arrow arrays or scalar constants and expects an Arrow-compatible result with the same row count for array output. The UDF guide explicitly states scalar UDFs get one or more Arrow arrays as input and produce an Arrow array with the same number of rows as output. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### 24.3.1 Minimal scalar UDF with `create_udf`

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::arrow::array::{ArrayRef, Int64Array};
use datafusion::arrow::datatypes::DataType;
use datafusion::common::{cast::as_int64_array, Result};
use datafusion::logical_expr::{create_udf, ColumnarValue, Volatility};
use datafusion::prelude::*;

fn add_one(args: &[ColumnarValue]) -> Result<ColumnarValue> {
    if args.len() != 1 {
        return datafusion::common::plan_err!("add_one expects exactly one argument");
    }

    // Simpler but less optimal: scalar constants are expanded into arrays.
    let arrays = ColumnarValue::values_to_arrays(args)?;
    let input = as_int64_array(&arrays[0])?;

    let output = input
        .iter()
        .map(|v| v.map(|x| x + 1))
        .collect::<Int64Array>();

    Ok(ColumnarValue::Array(Arc::new(output) as ArrayRef))
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let ctx = SessionContext::new();

    let udf = create_udf(
        "add_one",
        vec![DataType::Int64],
        DataType::Int64,
        Volatility::Immutable,
        Arc::new(add_one),
    );

    ctx.register_udf(udf);

    ctx.sql("SELECT add_one(41) AS answer")
        .await?
        .show()
        .await?;

    Ok(())
}
```

`create_udf` takes the SQL function name, accepted argument `DataType`s, return `DataType`, volatility, and function implementation; the resulting `ScalarUDF` must be registered with `SessionContext::register_udf` before SQL can call it by name. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### 24.3.2 Scalar UDF test against Arrow arrays

```rust
#[test]
fn add_one_direct_arrow_test() -> datafusion::common::Result<()> {
    let input = ColumnarValue::Array(
        Arc::new(Int64Array::from(vec![Some(1), None, Some(3)])) as ArrayRef,
    );

    let output = add_one(&[input])?;
    let output = output.into_array(3)?;

    let output = output
        .as_any()
        .downcast_ref::<Int64Array>()
        .expect("Int64Array");

    assert_eq!(output, &Int64Array::from(vec![Some(2), None, Some(4)]));
    Ok(())
}
```

The UDF guide demonstrates direct Arrow-array testing by constructing an `Int64Array`, wrapping it in `ColumnarValue`, invoking the function, converting the result back into an array, downcasting, and asserting null-preserving output. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 24.4 `ScalarUDFImpl`: production scalar UDF API

Use `ScalarUDFImpl` when the function needs advanced signatures, named arguments, return-type inference, custom return fields/nullability, scalar-fast paths, optimizer simplification, documentation metadata, aliases, or configuration-sensitive behavior. `ScalarUDFImpl` exposes the full API for scalar UDF implementation, while `ScalarUDF` is the logical wrapper DataFusion uses for planning and invocation. ([Docs.rs][3])

### 24.4.1 Required method skeleton

```rust
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct AddOne {
    signature: Signature,
}

impl AddOne {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            signature: Signature::uniform(
                1,
                vec![DataType::Int64],
                Volatility::Immutable,
            ),
        }
    }
}

impl ScalarUDFImpl for AddOne {
    // DataFusion 54: no `fn as_any` — `Any` is a supertrait of ScalarUDFImpl.

    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "add_one"
    }

    fn signature(&self) -> &Signature {
        &self.signature
    }

    fn return_type(&self, arg_types: &[DataType]) -> Result<DataType> {
        match arg_types {
            [DataType::Int64] => Ok(DataType::Int64),
            _ => plan_err!("add_one only accepts Int64"),
        }
    }

    fn invoke_with_args(&self, args: ScalarFunctionArgs) -> Result<ColumnarValue> {
        if args.args.len() != 1 {
            return plan_err!("add_one expects exactly one argument");
        }

        match &args.args[0] {
            ColumnarValue::Scalar(ScalarValue::Int64(Some(v))) => {
                Ok(ColumnarValue::Scalar(ScalarValue::Int64(Some(v + 1))))
            }
            ColumnarValue::Scalar(ScalarValue::Int64(None)) => {
                Ok(ColumnarValue::Scalar(ScalarValue::Int64(None)))
            }
            _ => {
                let arrays = ColumnarValue::values_to_arrays(&args.args)?;
                let input = as_int64_array(&arrays[0])?;

                let output = input
                    .iter()
                    .map(|v| v.map(|x| x + 1))
                    .collect::<Int64Array>();

                Ok(ColumnarValue::Array(Arc::new(output) as ArrayRef))
            }
        }
    }
}

let add_one = ScalarUDF::from(AddOne::new());
```

`ScalarUDFImpl` requires `name`, `signature`, `return_type`, and `invoke_with_args`; in DataFusion 54 the trait declares `Any` as a supertrait (`ScalarUDFImpl: Debug + DynEq + DynHash + Send + Sync + Any`), so no `as_any` method is written — the same applies to `AggregateUDFImpl` and `WindowUDFImpl`. The docs emphasize that `invoke_with_args` should handle `ColumnarValue::Scalar` for performance; `ColumnarValue::values_to_arrays` is simpler but can be slower because it expands constants into arrays. ([Docs.rs][4])

### 24.4.2 Register and invoke

```rust
let ctx = SessionContext::new();

let add_one = ScalarUDF::from(AddOne::new());
ctx.register_udf(add_one.clone());

// DataFrame / Expr invocation
let expr = add_one.call(vec![col("a")]);

// SQL invocation
let df = ctx.sql("SELECT add_one(a) AS a_plus_one FROM t").await?;
```

`ScalarUDF::call` creates an `Expr` that invokes the function, while `SessionContext::register_udf` registers the function for SQL and name-based resolution. ([Docs.rs][3])

---

## 24.5 Signatures

A `Signature` contains a `TypeSignature`, `Volatility`, and optional parameter names. It defines which argument types a function accepts and enables named-argument notation when parameter names are provided. ([Docs.rs][5])

### Common constructors

```rust
let sig = Signature::exact(
    vec![DataType::Int64, DataType::Utf8],
    Volatility::Immutable,
);

let sig = Signature::uniform(
    2,
    vec![DataType::Int64, DataType::Float64],
    Volatility::Immutable,
);

let sig = Signature::numeric(1, Volatility::Immutable);
let sig = Signature::string(2, Volatility::Immutable);
let sig = Signature::variadic(vec![DataType::Utf8], Volatility::Immutable);
let sig = Signature::variadic_any(Volatility::Volatile);
let sig = Signature::any(1, Volatility::Stable);
let sig = Signature::one_of(vec![/* TypeSignature variants */], Volatility::Immutable);
let sig = Signature::user_defined(Volatility::Immutable);
```

Current `Signature` constructors include `new`, `variadic`, `user_defined`, `numeric`, `string`, `variadic_any`, `uniform`, `exact`, `coercible`, `comparable`, `nullary`, `any`, `one_of`, and array-specialized signatures. ([Docs.rs][5])

### Named arguments

```rust
let signature = Signature::exact(
    vec![DataType::Float64, DataType::Float64],
    Volatility::Immutable,
)
.with_parameter_names(vec!["base", "exponent"])?;
```

```sql
SELECT power(base => 2.0, exponent => 3.0);
SELECT power(exponent => 3.0, base => 2.0);
```

Named arguments are supported for scalar, window, and aggregate UDFs; implementers enable them by adding parameter names to the signature with `.with_parameter_names()`. The number of names must match the signature arity, and variadic signatures cannot use parameter names. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rules:

```text
Signature::exact      -> strict type/arity API
Signature::uniform    -> fixed arity, all args same type among valid types
Signature::numeric    -> numeric coercion intent
Signature::string     -> string coercion intent
Signature::variadic   -> variable arity, common accepted types
Signature::any        -> fixed arity, any types
Signature::user_defined -> implement coerce_types yourself
```

---

## 24.6 Volatility

```rust
Volatility::Immutable
Volatility::Stable
Volatility::Volatile
```

Volatility controls optimizer eligibility. `Immutable` means same input always returns same output and can be evaluated during planning; `Stable` may vary across queries but is stable within a query; `Volatile` may change per evaluation and cannot be evaluated during planning or pushed into scans in the same way. ([Docs.rs][6])

| Volatility  | Example                                     | Optimizer stance                                            |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Immutable` | `abs(x)`, deterministic parse/normalize     | strongest optimization; constant folding safe               |
| `Stable`    | `now()`-like query timestamp                | stable within query; planning-time rules limited by context |
| `Volatile`  | `random()`, external mutable service lookup | evaluate at runtime; avoid folding/reordering/pushdown      |

Agent rules:

```text
Use the strictest correct volatility.
Do not mark external-state functions Immutable.
Do not mark random/time/per-row API functions Stable unless semantics guarantee it.
Wrong volatility can produce wrong query results.
```

---

## 24.7 Return type inference and return fields

### Basic type-based return

```rust
fn return_type(&self, arg_types: &[DataType]) -> Result<DataType> {
    match arg_types {
        [DataType::Int64] => Ok(DataType::Int64),
        [DataType::Float64] => Ok(DataType::Float64),
        _ => plan_err!("unsupported argument types: {arg_types:?}"),
    }
}
```

`return_type` computes the output `DataType` from already-coerced argument types. For most UDFs, this is enough. ([Docs.rs][4])

### Advanced return field / nullability

```rust
// Conceptual shape; exact args type should match your pinned DataFusion version.
fn return_field_from_args(
    &self,
    args: datafusion::logical_expr::ReturnFieldArgs,
) -> Result<datafusion::arrow::datatypes::FieldRef> {
    // choose data type, nullability, and metadata based on argument fields/values
    todo!()
}
```

`ScalarUDFImpl` can implement `return_field_from_args`; when this is implemented, DataFusion does not call `return_type`. The docs describe this path as useful for advanced cases such as specifying nullability or return types based on runtime argument values rather than only argument types. ([Docs.rs][4])

Agent rules:

```text
Use return_type for deterministic type-from-types behavior.
Use return_field_from_args for:
  output nullability control
  output metadata
  value-dependent return types
  field-name-aware typing
  nested/struct/list return fields
Do not panic in return_type; return DataFusionError instead.
```

---

## 24.8 Scalar UDF documentation metadata

`ScalarUDFImpl::documentation()` can return DataFusion documentation metadata. The docs.rs example uses `Documentation::builder(...)` with an argument description, and the official UDF guide shows `datafusion_doc::Documentation` / `datafusion_macros::user_doc` usage and `documentation(&self) -> Option<&Documentation>`. ([Docs.rs][4])

```rust
use std::sync::LazyLock;
use datafusion_doc::{Documentation, DOC_SECTION_MATH};

static ADD_ONE_DOC: LazyLock<Documentation> = LazyLock::new(|| {
    Documentation::builder(
        DOC_SECTION_MATH,
        "Add one to an Int64 value.",
        "add_one(41)",
    )
    .with_argument("value", "The Int64 value to increment.")
    .build()
});

impl ScalarUDFImpl for AddOne {
    // required methods...

    fn documentation(&self) -> Option<&Documentation> {
        Some(&ADD_ONE_DOC)
    }
}
```

Agent rules:

```text
Add docs for every public SQL UDF.
Include section, short description, example, and argument docs.
Treat parameter names and documentation as product API.
Use docs to support SHOW FUNCTIONS / information_schema-style discovery.
```

---

## 24.9 Async scalar UDFs

Async scalar UDFs support asynchronous execution inside a scalar function, such as network or I/O calls. DataFusion’s guide says to implement `AsyncScalarUDFImpl`, wrap it with `AsyncScalarUDF::new`, and register the converted scalar UDF with the `SessionContext`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Skeleton

```rust
use std::{any::Any, sync::Arc};

use async_trait::async_trait;
use datafusion::arrow::{
    array::{ArrayRef, ArrayIter, StringArray},
    datatypes::DataType,
};
use datafusion::common::{internal_err, Result};
use datafusion::logical_expr::{
    async_udf::{AsyncScalarUDF, AsyncScalarUDFImpl},
    ColumnarValue,
    ScalarFunctionArgs,
    ScalarUDFImpl,
    Signature,
    Volatility,
};

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct AsyncUpper {
    signature: Signature,
}

impl AsyncUpper {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            signature: Signature::uniform(
                1,
                vec![DataType::Utf8],
                Volatility::Volatile,
            ),
        }
    }
}

impl ScalarUDFImpl for AsyncUpper {
    fn name(&self) -> &str { "async_upper" }
    fn signature(&self) -> &Signature { &self.signature }

    fn return_type(&self, _arg_types: &[DataType]) -> Result<DataType> {
        Ok(DataType::Utf8)
    }

    fn invoke_with_args(&self, _args: ScalarFunctionArgs) -> Result<ColumnarValue> {
        internal_err!("async_upper must be invoked through async UDF execution")
    }
}

#[async_trait]
impl AsyncScalarUDFImpl for AsyncUpper {
    fn ideal_batch_size(&self) -> Option<usize> {
        Some(32)
    }

    async fn invoke_async_with_args(
        &self,
        args: ScalarFunctionArgs,
    ) -> Result<ColumnarValue> {
        let arrays = ColumnarValue::values_to_arrays(&args.args)?;
        let input = arrays[0].as_string::<i32>();

        let output = ArrayIter::new(input)
            .map(|v| v.map(|s| s.to_uppercase()))
            .collect::<StringArray>();

        Ok(ColumnarValue::Array(Arc::new(output) as ArrayRef))
    }
}

// registration
let udf = AsyncScalarUDF::new(Arc::new(AsyncUpper::new()));
ctx.register_udf(udf.into_scalar_udf());
```

Deployment rules:

```text
Use async UDF only for real async work.
Batch external calls; never one network request per row if avoidable.
Implement timeout, retry, and circuit-breaker policy.
Mark external-state functions Volatile unless stronger semantics are guaranteed.
Cache carefully: SQL semantics and volatility must remain correct.
```

---

## 24.10 Aggregate UDFs / UDAFs

Aggregate UDFs take a group of rows and return one value, similar to `SUM` or `COUNT`. DataFusion’s `Accumulator` API requires stateful methods including `update_batch`, `state`, `merge_batch`, `evaluate`, and `size`; the docs describe `Accumulator`s as stateful objects that aggregate values from multiple rows into a final output aggregate. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Accumulator skeleton: geometric mean

```rust
use datafusion::arrow::array::ArrayRef;
use datafusion::common::{Result, ScalarValue};
use datafusion::physical_plan::Accumulator;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct GeoMean {
    product: f64,
    count: u64,
}

impl GeoMean {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            product: 1.0,
            count: 0,
        }
    }
}

impl Accumulator for GeoMean {
    fn update_batch(&mut self, values: &[ArrayRef]) -> Result<()> {
        let input = values[0].as_primitive::<datafusion::arrow::datatypes::Float64Type>();

        for v in input.iter().flatten() {
            self.product *= v;
            self.count += 1;
        }

        Ok(())
    }

    fn state(&mut self) -> Result<Vec<ScalarValue>> {
        Ok(vec![
            ScalarValue::Float64(Some(self.product)),
            ScalarValue::UInt64(Some(self.count)),
        ])
    }

    fn merge_batch(&mut self, states: &[ArrayRef]) -> Result<()> {
        let products = states[0].as_primitive::<datafusion::arrow::datatypes::Float64Type>();
        let counts = states[1].as_primitive::<datafusion::arrow::datatypes::UInt64Type>();

        for (p, c) in products.iter().zip(counts.iter()) {
            if let (Some(p), Some(c)) = (p, c) {
                self.product *= p;
                self.count += c;
            }
        }

        Ok(())
    }

    fn evaluate(&mut self) -> Result<ScalarValue> {
        if self.count == 0 {
            Ok(ScalarValue::Float64(None))
        } else {
            Ok(ScalarValue::Float64(Some(
                self.product.powf(1.0 / self.count as f64),
            )))
        }
    }

    fn size(&self) -> usize {
        std::mem::size_of_val(self)
    }
}
```

### Register UDAF

```rust
let geo_mean = create_udaf(
    "geo_mean",
    vec![DataType::Float64],
    Arc::new(DataType::Float64),
    Volatility::Immutable,
    Arc::new(|_| Ok(Box::new(GeoMean::new()))),
    Arc::new(vec![DataType::Float64, DataType::UInt64]),
);

ctx.register_udaf(geo_mean);

let df = ctx.sql("SELECT region, geo_mean(amount) FROM t GROUP BY region").await?;
```

`create_udaf` wraps an accumulator implementation into an `AggregateUDF`, after which `SessionContext::register_udaf` makes it available to SQL. The state-type vector must correspond to the values emitted by `Accumulator::state()` and consumed by `merge_batch`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rules:

```text
UDAF state must be compact, serializable, mergeable, and deterministic.
update_batch handles raw input arrays.
state emits partial aggregate state.
merge_batch consumes partial states from other partitions.
evaluate emits final ScalarValue.
size reports memory footprint for planning/accounting.
```

---

## 24.11 Window UDFs / UDWFs

Window UDFs are scalar-like in output cardinality but have access to rows around the current row through window frames. DataFusion’s guide shows implementing `PartitionEvaluator`; `evaluate` is called once per row and is the simplest but slowest API, while `evaluate_all` or `evaluate_all_with_rank` should be implemented when possible for performance. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Moving-average UDWF

```rust
use datafusion::arrow::{
    array::{ArrayRef, AsArray, Float64Array},
    datatypes::{DataType, Float64Type},
};
use datafusion::common::{Result, ScalarValue};
use datafusion::logical_expr::PartitionEvaluator;

#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
struct MovingAverage;

impl PartitionEvaluator for MovingAverage {
    fn uses_window_frame(&self) -> bool {
        true
    }

    fn evaluate(
        &mut self,
        values: &[ArrayRef],
        range: &std::ops::Range<usize>,
    ) -> Result<ScalarValue> {
        let arr: &Float64Array = values[0].as_ref().as_primitive::<Float64Type>();

        let len = range.end - range.start;
        if len == 0 {
            return Ok(ScalarValue::Float64(None));
        }

        let sum: f64 = arr
            .values()
            .iter()
            .skip(range.start)
            .take(len)
            .sum();

        Ok(ScalarValue::Float64(Some(sum / len as f64)))
    }
}

fn make_partition_evaluator() -> Result<Box<dyn PartitionEvaluator>> {
    Ok(Box::new(MovingAverage))
}
```

### Register UDWF

```rust
let smooth_it = create_udwf(
    "smooth_it",
    DataType::Float64,
    Arc::new(DataType::Float64),
    Volatility::Immutable,
    Arc::new(make_partition_evaluator),
);

ctx.register_udwf(smooth_it);

let df = ctx.sql(
    r#"
    SELECT
      car,
      ts,
      speed,
      smooth_it(speed) OVER (
        PARTITION BY car
        ORDER BY ts
        ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
      ) AS smooth_speed
    FROM car_speeds
    "#,
).await?;
```

The guide’s `create_udwf` example takes the SQL function name, input `DataType`, return `DataType`, volatility, and a factory for `PartitionEvaluator`. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

Agent rules:

```text
Use UDWF when output row count equals input row count.
Implement evaluate_all/evaluate_all_with_rank when possible.
Test PARTITION BY, ORDER BY, frame bounds, empty frames, ties, and nulls.
Avoid unbounded-frame custom functions unless memory behavior is clear.
```

---

## 24.12 Table functions / UDTFs

A UDTF takes parameters and returns a `TableProvider`; DataFusion invokes the table provider inside a query plan. `TableFunctionImpl::call_with_args` receives `TableFunctionArgs`, whose arguments are `Expr`s, and returns `Result<Arc<dyn TableProvider>>`. In DataFusion 54, `TableFunctionImpl` declares `Any` as a supertrait (`TableFunctionImpl: Debug + Sync + Send + Any`, no `as_any` method), the legacy `call(&self, &[Expr])` is deprecated and default-bodied (it errors unless overridden), and `call_with_args` is the primary entry point — `TableFunctionArgs::exprs()` yields the call arguments and `TableFunctionArgs::session()` exposes the calling `Session`, so a table function can consult session configuration and state at planning time. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

### Minimal echo UDTF

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::arrow::{
    array::{ArrayRef, Int64Array},
    datatypes::{DataType, Field, Schema},
    record_batch::RecordBatch,
};
use datafusion::catalog::{TableFunctionArgs, TableFunctionImpl, TableProvider};
use datafusion::common::{plan_err, Result, ScalarValue};
use datafusion::datasource::memory::MemTable;
use datafusion::logical_expr::Expr;

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct EchoFunction;

impl TableFunctionImpl for EchoFunction {
    fn call_with_args(&self, args: TableFunctionArgs) -> Result<Arc<dyn TableProvider>> {
        let exprs = args.exprs();

        let Some(Expr::Literal(ScalarValue::Int64(Some(value)), _)) = exprs.get(0) else {
            return plan_err!("echo expects first argument to be an Int64 literal");
        };

        let schema = Arc::new(Schema::new(vec![
            Field::new("value", DataType::Int64, false),
        ]));

        let batch = RecordBatch::try_new(
            schema.clone(),
            vec![Arc::new(Int64Array::from(vec![*value])) as ArrayRef],
        )?;

        let table = MemTable::try_new(schema, vec![vec![batch]])?;
        Ok(Arc::new(table))
    }
}

ctx.register_udtf("echo", Arc::new(EchoFunction));

let df = ctx.sql("SELECT * FROM echo(42)").await?;
```

Agent rules:

```text
UDTF args are planning-time Exprs, not row-wise evaluated values.
Validate argument count and literal/type expectations.
Return stable schema for the same argument contract.
Use custom TableProvider for remote API/file/database table functions.
Do not perform large remote scans inside call_with_args; defer scanning to TableProvider::scan.
```

---

## 24.13 SQL and DataFrame invocation

### SQL invocation

```sql
SELECT add_one(id) AS id_plus_one
FROM events;

SELECT region, geo_mean(amount) AS gm
FROM events
GROUP BY region;

SELECT smooth_it(speed) OVER (
  PARTITION BY car
  ORDER BY ts
  ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
) AS smooth_speed
FROM car_speeds;

SELECT *
FROM echo(42);
```

### DataFrame invocation

```rust
let add_one = ScalarUDF::from(AddOne::new());
ctx.register_udf(add_one.clone());

let df = ctx
    .table("events")
    .await?
    .select(vec![
        col("id"),
        add_one.call(vec![col("id")]).alias("id_plus_one"),
    ])?;
```

`ScalarUDF::call` is the direct Rust expression path; SQL name resolution requires registration with `SessionContext`. ([Docs.rs][3])

---

## 24.14 Registration API map

```rust
ctx.register_udf(scalar_udf);
ctx.register_udaf(aggregate_udf);
ctx.register_udwf(window_udf);
ctx.register_udtf("echo", Arc::new(EchoFunction));
```

Registration must happen **before query planning**. A `DataFrame` or `LogicalPlan` already built before registration will not retroactively re-resolve unknown functions.

Agent rules:

```text
Register functions during engine/session construction.
Use consistent lowercase names for SQL-facing functions.
Document aliases and named arguments.
Avoid per-request registration unless functions are request-specific and isolated.
```

---

## 24.15 Aliases

```rust
let udf = ScalarUDF::from(AddOne::new())
    .with_aliases(["plus_one", "inc"]);
```

`ScalarUDF::with_aliases` adds additional names that can invoke the same function; when implementing `ScalarUDFImpl` directly, aliases can be returned from the implementation instead. ([Docs.rs][3])

Agent rules:

```text
Use aliases for dialect compatibility.
Do not overload aliases with different semantics.
Document aliases as API surface.
Avoid case-sensitive surprises; prefer lowercase function names.
```

---

## 24.16 Optimizer interaction hooks for scalar UDFs

`ScalarUDFImpl` includes optional hooks beyond basic invocation: `coerce_types`, `return_field_from_args`, `simplify`, `with_updated_config`, `evaluate_bounds`, `propagate_constraints`, `output_ordering`, `preserves_lex_ordering`, `documentation`, and `placement`. These hooks let advanced UDFs participate in type coercion, return-field inference, expression simplification, interval analysis, ordering inference, configuration changes, and documentation. ([Docs.rs][4])

Agent rules:

```text
Implement optional hooks only when semantics are precise.
simplify must preserve expression names and volatility semantics.
coerce_types must agree with Signature.
evaluate_bounds / propagate_constraints must be conservative.
output_ordering / preserves_lex_ordering must never overclaim.
```

---

## 24.17 Vectorized Arrow implementation rules

```text
Inputs:
  ScalarFunctionArgs.args: Vec<ColumnarValue>
  ColumnarValue::Array(ArrayRef)
  ColumnarValue::Scalar(ScalarValue)

Outputs:
  ColumnarValue::Array(ArrayRef) with row count = number_rows
  or ColumnarValue::Scalar(ScalarValue) when result is constant
```

### Scalar-fast path

```rust
match &args.args[0] {
    ColumnarValue::Scalar(ScalarValue::Int64(Some(v))) => {
        return Ok(ColumnarValue::Scalar(ScalarValue::Int64(Some(v + 1))));
    }
    ColumnarValue::Scalar(ScalarValue::Int64(None)) => {
        return Ok(ColumnarValue::Scalar(ScalarValue::Int64(None)));
    }
    _ => {}
}
```

### Array path

```rust
let arrays = ColumnarValue::values_to_arrays(&args.args)?;
let input = as_int64_array(&arrays[0])?;

let output = input
    .iter()
    .map(|v| v.map(|x| x + 1))
    .collect::<Int64Array>();
```

The `ScalarUDFImpl` docs note that handling scalar constant arguments is best for performance; converting all `ColumnarValue`s into arrays is simpler but likely slower. ([Docs.rs][4])

---

## 24.18 Error handling

```rust
fn return_type(&self, arg_types: &[DataType]) -> Result<DataType> {
    if arg_types != [DataType::Int64] {
        return plan_err!("add_one expects Int64, got {arg_types:?}");
    }
    Ok(DataType::Int64)
}
```

```rust
fn invoke_with_args(&self, args: ScalarFunctionArgs) -> Result<ColumnarValue> {
    if args.args.len() != 1 {
        return plan_err!("add_one expects one argument, got {}", args.args.len());
    }
    // ...
}
```

Agent rules:

```text
Return DataFusion errors, not panics.
Validate arity.
Validate downcasts.
Validate scalar/array cases.
Treat nulls deliberately.
Expose actionable error messages.
```

## 24.20 Deployment advisory

```text
UDFs are trusted code executing inside the DataFusion process.
Do not load arbitrary user-supplied native code without sandboxing.
Use function allowlists for public SQL services.
Mark volatility correctly; wrong volatility can change results.
Prefer vectorized Arrow kernels over row loops.
Avoid blocking I/O in sync scalar UDFs.
Use async UDFs only with concurrency/rate controls.
Track aggregate state memory.
Document SQL names, aliases, arguments, volatility, null behavior, and examples.
Pin DataFusion version for extension-heavy crates.
```

---

## 24.21 Anti-pattern inventory

* Sync scalar UDF performing blocking network I/O.
* Marking random/API/time-dependent functions `Immutable`.
* Expanding scalar constants into arrays in every hot-path call.
* Returning an array with the wrong row count.
* Ignoring `NULL` behavior.
* Panicking in `return_type` or `invoke_with_args`.
* UDAF `state()` not matching declared state datatypes.
* UDAF `merge_batch()` inconsistent with `update_batch()`.
* Window UDF using row-by-row `evaluate` when vectorized `evaluate_all` is feasible.
* UDTF performing expensive remote scan during planning.
* Registering UDFs after planning queries.
* Exposing volatile or expensive UDFs to public SQL without allowlists/resource limits.
* Missing documentation metadata for product-facing UDFs.
* Snapshot-testing function output without deterministic inputs.

---

```text
[ ] Choose UDF family: scalar / async scalar / aggregate / window / table.
[ ] Use create_udf for simple fixed-type scalar functions.
[ ] Use ScalarUDFImpl for production scalar functions.
[ ] Define Signature precisely.
[ ] Add named parameters if SQL ergonomics require them.
[ ] Set Volatility correctly.
[ ] Implement return_type or return_field_from_args.
[ ] Implement scalar fast path for ColumnarValue::Scalar.
[ ] Preserve null semantics.
[ ] Register with SessionContext before planning.
[ ] Expose SQL and DataFrame invocation examples.
[ ] Add Documentation metadata for public functions.
[ ] Test directly against Arrow arrays and through SQL.
[ ] For UDAFs, test update/state/merge/evaluate.
[ ] For UDWFs, test partitions, frames, and ordering.
[ ] For UDTFs, validate args and return TableProvider.
[ ] Add allowlist/resource policy for untrusted SQL environments.
```
