## 35.23 Build and compile-time guidance

```toml
[dependencies]
datafusion = { version = "=55.0.0", default-features = false, features = [
  "sql",
  "parquet",
] }
```

The crate-configuration docs describe using normal crates.io releases, unreleased Git dependencies for testing main-branch code, package-level Git dependencies for subcrates, and feature-controlled dependency declarations. They also warn build optimization settings can improve runtime performance while increasing compile time and binary size. ([datafusion.apache.org][7])

Agent rules:

```text
For fastest development:
  use default dev profile.
  depend on top-level datafusion.

For smaller binaries:
  use default-features=false and add only needed features.

For extension libraries:
  consider direct subcrates but pin versions.

For unreleased testing:
  use git dependency only in upgrade/testing branches.
```

---

## 35.24 Crate organization and API stability

```text
High-level, more stable:
  datafusion::prelude
  SessionContext
  DataFrame
  ctx.sql
  read/register file APIs

Mid-level:
  datafusion::logical_expr
  datafusion::catalog
  UDF APIs
  TableProvider

Lower-level / more upgrade-sensitive:
  datafusion::physical_plan
  datafusion::physical_optimizer
  datafusion::sql planner extension traits
  QueryPlanner / PhysicalPlanner
  custom ExecutionPlan
```

DataFusion’s own docs describe top-level `datafusion` as the main user-facing crate and list internal subcrates as modularity/compile-time boundaries. Lower-level crates are powerful but increase upgrade-surface area, especially where traits model execution/planning internals. ([Docs.rs][1])

Agent rule:

```text
The lower the crate layer, the more exact version pinning and upgrade testing you need.
```

---

## 35.25 Anti-pattern inventory

* Depending on both `datafusion` and mismatched `datafusion-expr`.
* Importing `arrow` directly with a version different from `datafusion::arrow`.
* Using direct subcrate dependencies in an app with no compile-time/binary-size reason.
* Implementing custom `ExecutionPlan` when `TableProvider` or `FileSource` is enough.
* Treating `datafusion_sql` parser extensions as runtime execution extensions.
* Putting physical execution logic in logical-expression crates.
* Letting public library APIs expose DataFusion subcrate types without pinning/versioning policy.
* Assuming function crates are available when `default-features = false`.
* Depending on CLI-only testing crates in production binaries.
* Using `datafusion_proto` for stable long-term plan storage without versioning the serialized format.
* Assuming every DataFusion logical feature maps cleanly to Substrait.
* Importing from `datafusion_*` direct crates and `datafusion::...` re-exports interchangeably without type/version audit.

---

## 35.26 Agent checklist

```text
[ ] Use top-level datafusion crate for ordinary apps.
[ ] Prefer datafusion::prelude for SessionContext/DataFrame workflows.
[ ] Prefer datafusion::arrow for Arrow types.
[ ] Use datafusion::common for Result, DataFusionError, ScalarValue, DFSchema.
[ ] Use datafusion::logical_expr for Expr, LogicalPlan, UDF metadata.
[ ] Use datafusion::sql only for SQL parser/planner extension work.
[ ] Use datafusion::optimizer only for logical/analyzer rule work.
[ ] Use datafusion::physical_plan only for custom physical operators/streams.
[ ] Use datafusion::execution for RuntimeEnv, TaskContext, memory/disk/object stores.
[ ] Use datafusion::catalog for custom catalogs, schemas, TableProviders, table functions.
[ ] Use datafusion::datasource for file/data IO abstractions and sinks.
[ ] Use function crates through datafusion::functions* re-exports when possible.
[ ] Use datafusion_proto directly for DataFusion plan serialization.
[ ] Use datafusion_substrait directly for Substrait interoperability.
[ ] Pin direct datafusion-* subcrates to the same version.
[ ] Run cargo tree -d after dependency changes.
[ ] Keep architecture boundaries clean: logical in expr, physical in physical_plan, runtime resources in execution, metadata in catalog, file IO in datasource.
```

# DataFusion Advanced — 36) Plan serialization and interoperability

## 36.0 Serialization mental model

```text
DataFusion plan interchange
  ├─ DataFusion-native protobuf
  │   └─ datafusion_proto
  │       ├─ Expr
  │       ├─ LogicalPlan
  │       ├─ ExecutionPlan
  │       ├─ PhysicalExpr
  │       ├─ bytes / JSON helpers
  │       └─ DataFusion-specific, broadest fidelity
  └─ Substrait
      └─ datafusion_substrait
          ├─ substrait::proto::Plan
          ├─ cross-language relational algebra format
          ├─ DataFusion producer / consumer
          └─ interoperability-oriented, incomplete coverage
```

`datafusion_proto` is the DataFusion-native serialization crate: it serializes and deserializes DataFusion `LogicalPlan`s, including `Expr`, and `ExecutionPlan`s, including `PhysicalExpr`, by converting them to Protocol Buffers with `prost`. Its serialized form is **not guaranteed to be compatible across DataFusion versions**. ([Docs.rs][1])

`datafusion_substrait` serializes/deserializes DataFusion `LogicalPlan` and `ExecutionPlan` values to and from generated `substrait::proto` types. Substrait is a cross-language relational-algebra serialization format based on Protocol Buffers, but it does not yet cover the full DataFusion plan/expression surface. ([Docs.rs][2])

---

## 36.1 Decision table

| Requirement                                 | Prefer                                   | Reason                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| highest DataFusion fidelity                 | `datafusion_proto`                       | DataFusion-specific; broad plan/expression coverage           |
| same-version distributed DataFusion service | `datafusion_proto`                       | native plan exchange; pair with exact version pin             |
| cross-language / cross-engine exchange      | `datafusion_substrait`                   | standard relational-algebra format                            |
| Python/Rust/FFI plan handoff                | Substrait or proto                       | Substrait for interoperability; proto for DataFusion fidelity |
| long-term archival                          | neither blindly                          | versioned format + migration layer required                   |
| custom logical/physical extension nodes     | proto + extension codec or custom format | default codecs may not know custom nodes                      |
| broad DataFusion physical plan transport    | `datafusion_proto` where supported       | native `ExecutionPlan` serialization helpers exist            |
| portable semantic query exchange            | Substrait                                | use standard plan model, accept feature gaps                  |

Agent default:

```text
Same DataFusion version, same application family:
  datafusion_proto

Cross-language / cross-engine:
  datafusion_substrait

Durable storage / long-lived cache:
  store SQL + version + config + catalog snapshot;
  serialize plans only with explicit versioning and invalidation policy.
```

---

## 36.2 Cargo setup

### DataFusion-native protobuf

```toml
[dependencies]
datafusion = "=55.0.0"
datafusion-proto = "=55.0.0"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["rt-multi-thread", "macros"] }
```

### Substrait

```toml
[dependencies]
datafusion = "=55.0.0"
datafusion-substrait = "=55.0.0"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["rt-multi-thread", "macros"] }
prost = "0.14"
```

`datafusion-proto 55.0.0` depends on the matching `datafusion-* 55.0.0` crate family, Arrow `59.2.0`, `prost 0.14`, and `object_store 0.13.2`; `datafusion-substrait 55.0.0` depends on the matching `datafusion 55.0.0`, the `substrait` protobuf crate, and `prost`. Keep these crate families aligned during upgrades. ([Docs.rs][1])

---

## 36.3 `datafusion_proto`: native DataFusion serialization

### Supported high-level structures

```text
datafusion_proto supports:
  LogicalPlan including Expr
  ExecutionPlan including PhysicalExpr

Encoding substrate:
  Protocol Buffers via prost

Format property:
  DataFusion-specific
  broadest fidelity for DataFusion-native plans
  not cross-version stable
```

The crate docs explicitly describe support for serializing/deserializing `LogicalPlan`s with `Expr`s and `ExecutionPlan`s with `PhysicalExpr`s; they also state the native binary format supports the full range of DataFusion plans but is DataFusion-specific. ([Docs.rs][1])

---

## 36.4 `datafusion_proto`: serialize `Expr`

```rust
use datafusion::prelude::*;
use datafusion::logical_expr::Expr;
use datafusion_proto::bytes::Serializeable;

fn expr_round_trip(ctx: &SessionContext) -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let expr: Expr = col("a").lt(lit(5i32));

    let bytes = expr.to_bytes()?;
    let decoded = Expr::from_bytes_with_ctx(&bytes, ctx.task_ctx().as_ref())?;

    assert_eq!(expr, decoded);
    Ok(())
}
```

The `datafusion_proto` crate provides `Expr::to_bytes()` for encoding. For decoding, DataFusion 54 changed the `Serializeable` trait: the registry-based `from_bytes_with_registry` is gone, and the required method is `from_bytes_with_ctx(&[u8], &TaskContext)`. A convenience `Expr::from_bytes(&bytes)` default method remains, but it decodes against `TaskContext::default()` and therefore errors if the serialized expression references any user-defined functions — pass the real `TaskContext` (`ctx.task_ctx().as_ref()`) whenever UDFs may appear. The same `&TaskContext` requirement applies to the lower-level `parse_expr`/`parse_exprs`/`parse_sorts` helpers in `datafusion_proto::logical_plan::from_proto`. ([Docs.rs][1])

Agent rules:

```text
Use Expr serialization for:
  predicate transport
  filter caches
  distributed query fragments
  expression-level testing

Do not use serialized Expr as:
  unvalidated user input
  cross-version durable cache
  public stable API
```

---

## 36.5 `datafusion_proto`: serialize `LogicalPlan`

```rust
use datafusion::prelude::*;
use datafusion_proto::bytes::{
    logical_plan_from_bytes,
    logical_plan_to_bytes,
};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let ctx = SessionContext::new();

    ctx.register_csv(
        "t1",
        "tests/testdata/test.csv",
        CsvReadOptions::default(),
    )
    .await?;

    let plan = ctx
        .table("t1")
        .await?
        .into_optimized_plan()?;

    let bytes = logical_plan_to_bytes(&plan)?;

    let decoded = logical_plan_from_bytes(&bytes, &ctx.task_ctx())?;

    assert_eq!(
        format!("{:?}", plan),
        format!("{:?}", decoded),
    );

    Ok(())
}
```

The docs show `logical_plan_to_bytes(&plan)` and `logical_plan_from_bytes(&bytes, &ctx.task_ctx())` for serializing an optimized logical plan and deserializing it with a `TaskContext`. ([Docs.rs][1])

### Logical-plan transport payload

```text
payload:
  datafusion_version
  serialized_logical_plan_bytes
  catalog_version
  function_registry_version
  config_hash
  optional sql_text
  optional plan_display_indent
```

Agent rules:

```text
Deserialize logical plans only in a compatible SessionState/TaskContext.
Ensure required tables, catalogs, object stores, UDFs, and functions exist on the receiver.
Re-optimize after deserialization if receiver config/catalog differs intentionally.
Validate table/function allowlists before execution.
```

---

## 36.6 `datafusion_proto`: serialize `ExecutionPlan`

```rust
use datafusion::prelude::*;
use datafusion_proto::bytes::{
    physical_plan_from_bytes,
    physical_plan_to_bytes,
};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let ctx = SessionContext::new();

    ctx.register_csv(
        "t1",
        "tests/testdata/test.csv",
        CsvReadOptions::default(),
    )
    .await?;

    let physical_plan = ctx
        .table("t1")
        .await?
        .create_physical_plan()
        .await?;

    let bytes = physical_plan_to_bytes(physical_plan.clone())?;

    let decoded = physical_plan_from_bytes(&bytes, &ctx.task_ctx())?;

    assert_eq!(
        format!("{:?}", physical_plan),
        format!("{:?}", decoded),
    );

    Ok(())
}
```

The native protobuf docs show `physical_plan_to_bytes(physical_plan.clone())` and `physical_plan_from_bytes(&bytes, &ctx.task_ctx())` for physical plan round-tripping. ([Docs.rs][1])

### Physical-plan transport risks

```text
ExecutionPlan serialization captures physical decisions:
  partitioning
  operator choices
  scan implementation
  physical expressions
  possibly source/sink-specific metadata

Receiver must be compatible in:
  DataFusion version
  function registry
  object-store registry
  table/source provider availability
  custom physical extension codecs
  runtime resource configuration
```

Agent rules:

```text
Prefer LogicalPlan exchange when receiver should choose physical strategy.
Use ExecutionPlan exchange when coordinator has already made physical decisions.
Do not use ExecutionPlan bytes as a portable cross-engine format.
Do not expect physical plan bytes to remain valid across DataFusion upgrades.
```

---

## 36.7 Native proto JSON helpers

The `datafusion_proto::bytes` module exposes byte and JSON helper functions for logical and physical plans, including logical-plan bytes/JSON conversion and physical-plan bytes/JSON conversion; extension-codec variants are available for plans containing extension nodes. ([Docs.rs][3])

Conceptual usage:

```rust
use datafusion_proto::bytes::{
    logical_plan_to_json,
    logical_plan_from_json,
    physical_plan_to_json,
    physical_plan_from_json,
};

let json = logical_plan_to_json(&plan)?;
let plan2 = logical_plan_from_json(&json, &ctx.task_ctx())?;
```

Agent rules:

```text
Use bytes for network/runtime efficiency.
Use JSON for debugging, review, test snapshots, and tooling.
Do not treat JSON as a stable public schema across DataFusion versions.
Redact paths, credentials, and tenant-private metadata before exposing JSON.
```

---

## 36.8 Custom extension nodes and codecs

```text
Problem:
  LogicalPlan::Extension / custom ExecutionPlan nodes are opaque to default serializers.

Solution:
  implement extension codecs
  use *_with_extension_codec APIs where available
  keep codec ordering/versioning stable
  test round trips for every custom node
```

The `datafusion_proto::bytes` API surface includes extension-codec variants for logical and physical plan bytes/JSON serialization in the module listing, and the DataFusion examples include composed physical extension codec examples where codec ordering matters for decoding. ([Docs.rs][3])

Codec manifest:

```text
extension_codec_manifest:
  codec_set_name: my-engine-codecs
  codec_set_version: 3
  codecs:
    - id: 0
      name: parent_exec
      version: 1
    - id: 1
      name: child_exec
      version: 2
```

Agent rules:

```text
Every custom logical node needs a logical serialization story.
Every custom physical node needs a physical serialization story.
Codec ordering is part of the wire contract if positional dispatch is used.
Include codec-set version in every cross-process payload.
Fail closed on unknown extension node IDs.
```

---

## 36.9 `datafusion_substrait`: interoperability serialization

### Supported purpose

```text
datafusion_substrait use cases:
  run Substrait plans produced by other systems
  create plans for other systems
  pass query plans over FFI boundaries
  pass query plans across node boundaries
```

The crate docs list those exact potential uses and state that Substrait provides a cross-language relational-algebra plan/expression serialization format based on Protocol Buffers. ([Docs.rs][2])

---

## 36.10 Substrait logical plan production / consumption

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use datafusion::arrow::{
    array::{ArrayRef, Int32Array},
    record_batch::RecordBatch,
};
use datafusion::prelude::*;
use datafusion_substrait::logical_plan::{
    consumer,
    producer,
};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let ctx = SessionContext::new();

    let batch = RecordBatch::try_from_iter(vec![(
        "x",
        Arc::new(Int32Array::from(vec![42])) as ArrayRef,
    )])?;

    ctx.register_batch("t", batch)?;

    let df = ctx.sql("SELECT x FROM t").await?;
    let plan = df.into_optimized_plan()?;

    let substrait_plan =
        producer::to_substrait_plan(&plan, &ctx.state())?;

    let logical_round_trip =
        consumer::from_substrait_plan(&ctx.state(), &substrait_plan)
            .await?;

    let logical_round_trip = ctx.state().optimize(&logical_round_trip)?;

    assert_eq!(
        format!("{:?}", plan),
        format!("{:?}", logical_round_trip),
    );

    Ok(())
}
```

The `datafusion_substrait` docs show `logical_plan::producer::to_substrait_plan(&plan, &ctx.state())` and `logical_plan::consumer::from_substrait_plan(&ctx.state(), &substrait_plan).await` for logical-plan round-tripping. ([Docs.rs][2])

---

## 36.11 Substrait bytes / JSON

`datafusion_substrait` re-exports the `substrait` crate, and the docs state that generated types such as `substrait::proto::Plan` and `substrait::proto::Rel` can be serialized/deserialized to bytes, JSON, and other protobuf ecosystem formats using `prost` and related Rust protobuf tooling. ([Docs.rs][2])

```rust
use prost::Message;
use datafusion_substrait::substrait::proto::Plan;

fn encode_substrait_plan(plan: &Plan) -> datafusion::error::Result<Vec<u8>> {
    let mut bytes = Vec::new();
    plan.encode(&mut bytes)
        .map_err(|e| datafusion::error::DataFusionError::External(Box::new(e)))?;
    Ok(bytes)
}

fn decode_substrait_plan(bytes: &[u8]) -> datafusion::error::Result<Plan> {
    Plan::decode(bytes)
        .map_err(|e| datafusion::error::DataFusionError::External(Box::new(e)))
}
```

Agent rules:

```text
Substrait bytes are better for transport.
Substrait JSON is better for inspection/debugging.
Always include producer, consumer, DataFusion, Substrait, and extension-version metadata.
```

---

## 36.12 `datafusion_proto` vs `datafusion_substrait`

| Dimension                 | `datafusion_proto`                  | `datafusion_substrait`                                      |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Format                    | DataFusion-specific protobuf        | Substrait standard protobuf                                 |
| Goal                      | DataFusion fidelity                 | interoperability                                            |
| LogicalPlan               | supported                           | supported for many plans                                    |
| ExecutionPlan             | supported where implemented         | supported by crate, but coverage is not full                |
| Expr / PhysicalExpr       | native DataFusion coverage          | mapped to Substrait expression model                        |
| Cross-version stability   | not guaranteed                      | standard format, but mapping coverage/version still matters |
| Cross-engine use          | poor                                | intended use case                                           |
| Custom DataFusion nodes   | extension codec needed              | Substrait extension mapping needed                          |
| Best use                  | same-version distributed DataFusion | cross-language/cross-engine exchange                        |
| Long-term durable storage | risky without versioning            | less risky, still requires compatibility testing            |

The native proto crate explicitly says its serialized forms are not guaranteed to be compatible across DataFusion versions, while the Substrait crate explicitly says Substrait does not yet support the full range of DataFusion plans/expressions and points to `datafusion-proto` for a DataFusion-specific format with broader coverage. ([Docs.rs][1])

---

## 36.13 Cross-process plan exchange

### Logical-plan exchange architecture

```text
Coordinator process:
  SQL / DataFrame / custom compiler
    → optimized LogicalPlan
    → serialize with datafusion_proto or datafusion_substrait
    → send bytes + metadata

Worker process:
  receive bytes + metadata
  validate version / tenant / catalog / function registry
  deserialize into LogicalPlan
  optionally optimize
  create physical plan
  execute with local RuntimeEnv
```

Use logical-plan exchange when workers own their runtime resources, object-store registry, memory/disk config, and physical-planning choices.

### Physical-plan exchange architecture

```text
Coordinator process:
  optimized LogicalPlan
    → create physical ExecutionPlan
    → serialize physical plan
    → send physical plan bytes + fragments

Worker process:
  receive physical fragment
  validate version / extension codecs / runtime compatibility
  deserialize ExecutionPlan
  execute partition(s)
```

Use physical-plan exchange when the coordinator must control operator selection, repartitioning, physical fragments, or distributed execution strategy.

### Payload envelope

```rust
#[derive(Debug, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)]
struct PlanEnvelope {
    format: String,              // "datafusion-proto" | "substrait"
    plan_kind: String,           // "logical" | "physical"
    datafusion_version: String,
    substrait_version: Option<String>,
    codec_version: Option<String>,
    catalog_version: String,
    function_registry_version: String,
    config_hash: String,
    plan_bytes: Vec<u8>,
}
```

Agent rules:

```text
Never send naked plan bytes without metadata.
Validate producer/consumer compatibility before deserialization.
Treat deserialized plans as untrusted until policy-validated.
Validate table/function access after deserialization.
```

---

## 36.14 Compatibility boundaries

### DataFusion-native proto

```text
Hard boundary:
  DataFusion version

Also material:
  Arrow version
  object_store version
  function registry
  catalog/schema/table availability
  custom extension codec set
  feature flags
  physical planner/runtime assumptions
```

The `datafusion_proto` docs state serialized forms are not guaranteed to be compatible across DataFusion versions. This is the most important operational constraint for native proto plan exchange. ([Docs.rs][1])

### Substrait

```text
Hard boundary:
  Substrait specification / protobuf version
  DataFusion ↔ Substrait mapping support
  function/type extension mapping
  unsupported DataFusion plan nodes
  engine-specific semantics not representable in Substrait
```

The `datafusion_substrait` docs explicitly warn that Substrait does not yet support the full range of DataFusion plans and expressions. ([Docs.rs][2])

### Agent rules

```text
Use compatibility checks before deserialization.
Use round-trip tests for every query shape you rely on.
Store SQL fallback where possible.
Treat serialization failures as expected for unsupported plans.
```

---

## 36.15 Feature and semantic drift

Plan serialization interacts with:

```text
DataFusion features:
  UDFs
  UDAFs / UDWFs
  UDTFs
  custom TableProviders
  custom logical nodes
  custom physical nodes
  custom optimizer rules
  SQL parser dialect
  data types / nested types
  Parquet scan config
  object-store config
  runtime memory/disk behavior

Substrait features:
  standard relational algebra
  function extension URIs
  type mappings
  engine-specific extension points
  protobuf schema evolution
```

Agent rules:

```text
If a query uses only portable relational algebra:
  Substrait is plausible.

If a query uses DataFusion-specific physical/source/custom nodes:
  datafusion_proto or custom envelope likely required.

If a query uses custom SQL syntax:
  serialize the resulting plan, not the SQL extension state;
  ensure receiver has matching UDFs/planners/codecs.
```

---

## 36.16 Catalog and table-provider concerns

```text
Serialized plan contains references and structures, not the entire world.

Receiver still needs:
  catalog entries
  table providers
  object stores
  credentials
  function registries
  UDF implementations
  runtime config
  extension codecs
```

Logical plan deserialization in the native proto example requires `ctx.task_ctx()`, and Substrait consumption requires `ctx.state()`; this reflects that deserialization occurs in a session/runtime context, not in a vacuum. ([Docs.rs][1])

Agent rules:

```text
Do not assume serialized plan contains data source credentials.
Do not assume receiver has matching table providers.
For distributed systems, register catalogs/object stores/functions before plan deserialization.
For portable plan exchange, prefer symbolic table references plus external catalog protocol.
```

---

## 36.17 Security model

```text
Serialized plan is executable intent.
Treat it like code, not passive data.
```

Risks:

```text
unauthorized table scans
object-store path disclosure
resource exhaustion
expensive joins/sorts
unsupported custom nodes
function execution with side effects
deserialization bugs
catalog bypass
version confusion
```

Policy gate after deserialization:

```rust
fn validate_plan_for_tenant(plan: &LogicalPlan, tenant: &TenantPolicy)
    -> datafusion::error::Result<()>
{
    validate_tables(plan, tenant)?;
    validate_functions(plan, tenant)?;
    validate_no_ddl_dml(plan)?;
    validate_no_direct_paths(plan)?;
    validate_complexity_limits(plan)?;
    Ok(())
}
```

Agent rules:

```text
Never execute deserialized plans from untrusted users directly.
Validate table/function/source access after deserialization.
Apply row/column policy after deserialization.
Apply complexity limits: join count, sort count, estimated scan size, output caps.
Log plan envelope metadata and query_id.
```

---

## 36.18 Versioning strategy

### Native proto envelope

```text
native_plan_cache_key =
  datafusion_version
  arrow_version
  datafusion_proto_version
  feature_flags_hash
  catalog_version
  function_registry_version
  optimizer_config_hash
  serialized_plan_hash
```

### Substrait envelope

```text
substrait_plan_cache_key =
  substrait_proto_version
  producer_name_version
  datafusion_substrait_version
  extension_uri_set_hash
  function_mapping_version
  catalog_version
  plan_hash
```

Agent rules:

```text
Invalidate native proto plans on DataFusion upgrade.
Invalidate on catalog/function registry changes.
Invalidate on extension-codec changes.
Do not reuse physical plans across runtime-resource profiles unless proven safe.
```

## 36.19 Durable storage guidance

### Store this

```text
sql_text
datafusion_version
session_config / SHOW ALL snapshot
catalog/schema version
function registry manifest
object-store logical source references
plan serialization bytes if useful
EXPLAIN FORMAT INDENT
creation timestamp
```

### Avoid storing only this

```text
plan_bytes
```

Reason:

```text
Plan bytes alone do not explain:
  SQL source
  catalog version
  function registry
  optimizer settings
  extension codec versions
  DataFusion version
```

Agent rule:

```text
For durable plan cache:
  store SQL + metadata + serialized plan.
  if plan deserialization fails, re-plan from SQL.
```

## 36.20 Testing plan serialization

### Native logical round-trip test

```rust
#[tokio::test]
async fn proto_logical_round_trip() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let ctx = SessionContext::new();

    ctx.register_csv("t", "tests/fixtures/t.csv", CsvReadOptions::new())
        .await?;

    let plan = ctx.sql("SELECT * FROM t WHERE a > 10")
        .await?
        .into_optimized_plan()?;

    let bytes = datafusion_proto::bytes::logical_plan_to_bytes(&plan)?;
    let decoded =
        datafusion_proto::bytes::logical_plan_from_bytes(&bytes, &ctx.task_ctx())?;

    assert_eq!(
        plan.display_indent_schema().to_string(),
        decoded.display_indent_schema().to_string()
    );

    Ok(())
}
```

### Native physical round-trip test

```rust
#[tokio::test]
async fn proto_physical_round_trip() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let ctx = SessionContext::new();

    ctx.register_csv("t", "tests/fixtures/t.csv", CsvReadOptions::new())
        .await?;

    let physical = ctx.sql("SELECT * FROM t")
        .await?
        .create_physical_plan()
        .await?;

    let bytes = datafusion_proto::bytes::physical_plan_to_bytes(physical.clone())?;
    let decoded =
        datafusion_proto::bytes::physical_plan_from_bytes(&bytes, &ctx.task_ctx())?;

    assert_eq!(
        format!("{:?}", physical),
        format!("{:?}", decoded)
    );

    Ok(())
}
```

### Substrait logical round-trip test

```rust
#[tokio::test]
async fn substrait_logical_round_trip() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let ctx = SessionContext::new();

    let batch = RecordBatch::try_from_iter(vec![(
        "x",
        Arc::new(Int32Array::from(vec![42])) as ArrayRef,
    )])?;

    ctx.register_batch("t", batch)?;

    let plan = ctx.sql("SELECT x FROM t")
        .await?
        .into_optimized_plan()?;

    let substrait_plan =
        datafusion_substrait::logical_plan::producer::to_substrait_plan(
            &plan,
            &ctx.state(),
        )?;

    let decoded =
        datafusion_substrait::logical_plan::consumer::from_substrait_plan(
            &ctx.state(),
            &substrait_plan,
        )
        .await?;

    let decoded = ctx.state().optimize(&decoded)?;

    assert_eq!(format!("{:?}", plan), format!("{:?}", decoded));
    Ok(())
}
```

### Test matrix

```text
[ ] Expr round trip
[ ] LogicalPlan round trip
[ ] optimized LogicalPlan round trip
[ ] physical ExecutionPlan round trip
[ ] Substrait logical round trip
[ ] unsupported-plan failure path
[ ] custom logical extension codec
[ ] custom physical extension codec
[ ] UDF-containing plan
[ ] nested type plan
[ ] object-store table scan plan
[ ] plan deserialized under missing catalog/table/function fails safely
[ ] plan deserialized under different config is invalidated or reoptimized
```

## 36.21 Interoperability cookbook

### Same-version coordinator/worker

```text
Use:
  datafusion_proto logical plan or physical fragments

Require:
  exact DataFusion versions
  exact extension-codec set
  matching function registry
  matching catalog provider protocol
  matching runtime/source registration
```

### Rust ↔ Python / FFI

```text
Use:
  Substrait for broad interoperability
  native proto for DataFusion-specific plan handoff

Require:
  byte envelope
  catalog/function agreement
  explicit version metadata
```

The Substrait crate docs list passing plans over FFI boundaries, such as Python to Rust, as a potential use case. ([Docs.rs][2])

### Cross-engine

```text
Use:
  Substrait

Require:
  function mapping
  type mapping
  unsupported node fallback
  golden cross-engine result tests
```

### Durable cache

```text
Use:
  SQL + metadata + optional native proto plan cache

Require:
  invalidation on DataFusion/catalog/function/config changes
  fallback to SQL replanning
```

## 36.22 Limitations and stability risks

### Native proto risks

```text
not guaranteed compatible across DataFusion versions
custom extensions require codecs
physical plans embed execution-specific choices
receiver context must provide required tables/functions/object stores
serialized plans may expose source paths or internal metadata
```

### Substrait risks

```text
incomplete coverage of DataFusion plans and expressions
function mapping gaps
type mapping gaps
engine-specific semantics
extension URI/version management
semantic drift between producers/consumers
```

### Operational risks

```text
deserializing untrusted plans
running stale cached plans after catalog changes
using physical plans after runtime config changes
missing UDF/table provider implementations on receiver
plan cache poisoning
resource exhaustion from valid but expensive plan
```

Agent rule:

```text
Serialization is an optimization/interoperability mechanism, not a substitute for:
  SQL validation
  catalog governance
  authorization
  resource limits
  query baselines
  versioning
```

---

## 36.23 Deployment advisory

```text
Distributed DataFusion:
  use native proto inside one versioned control plane.
  exchange logical plans when workers should choose physical plans.
  exchange physical plans/fragments when coordinator owns scheduling.

Cross-engine:
  use Substrait.
  keep a function/type extension manifest.
  add cross-engine result tests.

Plan cache:
  store SQL fallback.
  invalidate aggressively.
  include DataFusion/version/config/catalog/function hashes.

Security:
  deserialize only from trusted sources or validate after deserialization.
  apply table/function/complexity policies before execution.
```

---

## 36.24 Anti-pattern inventory

* Treating `datafusion_proto` bytes as cross-version stable.
* Treating Substrait as full-fidelity DataFusion serialization.
* Executing deserialized plans without authorization validation.
* Storing only plan bytes without SQL/config/catalog metadata.
* Reusing physical plan bytes after changing runtime resources or object-store registry.
* Forgetting UDF/function registry compatibility.
* Forgetting custom logical/physical extension codecs.
* Ignoring unsupported-plan errors in Substrait conversion.
* Comparing only debug-string round trips and not execution results.
* Using serialized plans as a public API without version envelopes.
* Assuming receiver has the same catalog/table providers.
* Transporting secrets inside plan metadata or display strings.
* Long-lived plan caches without invalidation on DataFusion upgrade.

---

## 36.25 Agent checklist

```text
[ ] Choose format: datafusion_proto or datafusion_substrait.
[ ] Use datafusion_proto for same-version DataFusion fidelity.
[ ] Use datafusion_substrait for cross-language/cross-engine exchange.
[ ] Pin datafusion/datafusion-proto/datafusion-substrait versions.
[ ] Serialize LogicalPlan when receiver should plan physical execution.
[ ] Serialize ExecutionPlan only when physical decisions must be preserved.
[ ] Include version/config/catalog/function/codec metadata in envelope.
[ ] Register catalogs, object stores, and UDFs before deserialization.
[ ] Validate deserialized plans against authorization and complexity policy.
[ ] Use extension codecs for custom logical/physical nodes.
[ ] Round-trip test Expr, LogicalPlan, ExecutionPlan, and Substrait plans.
[ ] Store SQL fallback for cached plans.
[ ] Invalidate native proto plans on DataFusion upgrades.
[ ] Treat Substrait conversion gaps as expected compatibility constraints.
[ ] Never execute untrusted plan bytes without validation.
```

## 36.26 Proto decode contexts in DataFusion 54

DataFusion 54 restructured `datafusion-proto` deserialization around **task-context-driven decoding**. Three changes matter for any plan-transport layer:

### 1. `from_bytes_with_ctx` replaces `from_bytes_with_registry`

The `Serializeable` trait's registry-based decode entry point is gone. The required method is now:

```rust
pub trait Serializeable: Sized {
    fn to_bytes(&self) -> Result<Bytes>;

    // default: delegates to from_bytes_with_ctx(bytes, &TaskContext::default());
    // errors if the bytes reference any user-defined function
    fn from_bytes(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<Self> { ... }

    fn from_bytes_with_ctx(bytes: &[u8], ctx: &TaskContext) -> Result<Self>;
}
```

```rust
use datafusion_proto::bytes::Serializeable;

let expr = Expr::from_bytes_with_ctx(&bytes, ctx.task_ctx().as_ref())?;
```

The same migration applies to the lower-level helpers in `datafusion_proto::logical_plan::from_proto`: `parse_expr`, `parse_exprs`, and `parse_sorts` all take `&TaskContext` where they previously took a `&dyn FunctionRegistry`. A `TaskContext` bundles the function registries *and* runtime/session state, which is what UDF and (new in 54) higher-order-function resolution needs during decode. Callers that only have a `SessionContext` get one via `ctx.task_ctx()`.

### 2. `PhysicalPlanDecodeContext<'_>` for physical decoding

Physical-plan deserialization threads a single decode context instead of separate task-context/codec/registry parameters:

```rust
use datafusion_proto::physical_plan::{
    DefaultPhysicalProtoConverter, PhysicalPlanDecodeContext,
    PhysicalProtoConverterExtension,
};

let codec = MyPhysicalExtensionCodec::default();
let converter = DefaultPhysicalProtoConverter {};
let decode_ctx = PhysicalPlanDecodeContext::new(task_ctx, &codec);
let plan = converter.proto_to_execution_plan(&proto_node, &decode_ctx)?;
```

`PhysicalPlanDecodeContext` exposes `task_ctx()` and `codec()` accessors and internally carries the shared scalar-subquery results container so decoded `ScalarSubqueryExec` / `ScalarSubqueryExpr` nodes re-link correctly. The `PhysicalProtoConverterExtension` trait (with `DefaultPhysicalProtoConverter`) is the hook for overriding how specific physical nodes/exprs decode — custom implementations receive the decode context on every recursive call (e.g. `proto_to_physical_expr(expr, input_schema, ctx)`).

### 3. New node kinds your transport must handle

Plans produced by 54 can contain nodes that 53-era codecs never saw:

* `ScalarSubqueryExec` / `ScalarSubqueryExpr` — physical uncorrelated scalar subqueries (§20.27).
* Higher-order function expressions with lambdas — `Expr::HigherOrderFunction` / `Expr::Lambda` / `Expr::LambdaVariable` (§24.23) on the logical side.
* Field-aware casts — `Cast` carries a full `FieldRef` (logical field name: `field`; physical: `target_field`), so extension-type metadata rides through serialization.

A custom `PhysicalExtensionCodec`/proto converter written against 53 will fail (or silently drop metadata) on these — round-trip test every plan shape you transport after upgrading, and remember the native proto format remains **not cross-version stable** (§36.14).

Agent rules:

```text
Decode with from_bytes_with_ctx + the real TaskContext whenever UDFs may appear.
Plain from_bytes is only safe for built-in-function expressions.
Thread PhysicalPlanDecodeContext through custom converter extensions; do not cache raw registries.
Round-trip test scalar-subquery, lambda, and metadata-cast plan shapes explicitly.
```

# DataFusion Advanced — 37) Distributed and ecosystem integrations

## 37.0 Scope boundary

```text
Core DataFusion:
  Rust library / embeddable query engine
  in-process execution
  multithreaded, vectorized, Arrow-native
  SQL + DataFrame APIs
  deep extension surface:
    TableProvider
    UDF/UDAF/UDWF/UDTF
    logical/physical operators
    optimizer rules
    SQL planner extensions

Ecosystem integrations:
  Ballista      -> distributed DataFusion execution
  Python        -> Python bindings over Rust DataFusion
  Java          -> JVM bindings over native Rust DataFusion
  Comet         -> Spark accelerator using DataFusion execution
```

The official DataFusion landing page distinguishes the **core DataFusion project** from related subprojects: Python provides Python SQL/DataFrame bindings, Java provides Java SQL/DataFrame bindings, Comet accelerates Apache Spark, and Ballista is a distributed processing extension. Core DataFusion itself is documented as a Rust/Arrow query engine for building custom data systems. ([Apache DataFusion][1])

---

## 37.1 Core DataFusion vs subprojects

| Need                                                    | Use                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| embeddable Rust query engine                            | core `datafusion` crate                                 |
| custom database/query service in Rust                   | core DataFusion                                         |
| custom source, catalog, UDF, optimizer, execution node  | core DataFusion                                         |
| Python SQL/DataFrame over local files/in-memory/PyArrow | DataFusion Python                                       |
| Java SQL/DataFrame over native DataFusion               | DataFusion Java                                         |
| distributed DataFusion-style execution cluster          | Ballista                                                |
| accelerate existing Spark jobs without rewriting them   | Comet                                                   |
| preserve Spark API/session/catalog/job semantics        | Comet, not core DataFusion                              |
| cross-language plan/data exchange                       | Python/Java bindings, Substrait, Arrow C Data Interface |
| production Spark workload compatibility                 | Spark + Comet fallback model                            |
| production Rust single-node/embedded engine             | core DataFusion                                         |

Core DataFusion is an **in-process** library that uses threads for parallel query execution, while Ballista is the distributed compute platform built on top of DataFusion. This distinction matters: core DataFusion is not itself a cluster scheduler. ([Apache DataFusion][2])

---

## 37.2 Integration selection matrix

| Workload / product                     | Recommended path                                                       | Reason                                     |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Rust SaaS analytics API                | core DataFusion                                                        | maximum extension/control                  |
| Rust lakehouse query engine            | core DataFusion + custom catalogs/providers                            | source/catalog governance                  |
| Python notebook / scripting            | DataFusion Python                                                      | Python-native ergonomics                   |
| Python pipeline needing Rust-speed SQL | DataFusion Python                                                      | SQL/DataFrame with PyArrow interop         |
| JVM service needing embedded SQL       | DataFusion Java                                                        | JVM binding to native Rust engine          |
| existing Spark ETL/BI estate           | Comet                                                                  | no Spark job rewrites                      |
| Spark + Iceberg/Parquet acceleration   | Comet                                                                  | native acceleration path where supported   |
| distributed query engine from scratch  | Ballista or custom DataFusion-based system                             | distributed scheduler/executor model       |
| need exact Spark semantics/fallback    | Comet                                                                  | Spark integration and fallback             |
| need arbitrary Rust extension nodes    | core DataFusion first; Ballista only if distributed lifecycle required | distributed codecs/planners add complexity |

Agent rule:

```text
If the user wants to build a custom engine:
  start with core DataFusion.

If the user wants Python ergonomics:
  use DataFusion Python.

If the user wants JVM embedding:
  use DataFusion Java, but account for early-development status.

If the user wants Spark acceleration:
  use Comet.

If the user wants distributed DataFusion execution:
  use Ballista, or build a DataFusion-based distributed system with explicit scheduler/executor design.
```

---

# 37.3 Ballista distributed execution

## 37.3.1 What Ballista is

```text
Ballista:
  distributed query execution engine
  built on DataFusion + Arrow
  scheduler / executor architecture
  distributed SQL / DataFrame execution
  Arrow-native shuffle / IPC
  gRPC / protobuf / Arrow Flight SQL-oriented interfaces
```

Ballista’s architecture docs state that its primary purpose is to provide a distributed SQL query engine in Rust using the Apache Arrow memory model. The docs also state that Ballista provides a DataFrame API in Rust and Python, uses Arrow during execution, uses Arrow IPC for shuffle files and executor exchange, and exposes scheduler/executor APIs based on open standards such as protocol buffers, gRPC, Arrow IPC, and Arrow Flight SQL. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

## 37.3.2 Architecture

```text
Client
  → submits logical/physical query

Scheduler
  → receives query
  → creates distributed execution graph
  → schedules stages/tasks
  → coordinates executors

Executors
  → execute partitions/tasks
  → read data
  → shuffle intermediate data
  → return final results

Shuffle
  → Arrow IPC / disk shuffle / exchange between executors
```

Ballista’s docs explicitly describe scheduler, executor, client, distributed scheduling, and shuffle as architecture components. The same docs emphasize that Ballista users often extend scheduler/executor processes with custom data formats, operators, expressions, SQL dialects, or DSLs. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

## 37.3.3 Minimal Rust migration shape

```rust
// Core DataFusion style
use datafusion::prelude::*;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let ctx = SessionContext::new();

    ctx.register_csv("example", "tests/data/example.csv", CsvReadOptions::new())
        .await?;

    let df = ctx
        .sql("SELECT a, MIN(b) FROM example WHERE a <= b GROUP BY a LIMIT 100")
        .await?;

    df.show().await?;
    Ok(())
}
```

```rust
// Ballista style
use ballista::prelude::*;
use datafusion::prelude::*;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> datafusion::error::Result<()> {
    let ctx = SessionContext::standalone().await?;

    ctx.register_csv("example", "tests/data/example.csv", CsvReadOptions::new())
        .await?;

    let df = ctx
        .sql("SELECT a, MIN(b) FROM example WHERE a <= b GROUP BY a LIMIT 100")
        .await?;

    df.show().await?;
    Ok(())
}
```

The Ballista crate docs show an existing DataFusion application using `SessionContext::new()` and then a distributed variant using `ballista::prelude::*` plus `SessionContext::standalone().await?`, while leaving registration, SQL, and display logic structurally similar. ([Docs.rs][4])

## 37.3.4 Cluster startup

```bash
cargo install --locked ballista-scheduler
cargo install --locked ballista-executor

RUST_LOG=info ballista-scheduler

RUST_LOG=info ballista-executor -c 4
```

The Ballista crate docs document installing `ballista-scheduler` and `ballista-executor`, starting the scheduler, and starting executors with a concurrency level; they also note default ports for scheduler and executor processes. ([Docs.rs][4])

## 37.3.5 Extension implications

```text
Core DataFusion extension:
  custom LogicalPlan::Extension
  custom ExecutionPlan
  custom TableProvider
  custom UDF
  custom optimizer rule

Ballista extension:
  all of the above
  plus:
    distributed serialization codecs
    distributed planner support
    scheduler/executor compatibility
    task/shuffle lifecycle compatibility
```

Ballista’s extension example states that extending Ballista with custom logical and physical operators requires codecs and planner logic so the new operation is supported through the distributed query lifecycle. ([Apache DataFusion][5])

## 37.3.6 Use Ballista when

```text
Use Ballista when:
  one process is insufficient
  query execution must scale across nodes
  distributed scheduling/execution is desired
  Arrow-native distributed execution is acceptable
  you can operate scheduler/executor services
  you can handle distributed shuffle and task lifecycle
```

## 37.3.7 Prefer core DataFusion when

```text
Prefer core DataFusion when:
  single-node execution is enough
  embedding simplicity matters
  extensions are still evolving
  deployment should avoid scheduler/executor operations
  data size fits node resources
  lower operational complexity is more valuable than cluster scale
```

---

# 37.4 DataFusion Python

## 37.4.1 What DataFusion Python is

```text
DataFusion Python:
  Python binding to Rust DataFusion
  SQL API
  DataFrame API
  CSV / Parquet / in-memory data support
  multithreaded Rust execution
  PyArrow / Pandas interoperability
  Python UDF / UDAF support
```

The Python docs describe DataFusion Python as a Python library binding to the Arrow in-memory query engine DataFusion. It supports SQL and DataFrame plan construction over in-memory data, Parquet, or CSV, runs in a multithreaded environment, and returns results to Python; it also supports UDFs and UDAFs. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

## 37.4.2 Installation and minimal use

```bash
pip install datafusion
```

The Python docs show installation with `pip install datafusion`. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

```python
import datafusion

ctx = datafusion.SessionContext()

df = ctx.read_parquet("yellow_tripdata_2021-01.parquet")

df = df.select(
    "trip_distance",
)

df.show()
```

The Python concepts docs state that `SessionContext` is the main interface for executing queries, creating DataFrames from data sources, registering data sources as SQL tables, and executing SQL. They also state that DataFrames are lazy and are only executed by actions such as `show()` or `collect()`. ([Apache DataFusion][7])

## 37.4.3 SQL pattern

```python
from datafusion import SessionContext

ctx = SessionContext()
ctx.register_parquet("taxi", "yellow_tripdata_2021-01.parquet")

df = ctx.sql("""
    SELECT passenger_count, COUNT(*) AS n
    FROM taxi
    WHERE passenger_count IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY passenger_count
    ORDER BY passenger_count
""")

result = df.to_pandas()
```

The Python repository example shows creating a `SessionContext`, registering a Parquet file as a table, executing SQL, and converting the result to Pandas. Its feature list includes SQL/DataFrame execution over CSV, Parquet, and JSON, query optimization, Python UDF execution from SQL, exchange with Pandas/PyArrow-compatible libraries, and Substrait plan serialization/deserialization. ([GitHub][8])

## 37.4.4 Python vs Rust core

| Concern                                | Python                                       | Rust core                            |
| -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| language ergonomics                    | Python notebooks/scripts                     | Rust systems/services                |
| extension depth                        | Python UDF/UDAF and Python-side catalog APIs | full Rust extension surface          |
| zero-copy                              | Arrow C Data Interface / PyArrow interop     | native Arrow arrays                  |
| performance-sensitive custom operators | limited by binding surface                   | full `ExecutionPlan`/`TableProvider` |
| deployment                             | Python packaging/environment                 | Rust binary/library                  |
| public API stability                   | Python package/version                       | Rust crate/version                   |
| agent use                              | quick experiments, notebooks, ETL scripts    | production engine internals          |

The Python docs state zero-copy between Python and the execution engine is achieved technically through the Arrow C Data Interface, while results can be obtained back in Python; this is a major difference from embedding DataFusion directly in a Rust service. ([Apache DataFusion][6])

## 37.4.5 Use Python when

```text
Use DataFusion Python when:
  user environment is Python
  query authoring is notebook/script oriented
  PyArrow/Pandas interchange matters
  DataFrame + SQL ergonomics matter more than Rust-level extension control
  UDFs/UDAFs in Python are sufficient
```

## 37.4.6 Prefer Rust core when

```text
Prefer core Rust when:
  implementing custom TableProvider / ExecutionPlan / optimizer rules
  resource governance is critical
  low-level memory/spill/runtime integration is needed
  running as high-throughput service
  minimizing Python packaging/runtime complexity
```

---

# 37.5 DataFusion Java

## 37.5.1 What DataFusion Java is

```text
DataFusion Java:
  Java/JVM binding to native Rust DataFusion
  SQL + DataFrame API surface
  results returned as Arrow batches
  Arrow C Data Interface boundary
  early-development API
```

The official Java docs describe DataFusion Java as Java bindings for Apache DataFusion where queries run in native Rust and results return to the JVM as Apache Arrow batches via the Arrow C Data Interface. The same page explicitly marks the project as early development and says the API will change. ([Apache DataFusion][9])

## 37.5.2 Installation status

```text
Official Java docs currently state:
  no published release yet
  build from source required
  JDK 17 or newer
  stable Rust toolchain
```

The Java installation page states that Apache DataFusion Java has not yet published a release, requires JDK 17 or newer plus stable Rust, and must currently be built from source; `make test` compiles the native Rust crate and then runs JUnit tests. ([Apache DataFusion][10])

```bash
git clone https://github.com/apache/datafusion-java.git
cd datafusion-java
make test
```

## 37.5.3 Minimal Java pattern

```java
import org.apache.arrow.memory.RootAllocator;
import org.apache.arrow.vector.ipc.ArrowReader;
import org.apache.datafusion.DataFrame;
import org.apache.datafusion.SessionContext;

try (var allocator = new RootAllocator();
     var ctx = new SessionContext()) {

    ctx.registerParquet("orders", "/path/to/orders.parquet");

    try (DataFrame df = ctx.sql(
            "SELECT o_orderpriority, COUNT(*) AS n " +
            "FROM orders GROUP BY o_orderpriority");
         ArrowReader reader = df.collect(allocator)) {

        while (reader.loadNextBatch()) {
            var batch = reader.getVectorSchemaRoot();
            // consume Arrow vectors
        }
    }
}
```

The Java docs’ quickstart uses `RootAllocator`, `SessionContext`, `registerParquet`, `ctx.sql`, `DataFrame.collect(allocator)`, and `ArrowReader` to load Arrow batches into the JVM. ([Apache DataFusion][9])

## 37.5.4 Java vs Rust core

| Concern              | Java binding                                               | Rust core                      |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| host language        | JVM                                                        | Rust                           |
| execution engine     | native Rust DataFusion                                     | native Rust DataFusion         |
| result transport     | Arrow batches via Arrow C Data Interface                   | Arrow `RecordBatch` directly   |
| API maturity         | early development; API will change                         | primary project                |
| installation         | currently build from source in official docs               | crates.io                      |
| extension depth      | Java-facing APIs emerging                                  | full Rust extension surface    |
| memory model         | JVM + Arrow allocator + native library                     | Rust ownership + Arrow buffers |
| UDF/provider support | Java docs include sections for scalar UDFs/table providers | full native support            |

The Java docs explicitly list user-guide sections for DataFrame/SQL, Parquet, logical plans via `datafusion-proto`, scalar UDFs, and Java table providers, but also say the project is early development and no release has been published in the official docs. ([Apache DataFusion][10])

## 37.5.5 Use Java when

```text
Use DataFusion Java when:
  JVM integration is product-critical
  Java service wants embedded SQL/DataFrame execution
  Arrow batches are acceptable JVM result format
  project can tolerate early-development API movement
  build-from-source native dependency is acceptable
```

## 37.5.6 Prefer Rust core when

```text
Prefer Rust core when:
  mature/stable DataFusion API matters
  deep extension is required
  native deployment is acceptable
  avoiding JNI/native-library packaging complexity is important
```

---

# 37.6 DataFusion Comet for Spark acceleration

## 37.6.1 What Comet is

```text
Comet:
  Spark accelerator
  built on DataFusion
  integrates into Spark workloads
  translates/executes supported Spark physical work natively
  aims for Spark-compatible behavior
  falls back to Spark for unsupported features
```

The Comet documentation describes Apache DataFusion Comet as a high-performance accelerator for Apache Spark built on DataFusion. It is designed to improve Spark workloads on commodity hardware without requiring code changes, accelerates Iceberg Parquet scans from Spark, and aims for Spark compatibility with fallback to Spark for unsupported features. ([Apache DataFusion][11])

## 37.6.2 Architecture position

```text
Spark application
  → Spark SQL / DataFrame plan
  → Spark physical plan
  → Comet extension
      ├─ identify supported operators/scans
      ├─ translate to DataFusion-native execution where possible
      └─ fall back to Spark where unsupported
  → Spark job semantics remain visible to user
```

Comet’s docs state that it aims for compatibility with supported Spark versions and that users should expect the same behavior with Comet turned on or off; unsupported features are detected and fall back to Spark. This is materially different from replacing Spark jobs with raw DataFusion SQL. ([Apache DataFusion][11])

## 37.6.3 Data-source support implications

```text
Comet scan paths:
  Parquet:
    native Comet scans when schema/data types supported

  Iceberg:
    accelerates Iceberg scans of Parquet files

  CSV:
    experimental native CSV scan support via spark.comet.scan.csv.v2.enabled
    or Spark CSV reader → Arrow conversion path

  JSON:
    no native JSON scan; optional Spark JSON reader → Arrow conversion path
```

The Comet data-source docs state that Parquet scans are performed natively when schema data types are supported, Iceberg Parquet scans are accelerated, native CSV scan support is experimental and gated by `spark.comet.scan.csv.v2.enabled`, and JSON does not have native scan support but can be converted from Spark JSON reader output into Arrow for native execution. ([Apache DataFusion][12])

## 37.6.4 Use Comet when

```text
Use Comet when:
  workloads already run on Spark
  Spark APIs/catalogs/deployment must remain
  no-code-change acceleration is desired
  Parquet/Iceberg-heavy workloads dominate
  fallback to Spark for unsupported operators is acceptable
  Spark compatibility matters more than Rust-level engine customization
```

## 37.6.5 Prefer core DataFusion when

```text
Prefer core DataFusion when:
  you are not already committed to Spark
  you are building a custom query engine/service
  full Rust extension control is needed
  you want to avoid Spark scheduler/runtime overhead
  you need direct DataFusion SQL/DataFrame semantics rather than Spark semantics
```

## 37.6.6 Comet behavior differences

| Dimension            | Comet                                   | Core DataFusion                    |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| user API             | Spark SQL/DataFrame                     | DataFusion SQL/DataFrame           |
| planner input        | Spark plan                              | DataFusion logical plan            |
| fallback             | Spark fallback for unsupported features | DataFusion error or alternate plan |
| compatibility target | Spark behavior                          | DataFusion behavior                |
| deployment           | Spark extension/plugin                  | Rust library/binary                |
| catalog semantics    | Spark catalogs/session                  | DataFusion catalogs/providers      |
| supported formats    | Spark/Comet integration-specific        | DataFusion file/source support     |
| extension model      | Spark + Comet internals                 | DataFusion Rust extension APIs     |

---

# 37.7 API and behavior differences across subprojects

## 37.7.1 SQL and DataFrame semantics

```text
Core Rust:
  DataFusion SQL + DataFrame semantics

Python:
  DataFusion SQL + DataFrame semantics exposed through Python API

Java:
  DataFusion SQL + DataFrame semantics exposed through JVM API

Ballista:
  DataFusion-like distributed SQL/DataFrame semantics plus distributed execution constraints

Comet:
  Spark SQL/DataFrame semantics and compatibility expectations
```

Core DataFusion’s docs describe SQL/DataFrame APIs, file-format support, extension points, object-store I/O, optimizer features, and Substrait support in the Rust project. Comet’s docs, by contrast, explicitly frame compatibility around Apache Spark behavior and fallback to Spark for unsupported features. ([Apache DataFusion][13])

## 37.7.2 Extension depth

| Extension type        |               Core Rust |                             Python |                              Java |                             Ballista |                         Comet |
| --------------------- | ----------------------: | ---------------------------------: | --------------------------------: | -----------------------------------: | ----------------------------: |
| scalar UDF            |               full Rust |                   Python-supported |                 emerging Java API |       distributed lifecycle required |          Spark/Comet-specific |
| aggregate UDF         |               full Rust |                   Python-supported |                          emerging |       distributed lifecycle required |          Spark/Comet-specific |
| custom TableProvider  |               full Rust | Python catalog/provider APIs exist | Java docs include table providers | distributed codecs/planners required | Spark data-source/plugin path |
| custom ExecutionPlan  |               full Rust |                    not primary API |                   not primary API |         codecs + distributed planner |               Comet internals |
| custom optimizer rule |               full Rust |                    not primary API |                   not primary API |       cluster compatibility required |               Comet internals |
| custom SQL syntax     | full Rust planner hooks |                    not primary API |                   not primary API | distributed query lifecycle required |   Spark parser/planner domain |

Python’s feature list includes UDFs/UDAFs, SQL/DataFrames, optimizer use, Pandas/PyArrow exchange, and Substrait plan serialization; Java’s docs are still early but include sections for scalar UDFs and Java table providers; Ballista extension docs show custom logical/physical operators require codecs and planner logic across distributed execution. ([GitHub][8])

---

# 37.8 Operational complexity comparison

| System            | Process model                                               | Operational burden              |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| core DataFusion   | embedded in one process                                     | lowest                          |
| DataFusion Python | Python process + Rust native library                        | low/medium                      |
| DataFusion Java   | JVM + native Rust library                                   | medium                          |
| Ballista          | scheduler + executors + shuffle + clients                   | high                            |
| Comet             | Spark cluster + Comet native components + fallback behavior | high, but fits Spark operations |

Ballista introduces scheduler/executor processes and distributed shuffle. Comet integrates with Spark deployments and targets Spark compatibility/fallback. Python and Java bindings add host-language packaging and FFI/native-library boundaries but do not by themselves imply a cluster scheduler. ([Docs.rs][4])

---

# 37.9 Compatibility and versioning risks

```text
Core DataFusion:
  Rust API / SQL semantics / crate features / Arrow version coupling

Python:
  Python package version
  bundled DataFusion version
  PyArrow/Pandas compatibility
  Python UDF behavior and GIL boundaries

Java:
  early API changes
  native Rust library build/version
  Arrow Java allocator/vector compatibility
  generated datafusion-proto Java classes

Ballista:
  scheduler/executor/client version match
  distributed plan/protobuf compatibility
  custom extension codecs
  shuffle format compatibility

Comet:
  Spark version compatibility
  Comet version compatibility
  fallback behavior
  supported operator/data-source coverage
  Spark config interactions
```

The Java docs explicitly warn the API will change and state there are no official releases yet in the current official installation page. Comet’s install docs emphasize supported Spark-version compatibility, and its overview describes fallback for unsupported features. ([Apache DataFusion][9])

---

# 37.10 Agent deployment decision procedure

```text
1. Is the product already Spark?
   yes -> evaluate Comet.
   no  -> continue.

2. Is cluster/distributed DataFusion execution required?
   yes -> evaluate Ballista.
   no  -> continue.

3. Is the host language Python?
   yes -> DataFusion Python.
   no  -> continue.

4. Is the host language JVM/Java?
   yes -> DataFusion Java if early-development risk acceptable.
   no  -> continue.

5. Is deep engine customization required?
   yes -> core DataFusion Rust.
   no  -> choose the binding matching host language.

6. Is exact DataFusion semantics required?
   yes -> core Rust / Python / Java / Ballista.
   no, Spark semantics required -> Comet.
```

---

## Core DataFusion

[ ] choose crate version
[ ] define SessionConfig / RuntimeEnv
[ ] register catalogs/tables/UDFs
[ ] define object-store registry
[ ] implement extension points if needed
[ ] run SQL/DataFrame tests
[ ] benchmark with release/native build
```

## Ballista

[ ] choose matching Ballista/DataFusion versions

[ ] start executors
[ ] configure executor concurrency
[ ] validate data locality / object-store access on every executor
[ ] validate shuffle storage
[ ] validate custom extension codecs if any
[ ] run EXPLAIN / distributed query smoke tests
[ ] test executor failure/retry behavior if supported by deployment
```

## Python

```text
[ ] pin Python package version
[ ] verify bundled DataFusion behavior
[ ] verify PyArrow/Pandas compatibility
[ ] test UDF/UDAF behavior
[ ] test zero-copy pathways where performance matters
[ ] compare query results with Rust baseline if needed
```

## Java

```text
[ ] confirm official release/build status
[ ] build native library if required
[ ] set JDK version
[ ] set Rust toolchain
[ ] validate Arrow memory allocator lifecycle
[ ] validate native library packaging
[ ] test SQL/DataFrame/parquet/UDF/provider APIs used
```

## Comet

```text
[ ] verify Spark version compatibility
[ ] install matching Comet release/build
[ ] enable Comet Spark configs
[ ] validate fallback behavior
[ ] test query result parity with Comet on/off
[ ] test Parquet/Iceberg/CSV/JSON paths used by workload
[ ] benchmark representative Spark jobs
[ ] monitor native execution/fallback ratio
```

---

# 37.12 Anti-pattern inventory

* Using Ballista just because data is large when one node with Parquet pruning is enough.
* Using Comet for non-Spark workloads where core DataFusion would be simpler.
* Expecting Comet to expose core DataFusion Rust extension APIs directly to Spark users.
* Expecting DataFusion Python or Java to have every low-level Rust extension hook.
* Treating Java bindings as mature despite official docs marking early development.
* Treating Ballista custom operators as core DataFusion custom operators without distributed codecs/planners.
* Assuming Spark and DataFusion SQL behavior are identical.
* Forgetting that Comet fallback can hide unsupported native execution.
* Ignoring object-store credentials on Ballista executors.
* Benchmarking Comet without comparing Comet-on vs Comet-off results.
* Expecting DataFusion Python UDFs to behave like Rust UDFs in all performance/resource cases.
* Mixing subproject versions without checking compatibility.

---

# 37.13 Agent checklist

```text
[ ] Separate core Rust embedding from subprojects.
[ ] Use core DataFusion for embedded Rust/custom engine work.
[ ] Use Ballista only when distributed scheduler/executor execution is required.
[ ] Use Python bindings for Python SQL/DataFrame/PyArrow workflows.
[ ] Use Java bindings for JVM embedding, while accounting for early-development status.
[ ] Use Comet for existing Spark workloads that need acceleration without job rewrites.
[ ] For Ballista, validate scheduler/executor/shuffle/object-store deployment.
[ ] For Python, validate PyArrow/Pandas/UDF behavior.
[ ] For Java, validate native library build, JDK, Arrow C Data Interface behavior.
[ ] For Comet, validate Spark compatibility, native coverage, and fallback behavior.
[ ] Do not assume every core DataFusion extension exists identically in every subproject.
[ ] Pin versions and run result-parity tests across the chosen integration boundary.
```
